Algeria.d:
Algeria today has no diplomatic relations with its neighbour Morocco. It broke them off in August 2021, and one of the reasons it gave was a report that Morocco had been spying on Algerian phones.

That report came from the Pegasus Project, a group of journalists working with Amnesty International in 2021. Pegasus is spyware sold by NSO Group, an Israeli company, to governments; once on a phone it can read messages and listen in. The journalists reported that Morocco had picked more than 6,000 Algerian phones as possible targets, among them politicians and senior military officers. The same reporting, in Le Monde, said Morocco had also selected the phone of France's President Macron and 14 French ministers. Morocco denied using Pegasus. Being on a target list does not prove a phone was actually hacked, and no court has ruled on it.

The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt, is also recorded as present in Algeria, but the map has no documented case of it inside the state.

On the map Algeria sits in the pattern "Spyware and elections for hire", as a country where the tool was turned on its officials from outside. Its overall score is minimal.
Algeria.imp: For Algerians, the case is about who can listen to the people running their country. If a foreign government can read the messages of generals and politicians, it can learn their plans, their weaknesses and their private lives, and none of that shows up in public. The quarrel over it helped close the border relationship with Morocco, which affects trade and families on both sides. What to watch: whether Algerian officials' phones are named in any later spyware investigations, and whether Algeria itself buys similar tools.

Angola.d:
Angola's finance ministry, which decides where the state's money goes, is run by Vera Daves de Sousa, who has held the post since 8 October 2019. She is listed among the alumni of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme. The World Economic Forum is the organisation behind the Davos meetings; each year it picks people under about 40 for a five-year network of meetings and courses. Belonging to it is not wrongdoing, but it ties a finance minister into a private circle of business and political leaders.

Angola's oil runs through Sonangol, the state oil company. In January 2025 a Swiss federal court convicted Trafigura, one of the world's largest oil and metals traders, and its former chief operating officer Mike Wainwright over €4.3 million in bribes paid in 2009–11 to an Angolan official linked to a Sonangol subsidiary. Trafigura was fined $3.3 million and ordered to pay $145.6 million; Wainwright got 32 months, 20 of them suspended. Trafigura has appealed, so the ruling is not yet final.

Religion is the third thread. The Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, a church run from Brazil, built a large following in Angola. After Angolan pastors accused its Brazilian leaders of racial discrimination and of pressing pastors into vasectomies, the government in June 2020 ordered the church's board dissolved and removed Bishop Honorilton Gonçalves. The church had already been suspended for 60 days in 2013 after a deadly crush at a stadium event in Luanda.

Angola appears in four patterns: "Global firms buying governments" (where officials were paid), "Private forums where officials meet money", "Churches and movements placing members in the state" and "Exposure, purge and reversal", the last two because the government acted against a foreign-run church.
Angola.imp: For people in Angola, the oil money that pays for schools and hospitals passes through Sonangol, and a foreign court has found that a trader paid an official there. That kind of payment usually means a worse deal for the state, and it surfaced in Switzerland, not at home. The finance minister's place in a Davos network is public but its conversations are not. Watch the outcome of Trafigura's appeal, whether Angola itself prosecutes the official, and how the state treats foreign churches after the 2020 order.

Burkina Faso.d:
Burkina Faso is ruled by a military government under Captain Ibrahim Traoré, and its main foreign military partner is Russia. Traoré's government ordered French troops out in early 2023. On 24 January 2024 personnel from Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry's unit for Africa, arrived; an initial 100 were to grow to 300, and they set up their first African base at Loumbila, north-east of the capital Ouagadougou. Ghana's president had earlier alleged that a mine was handed to the Wagner Group, the Russian private military company, as payment; Burkina's mines minister denied it.

Before the coups, power ran through a different kind of network. Blaise Compaoré ruled from 1987 to 2014. Jeune Afrique, the Paris-based news magazine on Africa, reported in 2012 that he was a former grand master of the Grande Loge du Burkina, the country's Masonic grand lodge, and that he had been succeeded in that office by his own foreign minister, Djibrill Bassolé. A grand master leads a lodge system; the foreign minister speaks for the country abroad. In that arrangement the head of state and his top diplomat held the leadership of the same private brotherhood one after the other. Freemasonry is lawful, and the report describes membership, not a crime.

Burkina Faso belongs to two patterns: "French lodges and African presidencies", for the Compaoré and Bassolé cases, and "Russia's networks in Europe and Africa", as a target country where Russian forces now sit beside the government. The Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic movement, and the Order of Malta are also recorded as present.
Burkina Faso.imp: For people in Burkina Faso, the state's security now depends partly on a foreign force that answers to Moscow, and the terms of that deal, including any payment in mines, are not public. Earlier, the president and his foreign minister shared leadership of a lodge whose meetings were closed to outsiders. In both cases decisions about the country were tied to a circle citizens could not see into. Watch for published agreements with Russia, for who receives mining permits, and for whether lodge ties survive among the new military leaders.

Cameroon.d:
Paul Biya is president of Cameroon, and the one documented case on the map concerns him and money from the state oil company.

In December 1999 the French newspaper Le Monde reported that Biya had given tens of millions of francs between 1988 and 1992 to two bodies run by Raymond Bernard: the Sovereign Order of the Initiatic Temple (OSTI), a Templar-style esoteric order, and a related group called CIRCES. Biya gave 40 million francs personally, Le Monde said, and 11.2 million francs moved from the SNH, Cameroon's state oil company, into Bernard's personal account. The presidency called Bernard an "old friend" and would not comment on the payments. Bernard was questioned in a separate French inquiry into the Order of the Solar Temple, but he was not charged. OSTI is listed on the map as headquartered in Cameroon.

Other organisations are recorded as present: Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life; the Order of Malta; the Gülen movement; Glencore, the Swiss-based commodity trader that admitted paying bribes in Cameroon among other countries; and the Prigozhin network, which ran fake Facebook accounts aimed at Cameroon. French lodges and the Wagner Group are listed as likely but unconfirmed.

Cameroon belongs to two patterns, "Churches and movements placing members in the state" and "French lodges and African presidencies", both through the Biya–OSTI case.
Cameroon.imp: For people in Cameroon, the report shows how oil money that belongs to the public could be sent to a private esoteric order on the word of the president, with no explanation given. The same president is still in office, and the conditions score suggests few institutions able to ask questions. Watch for audits of the state oil company, and for whether foreign firms that admitted bribery here are ever pursued by Cameroon's own courts.

Central African Republic.d:
In the Central African Republic, Russian fighters guard the president and fight alongside the army. About 1,000 Wagner Group fighters have been in the country since 2018, after a Russia–CAR military agreement signed in August that year. Wagner is a Russian private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, which Russia used to place fighters and advisers with African governments. Their tasks included close protection for President Faustin-Archange Touadéra and fighting rebels with the national army, for example at Boyali in January 2021. Reporting links the deployment to gold, diamond and timber concessions, including a logging operation in Lobaye. Russia's defence ministry is moving these forces under its Africa Corps, and the CAR remains its largest African deployment, estimated at 1,500–2,000.

The presence reaches into the president's office. Valery Zakharov, a Russian, served as Touadéra's security adviser from 2018 and in 2021 publicly told rebels to hand over their leaders. Ukraine's security service said in 2018 he headed Wagner's security firm in the country. The US Treasury put him on its sanctions list, noting he was "linked to" Wagner and held a Central African passport issued in June 2018.

An older network sat at the top too. François Bozizé, president from 2003 to 2013, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting, and a 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier said he joined under the sponsorship of Congo's president Denis Sassou-Nguesso.

The CAR belongs to "Russia's networks in Europe and Africa" as a target country, "French lodges and African presidencies", and "Exposure, purge and reversal", through the US sanctions on Zakharov.
Central African Republic.imp: For people in the Central African Republic, the safety of the president and the fight against rebels both depend on a foreign force that is reported to be paid partly in the country's gold, diamonds and timber. Those deals are not published, and the people living near the mines and forests have no say in them. The president's own adviser was a foreign national under sanctions. Watch who holds mining and logging concessions, how many Russian troops remain under Africa Corps, and whether civilians can report abuses.

Chad.d:
Chad's documented cases centre on Idriss Déby, who ruled from 1990 until his death in 2021, and show two different networks meeting the presidency.

The first is Freemasonry. Déby was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting on African heads of state in Masonic lodges, and again in a 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier. No lodge is named, so the claim stays at the level of reporting.

The second runs the other way: the state shutting a movement out. The Gülen movement, also called Hizmet, is a Turkish Islamic movement that ran schools in many countries; Turkey calls it a terrorist group ("FETÖ") and blames it for the 2016 coup attempt. In November 2017 a statement on the Chadian presidency's website said Déby had agreed to hand Gülen-run schools to the Maarif Foundation, Turkey's state education body, by 18 December 2017, and to expel people linked to the movement. Families whose children attended those schools saw them change hands on the strength of a request from Ankara.

Chad belongs to four patterns: "Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement", as a country that closed schools and expelled members; "Churches and movements placing members in the state" and "Exposure, purge and reversal", for the same order; and "French lodges and African presidencies", for Déby. The Order of Malta is recorded as present, and the Grande Loge Nationale Française as likely.
Chad.imp: For people in Chad, these cases show the presidency making decisions in response to private and foreign ties that are not debated in public. A foreign government's request was enough to hand over schools and expel teachers. A president's lodge membership was reported abroad, never discussed at home. Watch whether foreign governments can still ask for people living in Chad to be removed, and how schools run by outside groups are treated.

Congo, Dem. Rep..d:
In the Democratic Republic of Congo, the army is fighting in the east, and a private American security operator is helping it. Erik Prince founded Blackwater, the US private military company. A UN group of experts described a proposed Prince mercenary deal for North Kivu province in 2023, and in February 2026 Reuters reported that Prince had sent men and drones to help Congo's army secure the eastern city of Uvira. A private contractor with foreign staff is now part of how the state fights its war.

The country's minerals have drawn foreign money into the state for years. Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trader and one of the largest mining firms in Congo, was found by US authorities to have paid $27.5 million to third parties between 2007 and 2018, intending part of it to bribe Congolese officials. In December 2022 Glencore agreed to pay Congo $180 million to settle the claims. A settlement is not a conviction in Congo, and the officials who were the targets are not named in this record.

The Prigozhin network, which ran fake social-media accounts tied to the Russian businessman Yevgeny Prigozhin, also targeted Congo. Opus Dei, the Gülen movement and the Wagner Group are listed as likely but unconfirmed.

Congo belongs to the pattern "Global firms buying governments", as a place where officials were paid, through both the Glencore and the Prince cases.
Congo, Dem. Rep..imp: For people in Congo, the riches under the ground bring foreign firms that have paid officials to get access, and settlements are handled between the company and the state rather than in open trials. The war in the east now involves a private contractor whose terms are not public. Watch who signs mining contracts, what the $180 million settlement is spent on, and what Prince's men are allowed to do and who they answer to.

Congo, Rep..d:
The Republic of Congo's president, Denis Sassou-Nguesso, is reported to be Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Congo-Brazzaville, the country's main Masonic body, which is linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Française, one of France's Masonic federations. A grand master leads the lodge system, and here that role and the presidency are reported to sit in the same hands. The report goes back to 2009 and was repeated in a 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier.

The pattern is older than him. Pascal Lissouba, president from 1992 to 1997, was reported by Jeune Afrique in 2012 to have been initiated at a lodge of the Grand Orient de France, France's largest Masonic body, in the French city of Besançon. Sassou-Nguesso's reach also crosses borders: a 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier said François Bozizé of the Central African Republic joined Freemasonry under Sassou-Nguesso's sponsorship. Freemasonry is lawful, and none of these reports describe a crime; they describe a private network that connects the people at the top.

Gunvor, a commodity trading firm, and the Order of Malta are also recorded as present.

Congo belongs to the pattern "French lodges and African presidencies", with two heads of state as lodge members, one of them its leader.
Congo, Rep..imp: For people in Congo, the president also heads a private brotherhood linked to France, and other leaders in the region have joined under his sponsorship. Ministers, judges and business people who belong owe loyalty within that circle as well as to the public, and its meetings are closed. Watch which senior officials are reported as lodge members, and whether ties to French lodges shape relations with France.

Cote d'Ivoire.d:
In Côte d'Ivoire the documented case is a 2012 snapshot of who sat in Masonic lodges at the top of the state. Jeune Afrique, the Paris-based news magazine on Africa, reported that year that Prime Minister Jeannot Ahoussou-Kouadio and Interior Minister Hamed Bakayoko were Freemasons. The interior minister runs the police and internal security. The magazine also said that the state prosecutor, Simplice Koffi Kouadio, had been received by the Grande Loge de Côte d'Ivoire, the country's grand lodge. It said President Alassane Ouattara was not officially known to be a member. Membership is lawful; the report shows a prime minister, the minister over police and the chief prosecutor sharing ties in one private body.

Other organisations are recorded as present: Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life; the Order of Malta; Glencore and Gunvor, two commodity traders (Glencore admitted bribery in Côte d'Ivoire among other states); and the Prigozhin network, whose fake Facebook accounts targeted the country. French lodges are listed as likely.

Côte d'Ivoire belongs to the pattern "French lodges and African presidencies", through ministers rather than the head of state.
Cote d'Ivoire.imp: For people in Côte d'Ivoire, when the chief prosecutor and the minister over the police share a lodge with the head of government, a citizen bringing a complaint cannot know what ties exist behind closed doors. Commodity traders that admitted paying officials here also shape the cocoa and oil trades that much of the economy depends on. Watch for disclosure of senior officials' memberships and for any domestic follow-up on admitted bribery.

Egypt.d:
In Egypt today, membership of the Muslim Brotherhood can send a person to prison. The Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt and headquartered there, was declared a terrorist organisation by the interim cabinet on 25 December 2013. Deputy Prime Minister Hossam Eissa announced it two days after a car bomb at the Mansoura police headquarters killed 14 people; another group, Ansar Bait al-Maqdis, claimed the bombing. Membership became punishable by up to five years, and a court had already banned the group and seized its assets in September 2013.

The ban came after the Brotherhood briefly held the presidency. Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure and candidate of its Freedom and Justice Party, won the June 2012 presidential election. The army removed him on 3 July 2013, and most of the Brotherhood's leadership was jailed in the months that followed. Morsi was accused of passing state secrets to Qatar while president; on 16 September 2017 the Court of Cassation upheld his life sentence for leading an illegal group but threw out a 15-year term for stealing secret documents, and upheld three co-defendants' death sentences. Qatar denied the accusations.

The oldest case shows the state on the other side of a secret network. In 1976 General Kamal Hassan Ali, head of Egypt's intelligence service, signed the charter of the Safari Club, a pact of intelligence chiefs from France, Saudi Arabia, Morocco, Iran and Egypt. In 1977 France flew Egyptian and Moroccan troops into Zaire to back Mobutu, and Saudi Arabia paid Egypt $75 million for old Soviet weapons sent to Somalia.

Egypt belongs to "Movements that sought the state itself", "The anticommunist web, 1945–1990" and "Exposure, purge and reversal".
Egypt.imp: For people in Egypt, the line between a political movement and a crime is drawn by the state: a party that won the presidency in 2012 is now a terrorist organisation, and belonging to it carries prison. That shapes what people can say and who they can meet. The Safari Club case shows the intelligence service itself making secret foreign commitments without public debate. Watch how the terrorism label is applied to new arrests, and whether trials are open.

Equatorial Guinea.d:
Teodoro Obiang has ruled Equatorial Guinea since 1979, and Russian soldiers now help protect him. In autumn 2024 Russia deployed up to 200 troops from Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry's unit that operates in Africa, to guard his presidency and to train elite units in the cities of Malabo and Bata, according to the security journal CTC Sentinel and other analyses. Obiang officially received the Africa Corps commander in Malabo in November 2025.

A president's personal guard decides who can get close to him and how he responds to a threat from inside his own forces. Placing foreign troops in that role ties the survival of the government to the foreign state that sends them.

Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trader, is also recorded as present; the UK's Serious Fraud Office found it paid bribes in Equatorial Guinea, among other countries, between 2012 and 2016. The Order of Malta is recorded as present.

Equatorial Guinea belongs to the pattern "Russia's networks in Europe and Africa", as a target country.
Equatorial Guinea.imp: For people in Equatorial Guinea, a ruler in power since 1979 is now protected in part by a foreign army, which makes peaceful change harder and gives Russia a stake in who governs. The country's oil has also drawn a trader that admitted paying officials. Neither arrangement is open to public scrutiny. Watch how many Russian troops stay, what Russia receives in return, and who controls oil contracts.

Ethiopia.d:
Ethiopia's prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, is a Pentecostal Christian who sometimes preaches. He converted after the 1998–2000 war with Eritrea and attends the Ethiopian Full Gospel Believers' Church. He became prime minister in 2018 and in 2019 formed the Prosperity Party, which governs today. Pentecostal churches are a fast-growing family of evangelical churches; the record shows a head of government who is also active in one, not any church directing the state.

Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, is also home to the African Union, the body that brings the continent's states together, and the AU's building is the subject of the country's other case. China built and paid for the roughly $200 million headquarters, opened in 2012, and Huawei, China's largest telecoms equipment maker, supplied most of its computer and network equipment. In January 2018 Le Monde, later confirmed by the Financial Times, reported that the AU's IT staff had found in 2017 that the building's data were being copied each night to servers in Shanghai, from 2012 to January 2017, and that microphones were hidden in walls and furniture. The AU replaced its servers and declined Chinese offers to set them up again. China's ambassador called the report "ridiculous and preposterous", Huawei said its equipment was not the source, and no public evidence of a backdoor has been shown.

The Tony Blair Institute and Family Watch International, a US Christian lobbying group, are recorded as present. Ethiopia belongs to "China's long arm abroad" and "Churches and movements placing members in the state".
Ethiopia.imp: For people in Ethiopia, the case of the AU building shows how a gift of infrastructure can come with the risk that someone else is listening, and the people affected may not find out for years. The prime minister's faith is open and lawful, but it matters to know whether church networks shape appointments or policy. Watch who builds and runs government computer systems, and how religious groups are treated in public life.

Gabon.d:
Gabon's president, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, came to power in an August 2023 coup and was elected in April 2025. He is described in reporting as a non-practising Freemason. In November 2023, Gabonreview reported, citing the newsletter Africa Intelligence, that the Grand Master of the Grand Orient de France, France's largest Masonic body, Guillaume Trichard, met Oligui in secret in Libreville and offered support to his transitional council. Trichard also met the council of the Grande Loge symbolique du Gabon.

That meeting continues a long tradition. Omar Bongo, initiated in 1953, was president from 1967 until his death in 2009. He founded two Masonic bodies, one tied to the Grand Orient de France and the Grand Lodge of Gabon tied to the Grande Loge Nationale Française (GLNF), and held the grand mastership until he died. In 2009 the GLNF's Grand Master installed his son Ali Bongo as Grand Master of both; Ali Bongo became president the same year. Ministers Paul Toungui and Séraphin Moundounga and National Security Council head Léon Paul Ngoulakia attended the installation, Jeune Afrique reported. The police were included too: Antoine Embinga, grand master of the Grande Loge symbolique, was head of the police until January 2012.

After the 2023 coup, the grand mastership, which had traditionally gone to the head of state, passed to Jacques Denis Tsanga, governor of Haut-Ogooué province; Oligui reportedly declined it.

Gabon is a central case in "French lodges and African presidencies", and belongs to "Lodges inside police forces and courts" through Embinga.
Gabon.imp: For people in Gabon, for more than 50 years the head of state and the head of the country's lodges were the same person, and the police chief led another lodge. Decisions about who rose in government could be made among lodge brothers, out of public view. The 2023 coup changed the president but French Masonic leaders still sought him out. Watch whether ministers, judges and police chiefs under the new government are drawn from lodges, and what French Masonic bodies ask in return for support.

Gambia's conditions score is 5.9 out of 10: the map judges that insiders have wide room inside the state (7.0) but that defences such as courts and press are middling (5.1). As a best guess, the most likely route in is the one seen in Senegal, where presidents court the leaders of large religious brotherhoods for support.
Gambia.imp: For people in Gambia, the map has nothing documented yet. Religious brotherhoods can bring real followings, and politicians may seek their backing in ways that are not written down. Watch whether religious leaders are given state help or posts, and whether that is done in public. If it happens openly, voters can weigh it; if it happens privately, they cannot.

Ghana.d:
In Ghana, ministers say openly that they are Freemasons, and Parliament asks. At his vetting on 22 January 2025, the hearing where Parliament questions a nominee before approving him, George Opare Addo was asked by Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin whether he was a Freemason. He said yes and named his lodge as "Amity". He was then confirmed as Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment in President Mahama's government. Afenyo-Markin had himself said in February 2024: "I am a Freemason and a Catholic."

The year before, in May 2024, the Grand Lodge of Ghana honoured the Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, king of the Asante people, for 25 years in Freemasonry. GhanaWeb reported that National Security Minister Albert Kan-Dapaah and Transport Minister Kweku Ofori Asiamah took part as members, and that Afenyo-Markin, then Majority Leader, had said publicly he was a Freemason. Former President John Kufuor has said he joined in 1967.

The cases show a lodge whose members include a traditional king, ministers from successive governments and a former president, and whose membership is disclosed rather than hidden. Membership is lawful, and none of these reports allege wrongdoing.

The Tony Blair Institute, a London non-profit that places advisers in governments, is recorded as present; the United Grand Lodge of England and the Atlas Network are listed as likely. Ghana is not tied to a pattern on the map.
Ghana.imp: For people in Ghana, the useful part is that the question gets asked in public: Parliament can ask a nominee about lodge membership and he answers. That lets voters judge for themselves. What stays private is what happens inside lodge meetings, where a national security minister, a king and opposition leaders sit together. Watch whether vetting continues to ask about memberships, and whether lodge ties line up with appointments to security and transport posts.

Guinea.d:
Guinea's two documented cases come from the years of President Alpha Condé and show the presidency in two roles: as patron of a private network, and as the hand that shut another one down.

In 2012 Jeune Afrique, the Paris-based news magazine on Africa, reported that Condé oversaw ("chapeaute") the Grande Loge de Guinée, the country's Masonic grand lodge. The report does not say he was its formal grand master, only that he stood over it. Freemasonry is lawful, and the report describes a link, not a crime.

The Gülen movement, also called Hizmet, is a Turkish Islamic movement that ran schools in many countries; Turkey calls it a terrorist group and blames it for the 2016 coup attempt there. By June 2017 Gülen-linked schools in Guinea had been taken over by the Maarif Foundation, Turkey's state education body, after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry. Pupils and teachers found their schools under the control of a foreign government's foundation.

Guinea belongs to four patterns: "Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement", "Churches and movements placing members in the state" and "Exposure, purge and reversal", all through the school transfer; and "French lodges and African presidencies", through Condé. The Tony Blair Institute and the Order of Malta are also recorded as present.
Guinea.imp: For people in Guinea, these cases show decisions about schools and about who sits near the president being shaped by ties that were never put to a public vote: a lodge the president oversaw, and a request from Turkey. Watch who now runs the transferred schools, whether new leaders keep links to the grand lodge, and whether foreign governments can ask Guinea to act against their critics.

Guinea-Bissau.d: Nothing is documented on the map for Guinea-Bissau yet; this is an estimate. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic lay order with diplomatic relations to many states. Guinea-Bissau's conditions score is high, 7.9 out of 10: the map judges that insiders have wide room inside the state (8.5) and that defences such as courts and press are weak (2.7). As a best guess, the most likely route in is through the armed forces and the people around them, since in a state with few checks the officers who hold force can bring outside interests in.
Guinea-Bissau.imp: For people in Guinea-Bissau, weak courts and press mean that private deals with officials would be hard to uncover. The map has no case yet, which reflects limited investigation. Watch who gains influence with military leaders, and what foreign partners receive in return for support. In a state where officers have often decided who governs, those ties matter more than any party programme.

Kenya.d:
Kenya's president, William Ruto, is an evangelical Christian who led a church choir of the Africa Inland Church and married in that church. In July 2025 he announced he would build a church in the grounds of State House, the president's official home, with his own money. The Daily Nation published designs for a building seating 8,000 at about $9 million. Nairobi's Catholic archbishop and the Atheists in Kenya Society objected that it breached the secular state.

Kenya has one of the most varied records in Africa on the map. Patrick Njoroge, a celibate "numerary" member of Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life, governed the Central Bank of Kenya, which sets interest rates and manages the currency, from June 2015 to June 2023.

Elections have been shaped from outside. Cambridge Analytica, a British political-data firm, ran Uhuru Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 campaigns; its managing director said on undercover Channel 4 footage in 2018 that it rebranded the party twice and wrote its manifesto. In 2022 Team Jorge, an Israeli hacking and disinformation outfit, showed undercover reporters it had access to the Telegram account of Dennis Itumbi, Ruto's digital strategist; Itumbi confirmed it was compromised.

Foreign governments have reached in too. Turkish intelligence took Selahaddin Gülen, Fethullah Gülen's nephew, from Kenya in 2021, and on 18 October 2024 Kenya returned four Turkish refugees to Turkey "at the request of the government of Türkiye". In 2013 a Kenyan court convicted two Iranians alleged to be members of Iran's Quds Force of plotting attacks. A day after the Adani Group's directors were charged with bribery in New York in November 2024, Ruto cancelled Adani's airport and power deals.

Kenya belongs to six patterns, including "Spyware and elections for hire" and "Turkey's long arm".
Kenya.imp: For people in Kenya, the record shows that the votes, the central bank, refugees' safety and big public contracts have all been touched by outside networks, often discovered by foreign journalists or courts rather than Kenyan ones. Voters did not know a foreign firm wrote a winning party's manifesto. Refugees found that protection could end at another government's request. Watch for who runs digital campaigns in the next election, how airport and power contracts are awarded, and whether the State House church goes ahead.

Lesotho.d: Nothing is documented on the map for Lesotho yet; this is an estimate. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic lay order with diplomatic relations to many states. Lesotho's conditions score is 6.5 out of 10: the map judges that insiders have wide room inside the state (7.0) and that defences such as courts and press are on the weak side (3.9). As a best guess, the most likely route in is through business interests in South Africa, which surrounds Lesotho, seeking contracts or access through officials.
Lesotho.imp: For people in Lesotho, the map has nothing documented yet, and its checks on officials are rated as weak. A small state closely tied to a larger neighbour can be leaned on through trade and contracts. Watch how large contracts, including water and mining deals, are awarded, and whether parliament and the public can see the terms before they are signed.

Liberia.d:
Liberia is the place on the map where a Masonic lodge was most openly part of the ruling party, and where a coup turned on it. That history is the background to how the state works today, though no current case is recorded.

William Tolbert was vice-president from 1952 to 1971 and president from 1971 to 1980, and he was Grand Master of the Masonic Order of Liberia. Histories of the order say lodge membership was widely seen as a requirement for leadership in the True Whig Party, which ran the country, and that by the 1970s most high officials were Masons. On 12 April 1980 Samuel Doe seized power in a coup. Tolbert was killed, and much of the Masonic leadership was killed with him.

Doe then banned Freemasonry. He later lifted the ban; the order was formally reinstated in 1988, and Doe himself was initiated in 1989. Within a decade, the man who had overthrown the lodge's leaders had joined it.

The National Endowment for Democracy, a US government-funded foundation, and the Tony Blair Institute are recorded as present. Liberia belongs to "French lodges and African presidencies", for Tolbert and Doe, and "Exposure, purge and reversal", for the ban and its reversal.
Liberia.imp: For people in Liberia, the history shows how a private brotherhood can become the path to power, so that those outside it cannot rise, and how violently that can end. Doe's turn from banning the order to joining it shows that the network outlasted the purge. Watch whether lodge membership still predicts who gets senior posts, and whether officials disclose it.

Libya.d:
Libya is split between a government in Tripoli and the forces of Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army controls the east. Russia's Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry's unit in Africa, began replacing the Wagner Group there in spring 2024, and Russia uses eastern Libyan bases as logistics hubs.

Wagner, a Russian private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, came in to fight for Haftar. A May 2020 UN report counted 800 to 1,200 Wagner fighters with him, including sniper teams, and Syrians recruited by Wagner flown in on at least 33 flights. In July 2020 the US sanctioned Wagner people and firms over landmines planted around Tripoli, and in December 2020 a Pentagon report said the UAE was Wagner's main funder in Libya.

An American also tried to arm Haftar. Erik Prince founded Blackwater, the US private military company. A UN Panel of Experts found in February 2021 that he broke the UN arms embargo on Libya in a 2019 operation to supply aircraft and personnel to Haftar's forces; the planned $80 million deal collapsed in June 2019. Prince denies wrongdoing.

On the Tripoli side, the Justice and Construction Party, founded in 2012 as the political arm of the Libyan Muslim Brotherhood, won 17 party-list seats that year and had five ministers until 2014. Its member Khalid al-Mishri chaired the High Council of State, the Tripoli government's upper consultative body, from 2018 to 2023.

Libya belongs to "Russia's networks", "Global firms buying governments", "Movements that sought the state itself" and "Exposure, purge and reversal".
Libya.imp: For people in Libya, the armed forces on one side have been staffed and supplied by foreign private armies, paid for by other governments, while a movement on the other side held a top seat in Tripoli. Libyans have had little say over any of it, and the UN found the arms embargo broken. Watch how many Russian troops stay in the east, who pays for them, and whether the arms embargo is enforced.

Madagascar.d:
Madagascar's documented case is about its 2018 presidential election, and about Russian political strategists who worked inside it.

The Russian investigative outlet Proekt and the BBC reported in 2019 that 15 to 20 Russian political strategists tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the businessman behind the Wagner Group, worked in the race and dealt with as many as eight candidates, including the winner, Andry Rajoelina. Candidate André Mailhol said they gave him €5,000 in cash; former prime minister Omer Beriziky said he was promised $2 million. Rajoelina denied being Russia's candidate, and the BBC found no evidence that he took Russian money. Prigozhin's representatives denied any link.

The approach was to back several candidates at once, so that whoever won would owe something. In October 2019 Facebook also removed fake accounts tied to Prigozhin that meddled in Madagascar's election, along with those of other African states.

The Wagner Group and the Order of Malta are recorded as present, and French Masonic bodies as likely. Madagascar belongs to "Russia's networks in Europe and Africa", as a target country, and "Spyware and elections for hire".
Madagascar.imp: For people in Madagascar, the report means voters may have been choosing among candidates some of whom had taken help or cash from foreign strategists, without being told. The winner denied it and no evidence of his taking money was found, but the full list of who accepted what is unknown. Watch campaign funding in future elections, and whether candidates are required to disclose foreign advisers.

Malawi.d: Nothing is documented on the map for Malawi yet, and no organisation is recorded as present; this write-up is an estimate. Malawi has one of the lower conditions scores in Africa, 4.8 out of 10: the map judges that insiders have limited room inside the state (4.0) and that defences such as courts and press are middling (4.4). As a best guess, the most likely route in is through foreign firms or donors seeking contracts or policy influence through a handful of officials.
Malawi.imp: For people in Malawi, the map has nothing documented yet and rates the conditions as less open than most of its neighbours. Watch how large contracts and donor-funded programmes are awarded, and who in government decides them. Keeping those decisions public is what keeps the score low, and the record clean.

Mali.d:
Mali is ruled by a military government, and its main foreign military partner is Russia. Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry's unit that took over most of the Wagner Group's African operations after Prigozhin's death in 2023, deployed about 1,000 troops in December 2024. On 6 June 2025 Wagner announced it was leaving Mali, and Africa Corps became the only Russian force there, with about 2,000 Russian troops remaining. Several Wagner commanders moved across to it. Human Rights Watch and Le Monde have reported killings of civilians by Malian soldiers and Africa Corps members in 2025–26.

The US Treasury has named the officers who brought Wagner in. On 24 July 2023 it sanctioned the defence minister, Colonel Sadio Camara, saying he planned and organised Wagner's deployment and travelled to Russia several times in 2021 to finalise it. It also sanctioned the air force chief of staff, Colonel Alou Boi Diarra, who it said promoted Wagner inside the armed forces and worked with Wagner's Mali head Ivan Maslov, and his deputy, Lieutenant Colonel Adama Bagayoko. A month earlier Mali's government had asked UN peacekeepers to leave.

Before the coups, power ran through a different circle. Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that President Amadou Toumani Touré, removed in the coup of 21 March 2012, oversaw the Grande Loge du Mali, the country's grand lodge.

Mali belongs to "Russia's networks in Europe and Africa", "French lodges and African presidencies" and "Exposure, purge and reversal".
Mali.imp: For people in Mali, the country's security rests on a foreign force answering to Moscow, brought in by named officers in the defence ministry, and civilians have been reported killed in its operations. The terms of the deal are not public, and UN peacekeepers who could report on abuses have gone. Watch what Russia receives in return, how civilian deaths are investigated, and who in the military government keeps the Russian relationship going.

Mauritania's conditions score is 6.6 out of 10: insiders have fair room inside the state (6.5) and defences such as courts and press are weak (3.2). As a best guess, the most likely route in is through Islamist political parties or through foreign governments pressing the state to act against movements they oppose.
Mauritania.imp: For people in Mauritania, the map has no documented case yet, but several organisations active elsewhere in the region are present. With weak checks on officials, their influence would be hard to see. Watch how Islamist parties fare in government, and whether foreign governments ask Mauritania to close schools or hand over people, as happened in neighbouring states.

Mauritius.d: Nothing is documented on the map for Mauritius yet; this write-up is an estimate. Two organisations are recorded as present: the Grand Orient de France, France's largest Masonic body, and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic lay order with diplomatic relations. The Grande Loge Nationale Française and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, India's Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, are listed as likely. Mauritius has one of the lower conditions scores, 4.7 out of 10: insiders have moderate room inside the state (5.0) and defences are relatively strong (5.6). As a best guess, the most likely route in is through lodge ties to France or through organisations linked to India's large diaspora.
Mauritius.imp: For people in Mauritius, the map has nothing documented yet, and the country's checks are rated stronger than most in Africa. Its ties to France and India bring in networks from both. Watch whether senior officials disclose lodge or movement memberships, and whether those ties shape appointments, especially in the police, the courts and the offshore finance sector.

Morocco.d:
Morocco's Minister of Habous and Islamic Affairs, the minister who runs the country's mosques and religious endowments, is Ahmed Toufiq, who has held the post since November 2002 under five prime ministers. He is a historian who has said that a chance meeting with the sheikh of the Boutchichiya, Morocco's largest Sufi order and headquartered there, set him on the Sufi path. In August 2025 a leaked letter from Toufiq warned the order about "abuses" and "appetites" during a dispute over its leadership. The minister over all religious life also stands in a personal relationship to one order.

Politics has also run through Islamist movements. The Justice and Development Party (PJD), historically linked to the Muslim Brotherhood but never an official branch, won 107 seats in November 2011. Its leader Abdelilah Benkirane became head of government, followed by Saadeddine Othmani until 2021. In the September 2021 election it lost 113 seats.

Morocco has also acted against movements on foreign request: in 2017 the government ordered Gülen-linked schools shut, as Tunisia and Sierra Leone were reported to have done.

Two cases show the Moroccan state running secret networks abroad. In 1976 General Ahmed Dlimi, head of foreign intelligence, signed the Safari Club charter with the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Iran; in 1977 France airlifted Moroccan troops into Zaire to defend Mobutu. And the 2021 Pegasus Project reported that Morocco selected more than 6,000 Algerian phones and those of France's president and ministers as spyware targets; Morocco denied it.

Morocco belongs to five patterns, including "Movements that sought the state itself" and "The anticommunist web".
Morocco.imp: For people in Morocco, the official in charge of their mosques for over twenty years has a personal bond with one Sufi order, which matters when that order's leadership is disputed. The state has also used secret pacts abroad and was reported to target foreign phones. Watch how the Boutchichiya leadership dispute is settled and the ministry's role in it, and whether surveillance tools are used on people inside Morocco.

Mozambique.d:
Mozambique is still paying for a hidden debt. About $2 billion in loans, arranged by Credit Suisse and other banks, went to three Mozambican state companies set up for fishing and maritime security, and part of the debt was hidden from the IMF. The equipment came from Privinvest, an Emirati-Lebanese shipbuilding group. The scandal became known as the "tuna bonds".

The finance minister at the centre was Manuel Chang. In August 2024 a jury in Brooklyn, New York, convicted him of wire-fraud and money-laundering conspiracy; prosecutors said Privinvest paid him $7 million. He was sentenced to eight and a half years on 17 January 2025. Credit Suisse paid about $475 million in 2021, and London's High Court let Mozambique recover over $825 million from the estate of Privinvest's owner. The finance ministry is the office that signs the state's borrowing, so the minister who signed was paid by the company that profited.

The second case is online. On 30 October 2019 Facebook removed three networks of almost 200 fake and compromised accounts, with over a million followers, traced to entities tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the Russian businessman behind the Wagner Group. They targeted eight African countries and meddled in Mozambique's October 2019 election. Stanford Internet Observatory found the operators worked with local people.

Mozambique belongs to "Global firms buying governments", "Russia's networks in Europe and Africa" and "Spyware and elections for hire".
Mozambique.imp: For people in Mozambique, the hidden loans meant a debt taken out in their name without parliament or the IMF knowing, while the finance minister was paid. The cost fell on public budgets. The conviction came in a US court, not a Mozambican one. Watch how recovered money is used, whether other officials are tried at home, and who runs online campaigns during elections.

Namibia.d: Nothing is documented on the map for Namibia yet; this is an estimate. Two organisations are recorded as present: the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic lay order with diplomatic relations, and the Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Leadership School, a party school in Tanzania built with Chinese Communist Party money that trains cadres of Namibia's ruling SWAPO and five other ruling parties. The Afrikaner Broederbond, the secret Afrikaner society that ran apartheid South Africa, is listed as likely. Namibia's conditions score is 5.7 out of 10. As a best guess, the most likely route in is through party training abroad shaping the ruling party's officials.
Namibia.imp: For people in Namibia, the ruling party's officials are being trained at a school funded and taught by China's Communist Party, which can shape how they think about running the state. The map has no case yet. Watch who attends, what is taught, and whether it shows up in policy.

Niger.d:
Niger is ruled by a junta that took power in a July 2023 coup and then ended military cooperation with the United States and France. Russian troops now sit at the country's main air base. Dozens of Africa Corps troops, from the Russian defence ministry's unit for Africa, arrived in the capital Niamey in April 2024 and were stationed at Air Base 101 before US forces had left it. Estimates for 2025 put them at 200 to 300, mostly in intelligence, training and surveillance. Wikipedia's article says they took part in fighting during a January 2026 attack on Niamey airport.

Two earlier cases show other networks. Mamadou Tandja, president from 1999 to 2010, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting on African heads of state in Masonic lodges; no lodge was named. And by June 2017 schools run by the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic movement that Turkey calls a terrorist group, had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry, as also happened in Guinea, Sudan and Somalia.

The Archimedes Group, an Israeli political consulting firm removed from Facebook in 2019 for election meddling in Africa, is also recorded as present.

Niger belongs to "Russia's networks in Europe and Africa", "Turkey's long arm", "Churches and movements placing members in the state", "French lodges and African presidencies" and "Exposure, purge and reversal".
Niger.imp: For people in Niger, a foreign force now handles intelligence and surveillance for a government that came to power by force. Intelligence work is the hardest to see from outside, and it can be turned on the country's own people. Watch what Russian troops do beyond the air base, what agreement governs them, and whether foreign governments can still ask Niger to close schools or act against their critics.

Nigeria.d:
Nigeria's constitution bars members of secret societies from elected office. Under the 1999 Constitution, sections 66, 107, 137 and 182 disqualify them from the National Assembly, the state assemblies, the presidency and governorships, and section 38(4) bars anyone from belonging to one. The Code of Conduct for Public Officers says an official shall not belong to any society "incompatible with the functions or dignity of his office". Commentators name the Ogboni fraternities, along with Freemasons and AMORC, the Rosicrucian order, among the societies at issue. The rule was tested at once: after the February 1999 election, runner-up Olu Falae petitioned that Olusegun Obasanjo was an Ogboni member and so disqualified. The tribunal dismissed the petition.

Churches are present at the top in the open. Yemi Osinbajo, vice-president from 2015 to 2023 and twice acting president in 2017, is a senior pastor of the Redeemed Christian Church of God, a Nigerian Pentecostal church with branches abroad and headquartered in Nigeria.

Outside firms have worked on elections. Leaked emails reported in 2023 showed Cambridge Analytica worked with Israel's Team Jorge in 2015 to re-elect Goodluck Jonathan by discrediting Muhammadu Buhari, who won. In May 2019 Facebook removed networks of the Israeli Archimedes Group aimed at African elections including Nigeria's.

Money flowed in too. The UK's Serious Fraud Office found Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trader, paid more than $28 million in bribes in Nigeria and four other African states between 2012 and 2016; Glencore pleaded guilty in 2022. And Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala moved from a World Bank managing director's post to finance minister in 2011; she now heads the World Trade Organization.

Nigeria belongs to five patterns, including "Spyware and elections for hire" and "Global firms buying governments".
Nigeria.imp: For people in Nigeria, the constitution promises that secret-society members cannot hold elected office, but proving membership is hard, and the one major test failed in court. Meanwhile the clearer influences have come from outside: foreign firms working on campaigns without voters knowing, and a commodity trader admitting bribes in the oil trade. Watch how the secret-society rule is used in election petitions, who funds digital campaigns, and whether officials paid by Glencore are named and tried at home.

Rwanda.d:
Inside Rwanda's government, advisers from a foreign non-profit help run the units that plan and track the state's work. The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, a London-based organisation set up by the former British prime minister, places advisers inside governments; it reports work with more than 45 governments and had about 1,000 staff in 2026. In Rwanda it has supported a Strategy and Policy Unit and a Government Action Coordination Unit, and worked on Imihigo, the system of performance contracts that officials sign and are judged against. In Kenya it supported a Presidential Delivery Unit.

The Institute's largest donor is the foundation of Larry Ellison, the American technology billionaire, which gave over £52 million in 2023, according to The Guardian. The arrangement is public and lawful. The question it raises is who shapes a government's priorities when its central planning offices are supported by an outside organisation funded by a private donor.

Opus Dei and NSO Group, the Israeli maker of Pegasus spyware, are also recorded as present; the World Economic Forum is listed as likely.

Rwanda belongs to the pattern "Consultants and lobbyists inside the ministries".
Rwanda.imp: For people in Rwanda, decisions about which goals the government sets and how officials are judged are made partly with advisers paid by a foreign organisation. Those advisers are not elected, and the funders behind them are not Rwandan. Watch which policies these units push, whether the advisers' work is published, and how the Institute's donors' business interests line up with them.

Sao Tome and Principe.d: Nothing is documented on the map for São Tomé and Príncipe yet; this is an estimate. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic lay order with diplomatic relations to many states. The country has one of the lowest conditions scores on the map, 4.1 out of 10: the map judges that insiders have little room inside the state (3.0), though its defences such as courts and press are middling (4.8). As a best guess, the most likely route in for a small island state is through foreign investors or partner governments dealing with a few officials, for example over oil or fishing rights.
Sao Tome and Principe.imp: For people in São Tomé and Príncipe, the map finds little and the conditions look limited. Small states often deal with larger partners on unequal terms. Watch how fishing, oil and investment deals are agreed and whether their terms are published. With few officials making those decisions, a single deal can shape the country's income for years.

Senegal.d:
Senegal's president, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, makes regular visits to the leader of the Mouride Brotherhood. The Mourides are a Sufi Muslim brotherhood with millions of followers, centred on the holy city of Touba, which has run with wide autonomy from the state since 1928. Their leader, the caliph or Khalife général, is Serigne Mountakha Mbacké. Faye, sworn in on 2 April 2024, visited him on 15 April 2024, again in August 2024 and March 2025, and on 7 August 2025 ahead of the Grand Magal pilgrimage, and pledged state help with Touba's water and sanitation. The pre-Magal visit has become customary for heads of state. Abdoulaye Wade went to Touba the day after his 2000 election and put Mourides in his government. This is open politics, not a secret network, but it ties the presidency to a religious leader with a large following.

Other networks have reached the top. In February 2020, while president, Macky Sall accepted the Sunhak Peace Prize, a $1 million award funded by the Unification Church, the movement founded by Sun Myung Moon. Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Wade had been initiated into Freemasonry; Wade's camp accused Sall of membership, which Sall denied.

In 2017 Senegal closed more than a dozen schools linked to the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic movement, attended by about 3,000 children, after Turkish requests; Turkey's state Maarif Foundation took them on.

Senegal belongs to "Churches and movements placing members in the state", "Turkey's long arm", "French lodges and African presidencies" and "Exposure, purge and reversal".
Senegal.imp: For people in Senegal, the president's visits to Touba are public, but the promises made there, such as state money for the holy city, carry weight with millions of voters. A sitting president took $1 million from a prize funded by a foreign church, and 3,000 children's schools changed hands at another government's request. Watch what the state gives Touba and other brotherhoods, whether presidents disclose gifts and prizes, and how foreign requests to act against movements are handled.

The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic lay order with diplomatic relations to many states. Seychelles has one of the lower conditions scores, 4.3 out of 10: the map judges that insiders have limited room inside the state (4.0) and that defences such as courts and press are middling (5.4). As a best guess, the most likely route in is through foreign money, since small island states with financial services and tourism attract investors seeking access to officials.
Seychelles.imp: For people in Seychelles, the map finds little so far and rates the checks as fair. The main risk for a small state is outside money finding its way to a few decision-makers. Watch who owns major investments and how licences and land are granted. On a few islands, land and licences are limited, so who gets them is a direct measure of who has influence.

Sierra Leone.d: Nothing is documented on the map for Sierra Leone yet; this is an estimate. The United Grand Lodge of England, the main English Masonic body, is listed as likely. Its conditions score is 7.0 out of 10: insiders have wide room inside the state (8.0) and defences are on the weak side (4.0). As a best guess, the most likely route in is through foreign advisers in ministries, or through lodge ties to English Freemasonry.
Sierra Leone.imp: For people in Sierra Leone, foreign advisers working inside government help shape priorities without being elected, and lodge ties may link senior officials in ways that are not disclosed.
