Somalia.d:
Somalia's one documented case shows how far Turkey's campaign against the Gülen movement reached. The Gülen movement, also called Hizmet, is a Turkish Islamic movement that ran schools in many countries. Turkey lists it as a terrorist group ("FETÖ") and blames it for the 2016 coup attempt. By June 2017 Gülen-linked schools in Somalia had been taken over by the Maarif Foundation, Turkey's state education body, after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry. Guinea, Niger and Sudan did the same. The record does not say how many schools or pupils were involved.

The transfer shows the Somali government agreeing, at a foreign government's request, to give that government control over schools that had been run privately.

Other organisations are recorded as present: the Muslim Brotherhood, the Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt; Erik Prince's security companies, founded by the American who started Blackwater; and the Order of Malta. None of these has a documented case on the map in Somalia yet.

Somalia belongs to "Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement", "Churches and movements placing members in the state" and "Exposure, purge and reversal", all through the school transfer.
Somalia.imp: For people in Somalia, the case shows that a foreign partner can ask the government to hand over schools and get them, with no public debate. Watch who runs the transferred schools, what else foreign partners ask for, and what private security firms are hired to do. Each of those decisions affects Somali families directly, yet none of them has been put to a public vote.

South Africa.d:
South Africa is still dealing with what it calls "state capture": the takeover of parts of the state by a private network. The Zondo Commission, chaired by Chief Justice Raymond Zondo, heard over 300 witnesses from 2018 and published five reports in 2022. It found that ministers, senior ANC members and heads of state companies acted corruptly for the Gupta family, Indian-born businessmen close to President Jacob Zuma, naming former minister Malusi Gigaba and former Transnet chief Brian Molefe. Deputy Finance Minister Mcebisi Jonas said the Guptas offered him the finance minister's job shortly before Zuma sacked Nhlanhla Nene in December 2015; they deny it. The US sanctioned the brothers and their associate Salim Essa in 2019, and in 2023 the UAE refused to extradite two of them.

Foreign consultants helped. Zondo found Bain & Company worked with Zuma and tax commissioner Tom Moyane to take over the revenue service, SARS; the Treasury barred Bain for 10 years. McKinsey admitted in 2024 to a conspiracy to bribe officials at Eskom, the power utility, and Transnet, the freight rail firm, paying about $122 million. KPMG withdrew its SARS "rogue unit" report in 2017 and nine executives resigned. Bell Pottinger, a London PR firm paid by a Gupta company, was expelled from its industry body and collapsed.

The roots go back further. Every prime minister and state president from D. F. Malan in 1948 to F. W. de Klerk was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society founded in 1918; in 1979 all but two cabinet ministers belonged. Journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom published about 7,500 names in 1978. Before that, Alfred Milner's young Oxford staff, the "Kindergarten", ran the Transvaal after 1902 and pressed for the 1910 Union; the historian Carroll Quigley tied them to a secret society of Cecil Rhodes, a claim that rests on him.

Today, Education Minister Siviwe Gwarube is in the World Economic Forum's 2025 Young Global Leaders class, and ANC leaders attend a party school in Tanzania backed by China's Communist Party.

South Africa has the strongest record on the map and belongs to seven patterns.
South Africa.imp: For people in South Africa, state capture meant that the power utility, the freight railway and the tax service were run partly for a private family and paid consultants. A judicial inquiry exposed it, but the Guptas live abroad and the UAE refused to send two of them back. The country's history shows a secret society choosing its rulers for almost 50 years. Watch prosecutions arising from the Zondo findings, who wins contracts at Eskom and Transnet, and how foreign party schools and forums shape the next generation of leaders.

South Sudan.d: Nothing is documented on the map for South Sudan yet; this is an estimate. Three organisations are recorded as present: the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic lay order with diplomatic relations; the Atlas Network, a US-based network of free-market think tanks; and Glencore, the Swiss-based commodity trader, which the UK's Serious Fraud Office found paid bribes in South Sudan among other countries between 2012 and 2016. Its conditions score is among the highest, 8.5 out of 10: insiders have very wide room inside the state (9.0) and defences are very weak (2.0). As a best guess, the most likely route in is through the oil trade, where traders deal directly with a few officials.
South Sudan.imp: For people in South Sudan, oil is the state's main source of money, and a trader that admitted bribing officials here took part in that trade. With courts and press very weak, those deals stay hidden. Watch who sells the country's oil and on what terms, and whether any official is ever named or tried.

Sudan.d:
Sudan has been at war since April 2023 between its army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force that grew out of militias from Omar al-Bashir's rule. Both sides have foreign backers. A UN Panel of Experts report leaked in January 2024 found "credible" evidence that the UAE sent weapons to the RSF "several times per week" through Amdjarass in northern Chad; the UAE denied it. On the army's side, on 12 September 2025 the US sanctioned Sudan's finance minister, Gebreil Ibrahim, and the al-Baraa bin Malik Brigade, an Islamist militia that has supplied up to 20,000 fighters against the RSF. Treasury said the brigade got training and weapons from Iran's Revolutionary Guards. It used the word "Islamist", not "Muslim Brotherhood".

Those Islamists trace back to the Muslim Brotherhood. On 30 June 1989 Bashir seized power in a coup organised with Hassan al-Turabi's National Islamic Front, the Sudanese movement derived from the Brotherhood. Bashir ruled until 2019. In 2020 he and others were put on trial for the coup, and he admitted his role. The transitional government set up a committee in 2019 to remove people placed in state jobs under his rule; it dismissed judges and prosecutors, but in October 2021 the High Court overturned the dismissals. In September 2023 the US sanctioned Ali Karti, Bashir's former foreign minister and head of the Sudanese Islamic Movement, for obstructing a ceasefire.

Russia's network reached in too. In July 2020 the US sanctioned M Invest, a Prigozhin-linked company, and its gold-mining arm Meroe Gold, saying they tried to help suppress protesters in 2018–19. In 2017 Sudan handed Gülen-linked schools to Turkey's state foundation.

Sudan belongs to six patterns, including "Movements that sought the state itself".
Sudan.imp: For people in Sudan, the war is fed by foreign weapons and by Islamist networks rooted in the 1989 coup. An attempt to remove Bashir's appointees from courts was reversed, so those networks still hold posts. Sudan's gold has funded foreign forces. Watch who supplies weapons to each side, whether sanctioned officials stay in government, and who controls gold mines.

Tanzania.d:
In Kibaha, Tanzania, the Chinese Communist Party runs a school that trains officials of six African ruling parties. The Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Leadership School, headquartered there, took its first class on 22 February 2022. It was built with a $40 million grant from the Chinese Communist Party's Central Party School, the institution that trains China's own officials, and CCP theoreticians teach there. It is a joint project of the CCP and six ruling parties: Tanzania's CCM, South Africa's ANC, Angola's MPLA, Mozambique's FRELIMO, Namibia's SWAPO and Zimbabwe's ZANU-PF.

A party school shapes how cadres think about running a state: how to organise the party, how to hold power, and how the party relates to government. Here the curriculum comes from a foreign ruling party, and the students are the people who will staff the governments of six countries. The school's openness about its funding makes it one of the clearer cases on the map; what is taught is less public.

Opus Dei and the Gülen movement are also recorded as present.

Tanzania is not assigned a pattern on the map but is home to the school whose reach shows up in five other countries' records.
Tanzania.imp: For people in Tanzania, the ruling party's future officials are being trained by teachers from China's Communist Party, in a building China paid for. That can shape how government treats elections, dissent and the press. Citizens are not told what is taught. Watch which officials attend, what the course covers, and whether Chinese party methods appear in Tanzanian policy.

Togo.d: Nothing is documented on the map for Togo yet; this is an estimate. Three organisations are recorded as present: the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic lay order with diplomatic relations; NSO Group, the Israeli maker of Pegasus spyware; and the Archimedes Group, an Israeli political consulting firm removed from Facebook in 2019 for election meddling in Africa. French Masonic bodies and Russia's Africa Corps are listed as likely. Togo's conditions score is 6.5 out of 10: insiders have wide room inside the state (7.5) and defences are weak (4.4). As a best guess, the most likely route in is through surveillance tools and election consultants, given which firms are present.
Togo.imp: For people in Togo, the firms present are ones that elsewhere have been used to watch phones and shape elections. If used here, voters and journalists would be unlikely to know. Watch for reports of spyware on activists' phones and for who runs campaigns in elections. Neither would be visible unless someone inside or a foreign investigation brought it to light.

Tunisia.d:
Tunisia's best-known Islamist leader, Rached Ghannouchi, is in prison. On 5 February 2025 a Tunisian court sentenced him to a further 22 years for "plotting against state security" in what is called the Instalingo case. Ghannouchi leads Ennahda, an Islamist party, and was speaker of parliament from 2019 to 2021. The same verdict gave former foreign minister Rafik Abdessalem 34 years and former prime minister Hichem Mechichi 35 years in absentia. Ghannouchi has been jailed since April 2023, and in July 2025 he received another 14-year sentence. Ennahda calls the case political.

The background is Ennahda's time in power. Ennahda won the October 2011 Constituent Assembly election and led the government. Hamadi Jebali was prime minister from December 2011 to March 2013, followed by Ali Laarayedh until January 2014. Abdessalem, Ghannouchi's son-in-law, was foreign minister from 2011 to 2013. Ennahda grew out of the Muslim Brotherhood tradition, the Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt, but says it has no organisational link to the Egyptian Brotherhood.

Hizb ut-Tahrir, an Islamist group that calls for a caliphate, the Trilateral Commission and the Archimedes Group are also recorded as present.

Tunisia belongs to the pattern "Movements that sought the state itself", as a country where such a movement won government.
Tunisia.imp: For people in Tunisia, a party that won the first free election after 2011 now sees its leader and former ministers given decades in prison, and the party calls the cases political. Voters have to judge whether the courts are punishing crimes or removing opponents. Watch whether trials are open, how the security charges are defined, and whether other parties face similar cases.

Uganda.d:
Uganda's Anti-Homosexuality Act, passed in 2023, carries life imprisonment and in some cases death. Family Watch International, an Arizona-based Christian lobbying group with UN consultative status, has a strong presence in Africa, and a Ugandan activist named its president, Sharon Slater, as having lobbied for the law. The group earlier called its position on the 2009 bill "complicated". The World Bank halted new lending to Uganda in August 2023 over the law.

The law's roots run through an American prayer network. The Fellowship, also called The Family, is a US Christian network that runs national prayer breakfasts for politicians. David Bahati chairs Uganda's National Prayer Breakfast Fellowship. Journalist Jeff Sharlet reported that Bahati first floated his 2009 Anti-Homosexuality Bill, which proposed the death penalty, at the 2008 Uganda prayer breakfast, and Fellowship member Bob Hunter confirmed Bahati's link to NPR. Bahati has been a state minister since 2021, currently for trade, industry and cooperatives, and was re-appointed in 2026.

Surveillance is the other thread. In August 2019 the Wall Street Journal reported that Huawei technicians working inside Uganda's police headquarters helped its cyber unit get into the encrypted messages of opposition MP Bobi Wine. The Journal found no evidence that Huawei executives in China or the Chinese state directed this, and Huawei denied the report.

Uganda belongs to "China's long arm abroad" and "Churches and movements placing members in the state".
Uganda.imp: For people in Uganda, a law that can send people to prison for life began as a bill raised at a prayer breakfast tied to a US network and was lobbied for by a US group. Opposition politicians' messages were reportedly opened with help from a foreign company's staff inside police headquarters. Watch who sponsors prayer breakfasts and lobbying on family law, and what technology the police use to watch phones.

Zambia.d:
Zambia's constitution, adopted in 1996, declares it a Christian nation, and for five years that declaration had its own ministry. In September 2016 President Edgar Lungu turned a religious-affairs desk into a full Ministry of National Guidance and Religious Affairs and gave the post to Rev. Godfridah Sumaili, a cleric he appointed as a nominated member of parliament. She held it until August 2021. After the 2021 election President Hichilema dissolved the ministry into a department of the Vice-President's office.

The case shows a cleric sitting in cabinet, chosen by the president rather than elected to her seat, with a ministry built around religion. It is open, not secret, but it gave church networks a seat inside government. The record does not say which churches gained from it.

Huawei, China's largest telecoms equipment maker, is also recorded as present; the Wall Street Journal reported in 2019 that Huawei staff helped Zambia's government with domestic spying. Cambridge Analytica and the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, a Brazilian-run church, are recorded as present too.

Zambia belongs to the pattern "Churches and movements placing members in the state".
Zambia.imp: For people in Zambia, the Christian-nation clause means religion has a formal place in government, and for five years a minister appointed rather than elected spoke for it in cabinet. That can shape laws on families, schools and minorities. Watch what the religious-affairs department now does, which churches have access to it, and what technology foreign firms supply for watching citizens.

Zimbabwe.d:
Zimbabwe's documented case is about who watched its 2018 general election. AFRIC, the Association for Free Research and International Cooperation, presented itself as an independent African research and election-monitoring body and sent about 40 observers to the vote. Election observers matter because their reports tell the world whether a vote was fair, and governments and courts cite them. The European Platform for Democratic Elections reports that investigative journalists later found AFRIC was organised by people and structures linked to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the Russian businessman behind the Wagner Group. The finding rests on that reporting; the record does not say what AFRIC's observers concluded.

Zimbabwe's ruling party, ZANU-PF, is also one of six parties that send cadres to the Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Leadership School in Tanzania, built with Chinese Communist Party money. The United Grand Lodge of England, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International and the Rhodes Trust are listed as likely but unconfirmed.

Zimbabwe belongs to "Russia's networks in Europe and Africa", as a target country, and "Spyware and elections for hire".
Zimbabwe.imp: For people in Zimbabwe, an election verdict can be shaped by who is allowed to watch, and here a group presenting itself as independent was reported to be organised by Russian interests. Voters and courts relying on observer reports could not tell. Watch who is accredited to observe future elections and who funds them, and what the ruling party's officials learn at the CCP-funded school.

Afghanistan.d: Nothing is documented for Afghanistan on this map yet, so what follows is a best guess, not a finding. The only organisation with a recorded presence is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order that runs aid work and holds diplomatic status. Three others are likely present but undocumented: the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network; the Hojjatieh Society, an Iranian religious association; and the Asia Foundation, a US-funded development group. The conditions score is 8.75 out of 10, one of the highest anywhere: armed and unelected groups sit deep inside the state (9.0) and the institutions that could push back are very weak (1.5). The most likely route in is through neighbouring states' religious and security networks.
Afghanistan.imp: For people in Afghanistan, the map has no proven case of an outside network steering the government. That is not the same as there being none. With courts, a free press and elections largely absent, almost nothing that happens inside the state can be checked from outside. Watch for foreign-funded schools, aid groups and religious associations that gain access to officials, and for who controls the security services.

Armenia.d: Nothing is documented for Armenia on this map yet, so this is an estimate. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status that runs aid projects, has a recorded presence. The Russkiy Mir Foundation, set up by the Russian state to promote Russian language and culture abroad, is likely present but not documented. Armenia's conditions score is 3.94 out of 10, on the lower side: unelected groups are only moderately embedded in the state (3.5) and the country's institutions show middling strength (5.6). The most likely route in, as a best guess, is Russian cultural and political influence working through ties built up over the Soviet period and Armenia's continuing reliance on Russia.
Armenia.imp: People in Armenia have no proven case on this map of a secret society or foreign organisation steering their government. The likeliest pressure, if any, comes from Russia's state-backed cultural programmes, which are lawful but serve a foreign government's aims. Watch for who funds language centres, media and political groups, and whether that funding is declared.

Azerbaijan.d: Azerbaijan is the home of a network the map calls 'caviar diplomacy': the Azerbaijani state's practice of cultivating European politicians, which places it at the centre of the pattern 'Foreign money inside Europe's parliaments'. Its one documented case on this page, though, is about something else: how the government helped Turkey go after the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network best known for running schools abroad. On 18 June 2014 the movement's schools in Azerbaijan, 11 high schools, 13 university-entrance preparation centres and a private university, were taken over by the Azerbaijan International Education Company. The state oil company SOCAR, which holds shares in that company, sits at the heart of Azerbaijan's economy. The company said the reason was financial viability. The takeover came after Turkish Prime Minister Erdogan asked for help against the movement, according to Eurasianet. Also present on the record are the Grey Wolves, a Turkish ultranationalist youth movement, and the Tony Blair Institute, the former British prime minister's advisory group; the World Economic Forum is likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 7.27 out of 10, high: actors outside public view are strongly embedded in the state (8.5) and checks on power are weak (4.0). On the map, Azerbaijan belongs to 'Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement', where it is a country that closed schools; 'Churches and movements placing members in the state' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal', where it is a government that purged a movement; and it is the headquarters in 'Foreign money inside Europe's parliaments'.
Azerbaijan.imp: For people in Azerbaijan, the documented case shows how a state company can be used to carry out another government's political wishes, closing schools families relied on without a court ruling. The caviar diplomacy network points the other way: Azerbaijan's own state reaching into foreign parliaments. Watch for state-owned firms taking over private institutions, and for who in Europe speaks for the government.

Bahrain.d: Bahrain's documented case is about the use of Interpol, the international police cooperation body whose 'Red Notices' ask police worldwide to find and arrest a wanted person. Hakeem al-Araibi is a footballer and dissident who fled Bahrain in 2014 and became a refugee in Australia. Bahrain's Interior Ministry obtained a Red Notice for him, and when he flew to Bangkok in November 2018, Thai police arrested him on arrival. Interpol withdrew the notice days later, because a policy it adopted in 2015 bars notices requested by the country a refugee has fled. Thailand still held extradition proceedings until prosecutors dropped the case on 11 February 2019. The Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational Islamist movement, and the Tony Blair Institute, the former British prime minister's advisory group, also have a recorded presence; Iran's Quds Force and its allied militias are likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 4.58 out of 10, in the middle. On the map Bahrain belongs to 'Governments and industries inside international bodies', as a government that used an international body against someone it wanted back.
Bahrain.imp: For people from Bahrain who leave and speak out, this case shows that a request made at home can follow them into another country's airport. Interpol's own rules stopped it here, but only after an arrest and months of proceedings. Anyone who has fled should know whether a notice exists in their name and that refugee status is grounds to have it removed.

Bangladesh.d: Bangladesh's documented case is a coup attempt the army says it stopped. In January 2012 the Bangladesh army announced that serving and retired officers, whom it described as religious extremists, had planned to seize power. It named Hizb ut-Tahrir among those behind the plot. Hizb ut-Tahrir is an international Islamist party that aims to bring back a caliphate, a single Islamic state, and it has been banned in Bangladesh since 2009. Two retired officers were arrested and a serving major was named as a fugitive. The source is the army's own press briefing of 19 January 2012, reported by the BBC and Reuters; this is the army's account and the map does not record a court outcome. The Bank of Credit and Commerce International, a Pakistani-founded bank that collapsed in 1991 amid fraud, is likely to have had a presence but is not documented. The conditions score is 6.46 out of 10: groups outside public view are fairly embedded in the state (7.0) and institutions are on the weak side (4.1). The country belongs to two patterns: 'Movements that sought the state itself', as a place where a movement tried to take the army, and 'Religious nationalism in power'.
Bangladesh.imp: For people in Bangladesh, the case shows that the army is a target for movements that want to change the state outright, not just influence it. What the public knows comes almost entirely from the army's own statement. Watch for whether such cases go to open trial, and for how bans on movements are used.

Bhutan.d: Nothing is documented for Bhutan on this map yet, and no organisation is recorded as present or likely present. What follows is a best guess. The conditions score is 4.17 out of 10, on the lower side: unelected groups are not strongly embedded in the state (3.0) and institutions are of middling strength (4.7). With no foreign or secret network on record, the most likely route in, if one exists, would be through larger neighbours' state and business influence or through international aid and development programmes.
Bhutan.imp: People in Bhutan have no documented case on this map of an outside or secret network steering their government. The absence of records can also reflect how little outside reporting there is on a small country. Watch for who funds development projects and who advises ministries. A small country with few outside reporters can have influence that simply goes unrecorded.

Brunei.d: Nothing is documented for Brunei on this map yet, so this is an estimate. One organisation has a recorded presence: Chinese police 'overseas service stations', offices linked to Chinese police that have been found in many countries and are said to monitor and pressure Chinese citizens abroad. The conditions score is 4.19 out of 10, on the lower side: unelected groups are not strongly embedded (3.0) and institutions are of middling strength (4.6). As a best guess, the most likely route in is through China's overseas policing and community networks, reaching residents rather than ministers.
Brunei.imp: For people in Brunei, especially Chinese residents, the main point is that a foreign police presence has been recorded, even though no case has been documented. Such offices can pressure people without local officials being aware. Watch for who runs community associations and whether local police know of these stations.

Cambodia.d: Cambodia sits at the centre of the map's pattern on scam compounds: walled sites where trafficked workers are forced to run online frauds. Two Phnom Penh conglomerates headquartered here are now under sanctions, and both were close to the ruling family. Chen Zhi, born in Fujian in China, took Cambodian citizenship in 2014 and built the Prince Group into one of the country's largest firms. He held the honorary title Neak Oknha and advised Hun Sen, the long-serving prime minister, as well as interior minister Sar Kheng and National Assembly president Heng Samrin. On 14 October 2025 the US Justice Department indicted him for fraud and money laundering, calling him the head of a cyber-fraud empire, and seized about 127,271 bitcoin (about US$14 billion); the US and UK sanctioned 146 people and firms linked to the group. In January 2026 Cambodia said it had arrested him, revoked his citizenship and sent him to China to face charges. Huione Group's payment arm, Huione Pay, has Hun To, a cousin of current Prime Minister Hun Manet, as a major shareholder and director. Cambodia's central bank revoked its banking licence in March 2025, and in May 2025 the US Treasury's anti-money-laundering office found Huione had laundered over US$4 billion between August 2021 and January 2025, including money from North Korean hackers. A third case, reported in the press, involves the Unification Church, the Korean-founded church whose political arm is the Universal Peace Federation. Cambodia hosted its Asia-Pacific summit in November 2019, where church leader Hak Ja Han gave Hun Sen a governance award; in early 2022, still in office, he received the church's Sunhak Peace Prize Founders' Award. The conditions score is 7.77 out of 10: hidden actors are deeply embedded (9.0) and checks are weak (3.5). Cambodia belongs to 'Scam compounds and casino money inside Asian states', 'Churches and movements placing members in the state' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Cambodia.imp: For people in Cambodia, these cases show business empires built on fraud and laundering sitting next to the country's leaders as advisers and relatives. Action came mostly from abroad, through US and UK sanctions, before Cambodia moved against Chen Zhi. Watch for who replaces these firms, whether trafficked workers are freed, and whether other honorary titles go to people with similar records.

China.d: China mostly appears on this map as the country reaching outward. It is home to the Communist Party's United Front Work Department, which directs 'united front' work among overseas Chinese and foreign elites, and to Huawei, the Confucius Institutes, the overseas 'police service stations' and the China Association for International Friendly Contact. That places it as the sponsoring state in 'China's long arm abroad' and 'Governments buying officials in other countries'. It is also home to the Sun Kian Ip Group of Ng Lap Seng, which puts it in 'Global firms buying governments'. The documented cases here centre on Interpol, the international police body whose Red Notices ask police worldwide to arrest someone. In November 2016 Meng Hongwei, China's Vice-Minister of Public Security, was elected Interpol's first Chinese president. In February 2018, during his term, Interpol removed a Red Notice China had sought against Dolkun Isa, a World Uyghur Congress leader living in Germany whom China called a terrorist; no Western country had acted on it, and China protested. Rights groups record 1,546 detentions or deportations of Uyghurs from 28 countries since 1997. In September 2018 Meng himself disappeared after flying to China; the party's discipline commission said he was under investigation for bribery, and in January 2020 a Tianjin court sentenced him to 13 and a half years for taking more than 14.5 million yuan. His wife, granted asylum in France, says the case is political. The third case runs the other way. In December 2019 China sanctioned the National Endowment for Democracy, a US government-funded grant-maker, after Congress passed a Hong Kong rights law, having earlier named it a US intelligence front. That is the Chinese government's assertion, not an independent finding. The conditions score is 5.73 out of 10, with hidden actors fairly embedded (7.0).
China.imp: For people in China, these cases show that the same security ministry that sends officials into international bodies can also make them disappear at home. For Chinese and Uyghur people abroad, they show requests from Beijing following them across borders. Watch how foreign-funded groups are described, how Interpol handles requests, and who runs overseas community and police offices.

Cyprus.d: Nothing is documented for Cyprus on this map yet, so this is a best guess. Two organisations have a recorded presence: the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, and the Trilateral Commission, a private forum founded in 1973 that brings together political and business leaders from North America, Europe and Asia. The United Grand Lodge of England, the governing body of English Freemasonry, and the Grey Wolves, a Turkish ultranationalist movement, are likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 4.75 out of 10, middling. The most likely routes in are the island's divided politics, with Turkish nationalist networks in the north, and its role as a financial centre.
Cyprus.imp: People in Cyprus have no documented case on this map of a secret society or foreign group steering their government. The likeliest pressure points, as an estimate, are nationalist networks tied to the island's division and the flows of foreign money through its banks and company registry. Watch who owns companies and who funds political groups.

Georgia.d: Nothing is documented for Georgia on this map yet, so this is an estimate. Three organisations have a recorded presence: the Grand Orient de France, the main French Masonic body; the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status; and the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network known for its schools. The Atlas Network, a US-based group that links free-market think tanks around the world, is likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 4.50 out of 10, middling: unelected groups are moderately embedded (4.0) and institutions are of medium strength (5.0). As a best guess, the likeliest route in is foreign-funded think tanks and schools, given how strongly outside powers compete for influence there.
Georgia.imp: People in Georgia have no proven case on this map. With several foreign networks present and governments in Russia, Turkey and the West all seeking influence, the best protection is knowing who funds which schools, think tanks and lodges. Watch for laws that target foreign-funded groups as well as for undeclared foreign money.

India.d: India's government today is run largely by people who came up through one organisation: the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer group founded in 1925 from which the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) grew. Prime Minister Narendra Modi joined the RSS as a boy and worked as a full-time organiser (pracharak) from the early 1970s until the RSS sent him to the BJP in 1985; the RSS has acknowledged this. ThePrint counted in January 2020 that 38 of 53 BJP ministers in Modi's second government had RSS roots, along with all eight it listed on the cabinet's economic committee, including Amit Shah and Rajnath Singh. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar did not. C. P. Radhakrishnan, linked to the RSS since age 16, became Vice President in September 2025, which also makes him chair of Parliament's upper house. The RSS does not publish membership rolls; membership of it is lawful. Other cases show money and spying crossing borders. In November 2024 US prosecutors charged Gautam Adani, founder of the Adani ports and power conglomerate, alleging over $250 million in bribes to Indian officials for solar contracts; he denies it. US prosecutors also charged that Vikash Yadav, an employee of the office housing India's foreign intelligence agency, directed a 2023 plot to kill a Sikh separatist lawyer in New York; his go-between Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty in February 2026, while Yadav has not been brought to the US. The minister of civil aviation, Ram Mohan Naidu, is in the World Economic Forum's 2025 Young Global Leaders class. The oldest case is historical background: historian Carroll Quigley wrote that Lionel Curtis's Round Table group, a British imperial network, worked out the 'dyarchy' scheme enacted in the Government of India Act 1919. India's conditions score is 5.77 out of 10. It belongs to 'Religious nationalism in power', 'Churches and movements placing members in the state', 'Global firms buying governments', 'Governments buying officials in other countries', 'Private forums where officials meet money' and 'Rhodes, Milner and the Round Table network'.
India.imp: For people in India, the main point is that one movement with no public membership list supplies most of the cabinet, so its views reach policy without voters seeing how. Separately, the Adani charges allege that state officials took bribes on power contracts. Watch whether the Adani case is tested in court, and how RSS ties shape appointments to courts, universities and the civil service.

Indonesia.d: Indonesia's present-day cases are about religious movements and the state. Nahdlatul Ulama, the country's largest Muslim organisation, built on traditional Islamic boarding schools, saw its supreme leader Ma'ruf Amin chosen as President Joko Widodo's running mate in 2018; he left the post and served as vice-president from 2019 to 2024. At the other end, the government revoked the legal status of Hizb ut-Tahrir Indonesia, the local branch of an international party seeking a caliphate, in July 2017 under a new decree on mass organisations. Officials warned that civil servants who were members would be dismissed, and courts upheld the ban in 2018. The roots go back to the 1950s. The Ford Foundation, a large American charity, paid for University of Indonesia economists to take doctorates at the University of California, Berkeley. After Suharto took power in 1966 they became his economic team, later called the 'Berkeley Mafia'. Widjojo Nitisastro headed the planning agency BAPPENAS, which wrote the five-year plans, from 1967 to 1983. Ali Wardhana was finance minister from 1968 to 1983, deciding how state money was spent; Emil Salim and Mohammad Sadli also held ministries. Their 1966 programme cut inflation from 650% to 13% by 1969 and opened the country to foreign investors. John Perkins, chief economist at the Boston engineering firm Chas. T. Main, later claimed his job was to inflate growth forecasts so countries like Indonesia would take large loans; a New York Times check found his career described accurately but no evidence for his larger claims, and the US State Department called much of it fabrication. The conditions score is 6.86 out of 10: hidden actors are well embedded (8.0) and checks are weak (4.3). Indonesia belongs to 'Lenders, aid programmes and trained technocrats', 'Churches and movements placing members in the state', 'Religious nationalism in power', 'Movements that sought the state itself' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Indonesia.imp: For people in Indonesia, the long-run point is that the economy was shaped for two decades by a team trained through one foreign charity's programme, and that religious organisations reach the top offices today. Bans can protect the state but can also be used against civil servants for membership alone. Watch who advises economic ministries and how the mass-organisations decree is used.

Iran.d: The cases recorded for Iran are mostly background to how the state works today. Iran is the home of the Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force and its allied militias, which places it as the sponsoring state in the map's pattern 'Iran's armed allies inside governments'; that story is told mainly under Iraq and Lebanon. Inside Iran, the record goes back to the Shah. Jafar Sharif-Emami, for several years Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Iran, the country's main Masonic body, was the Shah's prime minister in 1960–61 and again in the autumn of 1978, the last months before the revolution. In 1976 General Nematollah Nassiri, head of the Shah's secret police SAVAK, signed the charter of the Safari Club, a secret alliance of the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Morocco and Iran to counter Soviet influence in Africa. Its papers were found in the Shah's archives after 1979, according to the journalist Mohamed Heikal. After the revolution, the Hojjatieh Society, a religious association founded to oppose the Baha'i faith, had members across government bodies. On 12 July 1983 Ayatollah Khomeini attacked it in a speech; its founder suspended it the same day, and its affiliates were purged from decision-making and educational bodies. Former members are reported to have later held judicial and security posts; claims about senior figures and influence under President Ahmadinejad are contested. The conditions score is 8.21 out of 10: unelected actors are very deeply embedded (9.5) and checks are weak (3.1). Iran belongs to 'Churches and movements placing members in the state', 'The anticommunist web, 1945–1990' and 'Iran's armed allies inside governments'.
Iran.imp: For people in Iran, the record shows that whoever holds power has long worked through closed networks, a Masonic lodge and a secret police under the Shah, and religious associations afterwards. Ordinary citizens cannot see who belongs to which network inside the judiciary or security services. Watch for how the Revolutionary Guards' allies abroad shape decisions at home.

Iraq.d: In Iraq today, armed groups loyal to Iran are part of the state's own armed forces and are paid from its budget. The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) formed in June 2014 to fight Islamic State and are made up of about 67 mostly Shia factions, almost all backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards. A law passed in November 2016 and signed by President Fuad Masum on 19 December 2016 made them a branch of the armed forces under the prime minister. In 2024 the PMF chief of staff said publicly that it took orders from Iran's supreme leader. A 2025 reform bill to tighten state control was tabled under US pressure. One faction, Kata'ib Hezbollah, has been listed by the US as a terrorist organisation since 2009. It staffs the PMF's 45th, 46th and 47th Brigades, and its commander Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis led the PMF in the field until a US strike killed him in January 2020. The US linked it to the January 2024 drone attack on Tower 22 that killed three US soldiers. Falih al-Fayyadh chairs the state body that runs the PMF and was also national security adviser. On 8 January 2021 the US Treasury sanctioned him over the killing of protesters in 2019; Iraq's foreign ministry said it was 'surprised', and he remains chairman. These designations are US government decisions, not court verdicts. The Muslim Brotherhood, Hizb ut-Tahrir and Hezbollah also have a recorded presence. The conditions score is 7.58 out of 10: hidden actors are deeply embedded (8.5) and checks are weak (3.3). Iraq is where these allies sit in the state in 'Iran's armed allies inside governments', and it also belongs to 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Iraq.imp: For people in Iraq, the force paid from their taxes to protect them includes units that answer, by their own officials' account, to another country's leader. The man running that force stays in post despite US sanctions over protesters' deaths. Watch whether the 2025 reform bill passes and whether PMF brigades come under real state command.

Israel.d: Israel appears on this map mainly as the home of companies that sell surveillance and election-influence services to other governments: NSO Group, Team Jorge and Archimedes Group. That makes it the firms' home in the pattern 'Spyware and elections for hire'. The documented case concerns NSO Group, which sells Pegasus, spyware that can take over a phone, only to governments and under export licences from Israel's defence ministry. Investigations by Citizen Lab and others tied its use by state clients to surveillance of journalists and dissidents, including people around the journalist Jamal Khashoggi before Saudi agents killed him in 2018. In November 2021 the US Commerce Department added NSO to its Entity List, a trade blacklist, for acting against US interests. A New York Times investigation found that Pegasus sales coincided with some governments' warmer ties with Israel. Several other organisations have a recorded presence, including the Legion of Christ, a Catholic religious order; the Unification Church; the Trilateral Commission, a private forum of political and business leaders; and Uber. The Church of Scientology and the World Economic Forum are likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 4.98 out of 10, middling. Israel also belongs to 'Exposure, purge and reversal', for the US blacklisting.
Israel.imp: For people in Israel, the main question is that a private company's sales, licensed by their own defence ministry, are linked to spying on journalists and dissidents abroad and appear tied to diplomacy. Export decisions are made with little public view. Watch who gets licences, which governments buy, and whether the same tools are used at home.

Japan.d: Japan has the fullest record on this map, and most of it is about religious and nationalist groups inside the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). The prime minister since 21 October 2025, Sanae Takaichi, has sat in the Diet league of Nippon Kaigi, Japan's largest nationalist lobby, which campaigns for constitutional revision and patriotic education. A Communist Party paper, Akahata, reported that 10 of her 19 ministers belong to that league, 12 to the league of Shinto Seiji Renmei (the political arm of the Association of Shinto Shrines), and five have ties to the Unification Church; in 2014, press counts put 15 of Abe's 19 ministers in Nippon Kaigi. The cabinet was reshuffled in September 2026 and has not been recounted. The Unification Church, a Korean-founded church, goes back a long way here. In 1968 former prime minister Nobusuke Kishi, Abe's grandfather, co-founded the anti-communist body that ran its political work in Japan. Its ties came into the open after Tetsuya Yamagami shot Shinzo Abe dead in July 2022, saying he blamed the church for ruining his family; he was sentenced to life in January 2026. The LDP's own survey that September found 179 of its 379 Diet members had ties to the church; 17, including Abe's brother, Defense Minister Nobuo Kishi, used its followers as campaign volunteers. Minister Daishiro Yamagiwa resigned in October 2022. Church documents seized in Korea are reported to say it backed 290 LDP candidates in 2021. Tokyo courts ordered the church dissolved for harm to 1,559 donors, upheld on 4 March 2026; that is a finding against the church, not against any official. Soka Gakkai, a Buddhist lay movement, supplies the votes of Komeito, which governed with the LDP from 1999 until it quit on 10 October 2025. Older cases include Aum Shinrikyo, the cult behind the 1995 sarin attack, which counted a Tokyo police officer and former soldiers among its followers, and a Tokyo 2020 Olympic board member, Haruyuki Takahashi, charged with taking about ¥198 million in bribes; he pleaded not guilty. The conditions score is low at 2.25 out of 10: strong institutions (7.5) are what brought most of this to light. Japan belongs to 'Churches and movements placing members in the state', 'Religious nationalism in power', 'Governments and industries inside international bodies' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Japan.imp: For people in Japan, the main point is that lobbies and churches most voters never deal with have members across the cabinet, and their views on the constitution, education and shrines reach policy through those lawmakers. Much of what is known came from a killing, a party's self-reporting and an opposition paper. Watch the recount for the reshuffled cabinet and the church's liquidation.

Jordan.d: In Jordan, the country's largest party in parliament is tied to a movement the government has banned. The Muslim Brotherhood is a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928, with branches across the region. Its political arm in Jordan, the Islamic Action Front, won 31 of 138 seats in the September 2024 election, more than any other party. On 23 April 2025 Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya banned all activities of the Brotherhood and said its assets would be seized. The ban followed the arrest of 16 people, including Brotherhood members, over an alleged plot involving weapons; the group denied knowing about it. On 13 January 2026 the US Treasury designated the Egyptian and Jordanian branches as Specially Designated Global Terrorists. Jordan's government spokesman responded that the group 'has been dissolved for years'. The record does not say whether the Islamic Action Front itself has been banned. Hizb ut-Tahrir, a party seeking a caliphate, and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta also have a recorded presence; Le Cercle, a private foreign-policy discussion club, is likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 5.19 out of 10, middling. Jordan belongs to 'Movements that sought the state itself' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal', as a country that banned the movement.
Jordan.imp: For people in Jordan, the case raises a hard question: the movement behind the party many voted for in 2024 is now banned at home and listed as terrorist by the US. Voters cannot easily see how far the party and the banned group are separate. Watch what happens to the Islamic Action Front's seats and to the 16 people arrested.

Kazakhstan.d: Kazakhstan's one documented case is about how it handled Turkey's campaign against the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network known for its schools abroad. After Turkey's July 2016 coup attempt, which Ankara blames on the movement, Turkey asked Central Asian governments to close Gülen-linked schools. Kazakhstan declined. On 18 October 2016 the foundation that sponsors the schools, KATEV, announced that its 33 Turkish-Kazakh lyceums, co-founded by the movement, would be renamed 'Bilim' Innovative Lyceums. Radio Free Europe reported that no Kazakh government order lay behind the change. Other organisations with a recorded presence include Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life; the Sovereign Military Order of Malta; Hizb ut-Tahrir, a party seeking a caliphate; and the Grey Wolves, a Turkish ultranationalist movement. The World Economic Forum, Russia's Russkiy Mir Foundation and Interpol are likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 5.67 out of 10, middling: hidden actors are fairly embedded (6.0) and institutions are on the weak side (4.7). Kazakhstan is listed in 'Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement' and 'Churches and movements placing members in the state', though here the record shows a government that kept the schools open.
Kazakhstan.imp: For people in Kazakhstan, the case shows the government resisting a foreign request to close schools, while the schools changed their names. Families sending children there may not know who founded them. Watch for further requests from Ankara and how Russian and Turkish networks compete for influence. A decision made by a foundation, not by officials, kept the schools running, so the record shows no state action against them.

Korea, DPR.d: Nothing is documented for North Korea on this map yet, so this is an estimate. One organisation has a recorded presence: the Unification Church, a Korean-founded church whose leaders have pursued business and political contacts with the North. The conditions score is 9.19 out of 10, among the highest anywhere: the ruling party and security services control the state completely (10.0), and there is almost nothing that could check them (1.6). In a closed one-party state, the route in for any outside network, as a best guess, is through deals approved at the top, such as the church's business ties, rather than infiltration from below.
Korea, DPR.imp: For people in North Korea, there is no independent press, court or parliament to expose any network inside the state, so the absence of documented cases says little. Any outside group operates only with the leadership's permission. Watch for joint business ventures and which foreign organisations are allowed in. People inside the country have no way to learn of such arrangements.

Korea, Rep..d: South Korea is now prosecuting the churches that reached into its last government. The Unification Church, founded in Korea by Sun Myung Moon and led by his widow Han Hak-ja, used money to buy political influence around the 2022 presidential election, a Seoul court found. On 28 January 2026 Kim Keon-hee, wife of former president Yoon Suk Yeol, was sentenced to one year and eight months for receiving a Chanel bag and a diamond necklace from the church in July 2022, passed through a shaman on behalf of church official Yun Young-ho. Kweon Seong-dong, a five-term lawmaker and Yoon ally who led his party in parliament, took 100 million won from Yun in January 2022; the Supreme Court upheld his two-year term on 16 July 2026 and he lost his seat. On 31 August 2026 Han Hak-ja was sentenced to two years for arranging both; the church says it will appeal. The money also reached the other side: Chun Jae-soo, oceans minister under President Lee Jae-myung of the Democratic Party, resigned in December 2025 after Yun said the church gave him cash and watches in 2018–2020. Police booked him as a bribery suspect; he denies it. A second church, Shincheonji, a Korean sect, is accused of signing at least 56,472 members into Yoon's People Power Party between 2021 and 2023; founder Lee Man-hee, 94, was indicted in July 2026. The roots go back to 1978, when a US House committee found Moon's organisation had allies in the Seoul government, made M-16 rifles and acted as a secret envoy, during the 'Koreagate' scandal in which Korean intelligence paid US congressmen. The conditions score is 3.00 out of 10, low, with strong institutions (8.0). South Korea is the sponsoring state in 'Governments buying officials in other countries' and belongs to 'Churches and movements placing members in the state' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Korea, Rep..imp: For people in South Korea, these verdicts show a church buying access to a first lady and a party leader, and a sect filling a party's membership to sway its primaries. Courts acted, across both main parties. Watch the appeals, the Chun Jae-soo investigation, and the Shincheonji trial. Most of what is known came from a special counsel investigation, not from the parties themselves.

Kuwait.d: Kuwait's documented case shows a religious movement entering politics openly through elections. The Muslim Brotherhood is a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 with branches across the region. After Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, the Kuwaiti Brotherhood broke with the international organisation and founded its own party, the Islamic Constitutional Movement, known as Hadas. Through the 1990s and 2000s Hadas regularly won several seats in parliament and now and then sent members into the cabinet. A coalition including Hadas left parliament after it boycotted the 2013 elections, according to a 2013 Carnegie analysis; the record does not show what has happened since. The Trilateral Commission, a private forum of political and business leaders, and Gulf state and private networks that fund Salafi missionary work also have a recorded presence. The conditions score is 5.29 out of 10, middling. Kuwait appears in 'Movements that sought the state itself' as a country where such a movement won a share of government, by vote.
Kuwait.imp: For people in Kuwait, this case is about a movement seeking power in the open, through elections, not in secret. Voters could see whom they were electing. What is less visible is how funding networks for religious missionary work shape politics. Watch whether Brotherhood-linked candidates return to parliament and where religious funding comes from.

Kyrgyzstan.d: In Kyrgyzstan, a citizen was taken out of the country by a foreign state, and the officers who let it happen are under investigation. Orhan Inandi, a Kyrgyz citizen, ran Sapat, a network of Turkish-founded schools linked to the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network the Turkish government blames for its 2016 coup attempt and calls 'FETÖ'. He disappeared in Bishkek in mid-2021. On 5 July 2021 President Erdogan said on Turkish television that Inandi, whom he called a FETÖ leader, had been 'captured and taken to Turkey'. In August 2021 Kyrgyzstan's Military Prosecutor's Office opened proceedings for negligence and breach of border rules against officers of the State Committee for National Security, the country's main security service, who allowed him to be taken out. The record does not show the outcome. Hizb ut-Tahrir, a party seeking a caliphate, and the Grey Wolves, a Turkish ultranationalist movement, are likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 7.36 out of 10, high: hidden actors are deeply embedded (8.5) and checks are weak (3.8). Kyrgyzstan belongs to 'Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement', 'Churches and movements placing members in the state' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Kyrgyzstan.imp: For people in Kyrgyzstan, the case shows that citizenship did not protect a school director from being taken abroad by another government, and that border guards let it happen. Families using Sapat schools live with that risk. Watch whether the prosecution of the border officers leads anywhere and whether other teachers are targeted.

Laos.d: Nothing is documented for Laos on this map yet, and no organisation is recorded as present or likely present. This is a best guess. The conditions score is 7.06 out of 10, high: the ruling party and security services sit deep in every part of the state (7.5), and there are few independent courts, newspapers or civil groups to check them (3.4). In a one-party state like this, the most likely route in for outside networks is through foreign state-backed investment and the business deals that come with it, agreed directly with party leaders.
Laos.imp: For people in Laos, the lack of a documented case partly reflects how little can be reported freely. Large foreign-funded projects are agreed at the top with little public detail. Watch who signs infrastructure and land deals, and on what terms. People affected by those deals, such as families moved off their land, often learn the terms only afterwards.

Lebanon.d: Lebanon's government is trying to disarm an armed party that also sits in its cabinet. Hezbollah is a Shia party with an armed wing, aligned with Iran and listed as a terrorist group by at least 28 countries including the US and UK. It holds about 14 of 128 seats in parliament, and in the government formed by Prime Minister Nawaf Salam in February 2025 its picks run the health ministry and the labour ministry; with its ally Amal it controls six portfolios. On 7 August 2025 the cabinet agreed that only the state should hold weapons, and Hezbollah and Amal ministers walked out. On 5 September the army chief presented a plan to disarm all militias, which the cabinet welcomed without a timeline. Hezbollah's leader Naim Qassem rejected it, and in March 2026 Salam said its rocket and drone strikes were outside the state's authority. In July 2019 the US Treasury sanctioned two sitting Hezbollah MPs, Amin Sherri and Muhammad Raad, and the head of its unit that deals with Lebanon's security agencies; Raad is now the party's deputy leader. Other states reach in too. On 4 November 2017 Prime Minister Saad Hariri announced his resignation on television from Saudi Arabia; President Aoun said the Saudis were holding him, which Saudi Arabia denied. He withdrew the resignation on 5 December. In January 2026 the US listed al-Jamaa al-Islamiya, the Lebanese branch of the Muslim Brotherhood, as a terrorist organisation. The conditions score is 8.21 out of 10: armed and unelected actors are very deeply embedded (9.5) and checks are weak (3.1). Lebanon is where Iran's allies sit in the state in 'Iran's armed allies inside governments', a target in 'Governments buying officials in other countries', the headquarters of Hizb ut-Tahrir in 'Religious nationalism in power', and also belongs to 'Movements that sought the state itself' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Lebanon.imp: For people in Lebanon, a party with its own army helps run the ministries that provide health care and labour protection, while the state cannot control its weapons. Foreign governments, Iran on one side and Saudi Arabia and the US on another, press on the government from outside. Watch whether the army's disarmament plan gets a timeline.

Malaysia.d: Malaysia's largest case involves a state fund, a global bank and a former prime minister now serving a prison sentence. 1MDB was a Malaysian state investment fund. Goldman Sachs bankers Tim Leissner and Roger Ng arranged its bond deals together with the financier Jho Low, and US authorities say money was diverted and used to bribe officials in Malaysia and the UAE. Goldman settled with Malaysia in July 2020 for about $3.9 billion. Leissner pleaded guilty and Ng was convicted in New York in 2022. On 26 December 2025 Malaysia's High Court found Najib Razak, prime minister from 2009 to 2018, guilty on all 25 counts tied to over $1 billion that reached his personal accounts, and sentenced him to 15 years. He is appealing. The second case involves Turkey's campaign against the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network. In May 2017 Malaysian police arrested Turgay Karaman, Ihsan Aslan and academic Ismet Ozcelik under a security law that allows 28 days' detention without trial, and deported them to Turkey on 11 May. The police chief said Ankara had cancelled their travel documents, so they were treated as illegal immigrants; Human Rights Watch condemned it. Opus Dei has a recorded presence; Freemasonry's English grand lodge, Hizb ut-Tahrir and China's United Front are among those likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 5.64 out of 10. Malaysia belongs to 'Global firms buying governments', 'Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement', 'Churches and movements placing members in the state' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Malaysia.imp: For people in Malaysia, 1MDB meant public money borrowed in their name was diverted, with a major foreign bank arranging the deals. A court has now convicted the man who led the government. Separately, the 2017 deportations show security laws used to hand people to another government. Watch Najib's appeal and how detention-without-trial laws are used.

Mongolia.d: Mongolia's one documented case is an attempted abduction that was stopped on the airport runway. On 27 July 2018 Veysel Akcay was seized in Ulaanbaatar, the capital. He was general manager of the Empathy Worldwide Educational Institution, which ran Turkish-Mongolian schools linked to the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network the Turkish government blames for its 2016 coup attempt. Mongolian authorities temporarily grounded a plane at the airport, and he was released the same day. Turkish Minute and the Stockholm Center for Freedom reported that Turkey's intelligence service, MIT, carried out the abduction; Mongolian authorities said they had no specific knowledge of an abduction and were investigating. Chinese police 'overseas service stations', offices linked to Chinese police that are said to monitor Chinese citizens abroad, also have a recorded presence, and the Unification Church is likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 5.11 out of 10, middling. Mongolia is listed in 'Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement' and 'Churches and movements placing members in the state'.
Mongolia.imp: For people in Mongolia, the case shows foreign security services operating on its soil, and Mongolian officials stepping in to stop a removal. Public pressure that day mattered. Watch for further foreign police or intelligence activity, from Turkey or from China's overseas police offices. Teachers and staff of foreign-linked schools are the people most exposed.

Myanmar.d: Under Myanmar's military government, a Buddhist nationalist monk once on trial for sedition now holds one of the country's highest honours. The story runs through Ma Ba Tha, the Association for the Protection of Race and Religion, a Buddhist nationalist monks' group formed in 2014. In 2013–14 the Ministry of Religious Affairs, which oversees religious life, drafted four 'Race and Religion Protection Laws' based on texts proposed by its members. They cover religious conversion, marriage between Buddhist women and non-Buddhist men, monogamy and birth spacing. Parliament passed them in 2015. In May 2017 the state Buddhist clergy council ordered Ma Ba Tha disbanded, and officials said its renamed successor was also outlawed. In June 2019, after its members protested a sedition case the civilian government had brought against the monk Wirathu, army spokesman Brigadier General Zaw Min Tun gave 30 million kyats to the successor group, the Buddha Dhamma Parahita Foundation. Zaw Min Tun is now spokesman of the military government that took power in 2021. Wirathu, known for anti-Muslim sermons, saw his sedition charges dropped in September 2021, seven months after the coup, and in November 2022 he received the title Thiri Pyanchi. The Congress for Cultural Freedom, a Cold War cultural body later shown to be CIA-funded, and Chinese police 'overseas service stations' also have a recorded presence. The conditions score is 8.77 out of 10, among the highest: the military is embedded everywhere (9.0) and checks are almost absent (1.5). Myanmar belongs to 'Religious nationalism in power'.
Myanmar.imp: For people in Myanmar, especially Muslims and other religious minorities, laws drafted from a nationalist group's texts now govern whom they may marry and how they may convert. The army backed that group even after the clergy banned it, and has honoured its best-known monk. Watch how the race and religion laws are enforced.

Watch for politicians attending events run by these groups, and for campaigns over religion in the constitution.
