Pakistan.d: Pakistan's cases cover the army, the courts, the central bank and old religious families. The most recent concerns the State Bank of Pakistan, the central bank, which sets interest rates and manages the currency. On 4 May 2019, a day after the previous governor was abruptly removed and while Pakistan was negotiating a bailout from the International Monetary Fund (the lender that attaches policy conditions to its loans), the government appointed Reza Baqir, an IMF staff member who had led its missions to Romania and Bulgaria. He served until May 2022. In December 2018 the Supreme Court, under Chief Justice Saqib Nisar, ordered the government to ban the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network Turkey calls 'FETÖ', and to hand the Pak-Turk schools it ran to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation, saying Pakistan was bound by an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation declaration. Shah Mahmood Qureshi, foreign minister in 2008–11 and again in 2018–22, comes from a family that holds hereditary custody of the Shrine of Bahauddin Zakariya in Multan; such families draw income and votes from devotees. His brother accused him in 2014 of using the saints' names for politics, which he denied. In August 2012 a military court convicted Brigadier Ali Khan and four majors of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a banned party seeking a caliphate; the army said it tried to recruit officers for a coup. The conditions score is 6.77 out of 10. Pakistan belongs to 'Governments and industries inside international bodies', 'Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement', 'Churches and movements placing members in the state', 'Religious nationalism in power', 'Movements that sought the state itself' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Pakistan.imp: For people in Pakistan, the central bank governor who set their interest rates during an IMF bailout came straight from the lender's staff. Students at the Pak-Turk schools saw them handed to a foreign state body by court order. Watch who runs the central bank during future loan talks, and how shrine families and the army shape who holds office.

Philippines.d: The Philippines has just banned an industry that drew its officials into trafficking. POGOs were Chinese-run online gambling firms licensed from 2016 to serve players in China; Senate hearings in 2024 tied many to fraud, trafficking and torture. President Marcos announced a ban in July 2024, and Congress wrote it into law in October 2025. Alice Guo, elected mayor of Bamban in 2022, was linked to a POGO hub raided in her town; a court ruled she is a Chinese citizen, Guo Hua Ping, and on 20 November 2025 she was sentenced to life for human trafficking. A self-confessed Chinese spy says she is a Chinese intelligence asset; she denies it and that claim is untested. In May 2025 a court issued an arrest warrant for Harry Roque, President Duterte's former spokesman, over another hub; he denies the charge and has sought asylum in the Netherlands. In a separate case, Pharmally, a firm founded in 2019 with ₱625,000 in capital, won ₱8.68 billion in pandemic contracts; the anti-graft court issued an arrest warrant for the procurement chief in 2024. Churches are the other thread. Iglesia ni Cristo, a Philippine church of about 2.6 million members, votes as a bloc; in 2022 it backed Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Sara Duterte and 12 Senate candidates. Duterte made its head a presidential special envoy in 2018, and in June 2026 about 12,000 members rallied for Senator Rodante Marcoleta, a member facing a charge over undeclared campaign money. Eddie Villanueva, founder of Jesus Is Lord Church, was a deputy speaker of the House in 2019–22. Apollo Quiboloy, whom Duterte called his spiritual adviser, was indicted in the US for sex trafficking and arrested in 2024 on Philippine charges. The conditions score is 6.77 out of 10. The Philippines belongs to 'Scam compounds and casino money inside Asian states', 'Churches and movements placing members in the state', 'Global firms buying governments' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Philippines.imp: For people in the Philippines, these cases show a foreign gambling industry able to put a mayor in office and draw in a president's spokesman, and churches that deliver votes and expect protection in return. The Senate and courts exposed much of it. Watch how the POGO ban is enforced and whether church endorsements shape the Sara Duterte impeachment vote.

Qatar.d: Nothing is documented for Qatar on this map yet, so this is an estimate. Two organisations have a recorded presence: Fight Impunity, a Brussels-based NGO at the centre of the European Parliament bribery inquiry known as 'Qatargate', and Gulf state and private networks that fund Salafi religious missionary work abroad. The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement, and Interpol are likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 5.52 out of 10, middling: unelected actors are fairly embedded (6.5) and institutions are of medium strength (5.5). As a best guess, the main route runs outward: Qatar's state wealth reaching into other countries' politics, rather than outside networks reaching into Qatar's.
Qatar.imp: People in Qatar have no documented case on this map of a network steering their own government. The more likely story, as an estimate, is the state's money and religious funding reaching abroad. Inside Qatar, decisions rest with the ruling family, so little is visible. Watch where foreign funding inquiries lead.

Saudi Arabia.d: Saudi Arabia appears on this map mainly as a state that sends money and religion outward. It is home to the Muslim World League and to state and private networks that fund Salafi missionary work abroad, which places it as the sponsoring state in 'Governments that export religion'. At home, it listed the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement, as a terrorist organisation on 7 March 2014, a day after it, the UAE and Bahrain withdrew their ambassadors from Qatar; the listing named no Saudi officials. The older cases show how the kingdom's oil money and intelligence service tied into Western ones. In 1974, after the Arab oil embargo, the US and Saudi Arabia set up a Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation, co-chaired by the US Treasury Secretary and the Saudi finance minister. A 1979 US Government Accounting Office report found its US technical help was paid almost entirely from a Saudi account held in the US Treasury, recycled oil dollars, and steered US goods and services to the kingdom. John Perkins says his firm, Chas. T. Main, worked on Saudi projects then; that part is only his claim. Kamal Adham, head of Saudi intelligence from 1965 to 1979, signed the 1976 charter of the Safari Club, a secret alliance of the intelligence chiefs of France, Egypt, Morocco, Iran and Saudi Arabia against Soviet influence in Africa; a later Saudi intelligence chief confirmed it publicly in 2002. Adham was also a major shareholder of BCCI, a bank that collapsed in 1991 amid fraud; US prosecutors said he helped it secretly take over Washington's First American bank, and he paid a $105 million fine under a plea deal. NSO Group, the Israeli spyware firm, also has a recorded presence. The conditions score is 7.61 out of 10. Saudi Arabia belongs to 'The anticommunist web, 1945–1990', 'Banks that carried the hidden money', 'Lenders, aid programmes and trained technocrats', 'Movements that sought the state itself' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Saudi Arabia.imp: For people in Saudi Arabia, the record shows state money and the intelligence service working with foreign governments and banks out of public view, while decisions at home rest with the ruling family. Citizens had no say in the oil-money arrangements made in their name. Watch where religious funding goes abroad and how terrorist listings are used against political movements.

Singapore.d: Singapore is one of the few countries on this map that has written a law to name people at risk of being used by foreign governments. The Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act of 2021 lets the Home Affairs Ministry designate such people, who must then disclose donations and foreign links. On 26 February 2024 it listed its first: Philip Chan Man Ping, a Hong Kong-born businessman who led the Hong Kong Chamber of Commerce in Singapore and was a patron of two government-linked grassroots bodies. He had attended China's Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, part of the Communist Party's 'united front' system for winning over people outside the party, as an overseas delegate. The ministry said he had shown he could be cultivated by foreign actors. Earlier, on 4 August 2017, the ministry cancelled the permanent residence of Huang Jing, a US-citizen professor at the National University of Singapore's Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, and banned him and his wife from returning. It called him an agent of influence of a foreign country working with its intelligence agents to sway Singapore's foreign policy, without naming the country. Huang denied it. These were government decisions, not court verdicts. Opus Dei, the Shincheonji church and the Prince Group, a Cambodian conglomerate under US sanctions, also have a recorded presence. The conditions score is 1.85 out of 10, among the lowest: strong institutions (7.8) and few hidden actors in the state (1.5). Singapore is a target country in 'China's long arm abroad' and belongs to 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Singapore.imp: For people in Singapore, the government now publicly names people it believes foreign states are cultivating, which brings some influence into the open. The same power rests with a ministry rather than a court, and the evidence is not published. Watch who else is designated, and whether those named can challenge it.

Sri Lanka.d: In September 2026 Sri Lanka's Supreme Court voided a president's pardon of a Buddhist nationalist monk, and the monk is back in prison. Bodu Bala Sena (BBS, 'Buddhist Power Force') is a Sinhala Buddhist nationalist monks' group founded in 2012 and accused of stirring anti-Muslim violence. Its leader, Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara, told a 2013 rally that followers must become 'an unofficial civilian police force against Muslim extremism'. The group had friends at the top early. On 9 March 2013 Defence Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa, the president's brother, opened its training centre in Galle District as chief guest. In 2018 the Court of Appeal jailed Gnanasara for six years for contempt of court in the case over the disappearance of journalist Prageeth Eknaligoda; President Maithripala Sirisena pardoned him in May 2019. That year Gotabaya Rajapaksa became president, and on 26 October 2021 he appointed Gnanasara to chair a presidential task force on 'One Country, One Law', to draft proposals for a single legal code. The justice minister said he had not been consulted, and the Bar Association said it took over Parliament's work. Gnanasara was jailed again in 2024 and 2025 over statements about Islam. On 10 September 2026, on petitions from the Centre for Policy Alternatives and the journalist's wife, the Supreme Court ruled the 2019 pardon arbitrary and invalid. Separately, Ranil Wickremesinghe, several times prime minister and president from 2022 to 2024, is listed as a member of the Mont Pelerin Society, a private forum of free-market economists; no forum has found the society directed his decisions. The conditions score is 6.64 out of 10. Sri Lanka belongs to 'Religious nationalism in power' and 'Private forums where officials meet money'.
Sri Lanka.imp: For people in Sri Lanka, especially Muslims, a monk whose group was accused of stirring violence was pardoned and then asked to draft the country's legal code. The courts have since checked that. Watch whether pardon powers are limited and whether the 'One Country, One Law' proposals return. Ordinary citizens and a journalist's wife brought the petitions that reversed the pardon.

Syria.d: Nothing is documented for Syria on this map yet, so this is an estimate. Several armed and political groups have a recorded presence: the Muslim Brotherhood; Hizb ut-Tahrir, a party seeking a caliphate; the Grey Wolves, a Turkish ultranationalist movement; the Wagner Group, a Russian mercenary force; Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed party; and Iran's Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force with its allied militias. The conditions score is 9.00 out of 10, among the highest: armed and unelected actors are embedded throughout the state (10.0) and there is little to check them (2.0). As a best guess, the route in is not secret membership but foreign-backed armed groups taking a place inside the state's security forces, as in Iraq and Lebanon.
Syria.imp: For people in Syria, many foreign armed groups have operated on their soil, and few institutions can hold any of them to account. No case has been documented on this map. Watch which armed groups are folded into the new army and police, and which foreign governments pay for them.

Taiwan.d: Taiwan's courts are convicting people for carrying out China's influence work, with more cases in recent years than almost anywhere on this map. China's Communist Party runs a 'united front' system to win over or recruit people outside the party, including in Taiwan, which Beijing claims. Taiwan passed an Anti-Infiltration Act to make taking instructions or money from it in politics a crime. In June 2025 a Taipei court sentenced Chou Ke-chi, chairman of the small Gong He Party, to two years for taking money from Fujian to fund the party's 2022 local campaigns. In May 2025 Lin Hsueh-feng, a former Kuomintang (KMT) council candidate, got four years for taking village and ward chiefs on trips paid for by a Chinese city's Taiwan Affairs Office, where officials urged them to vote for a particular party. In September 2025 four former members of the governing Democratic Progressive Party, including an aide to the foreign minister and a Presidential Office consultant, were convicted of spying for Chinese military intelligence, passing on William Lai's travel schedules. In September 2026 the High Court jailed a retired cabinet official, Hu Peng-nien, for five years for trying to recruit military personnel. Other cases are at the charge stage: former lawmaker Chang Hsien-yao, indicted in February 2025 for working with Chinese officials on the 2024 election, and two people accused of funding a 2022 council candidate from Jiangsu. In 2018 prosecutors raided the Chinese Unity Promotion Party, founded by former Bamboo Union gang leader Chang An-le. Most of the verdicts can be appealed. Taiwan is also home to the World Anti-Communist League. Its conditions score of 3.00 is borrowed from South Korea because Taiwan is not scored by the source index. Taiwan is a target country in 'China's long arm abroad' and the headquarters in 'The anticommunist web, 1945–1990'.
Taiwan.imp: For people in Taiwan, the cases show influence reaching every level: village chiefs, small parties, council candidates and aides in the president's and foreign minister's offices, from more than one party. Courts have been able to act. Watch the appeals, and how trips and funding from China to local officials are reported.

Tajikistan.d: Tajikistan's one documented case is the closure of schools by order of the president. The schools belonged to the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network known for running schools abroad, which the Turkish government blames for its 2016 coup attempt and calls 'FETÖ'. A 1994 cabinet decision had let seven Gülen-linked Turkish schools operate in Tajikistan. They came under investigation in January 2015, and in May 2015 President Emomali Rahmon issued a decree overruling that decision and closing them from September 2015. The schools were transferred to the state and renamed as schools for gifted children. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, also has a recorded presence; Hizb ut-Tahrir, a party seeking a caliphate, and Interpol are likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 8.23 out of 10, high: power is concentrated in the state and those around it (9.0), and checks are very weak (2.5). Tajikistan belongs to 'Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement', as a country that closed schools, and to 'Churches and movements placing members in the state' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Tajikistan.imp: For people in Tajikistan, the case shows schools that families had chosen being taken over by a single presidential decree, with no court involved. Teachers and pupils had little say. Watch how other foreign-linked schools and religious groups are treated, and whether decisions like this are made in the open.

Thailand.d: Thailand's one documented case concerns the World Economic Forum, the organisation behind the annual Davos meeting of business and political leaders. Each year it picks people under about 40 for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Its class of 2025 included Paetongtarn Shinawatra while she was Thailand's prime minister. The Constitutional Court removed her from office in August 2025. Being named to the programme is not wrongdoing, and the record does not say the Forum shaped her decisions. Other organisations with a recorded presence are the Sovereign Military Order of Malta; the Unification Church, a Korean-founded church; and the World Anti-Communist League, a Cold War alliance of anti-communist groups. Nugan Hand Bank, an Australian bank with intelligence ties that collapsed in 1980, China's United Front, and the Asia Foundation are likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 6.02 out of 10: hidden actors are fairly embedded (7.0) and institutions are of medium strength (5.0). Thailand belongs to 'Private forums where officials meet money', where heads of government meet business leaders through such networks.
Thailand.imp: For people in Thailand, the case shows a sitting prime minister taking part in a private network that links political leaders to global business, outside public view. That is lawful, but voters cannot see what is discussed. Watch which officials join such programmes and whether their policies favour the firms they meet there.

Timor-Leste.d: Nothing is documented for Timor-Leste on this map yet, so this is an estimate. Two organisations have a recorded presence: the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status that runs aid work, and Aginter Press, a Cold War-era agency based in Portugal, the former colonial power. The conditions score is 5.31 out of 10, middling: unelected actors are moderately embedded (4.5) and institutions are on the weak side (3.9). As a best guess, the most likely route in for outside networks is through aid, the Catholic Church's strong place in public life, and larger neighbours' interest in the country's oil and gas.
Timor-Leste.imp: People in Timor-Leste have no documented case on this map. A young state with weak institutions depends heavily on outside aid and advisers, which can bring influence with it. Watch who advises ministries and who negotiates oil and gas deals. Those negotiations shape the money the state has to spend on everyone.

Turkiye.d: In Turkey, the state has spent the last decade removing people it says belong to one movement, and it pursues them abroad as well. The Gülen movement, which calls itself Hizmet ('service'), is a Turkish Islamic network led by the preacher Fethullah Gülen, known for schools and for placing followers in the police and courts; the government calls it 'FETÖ' and lists it as terrorist. The break came in December 2013, when Istanbul prosecutors opened a corruption investigation reaching Prime Minister Erdogan's inner circle; four ministers left office. The government called it a Gülenist plot, about 1,000 police were moved, the four lead prosecutors were sacked, and the case was dropped. After the failed coup of 15 July 2016, the purge widened: 2,745 judges, about 36% of the bench, were removed the next day; about 15,000 military personnel and roughly 23,000 police were dismissed; around 150,000 people lost public jobs by decree. Courts gave former air force commander Akin Ozturk multiple life terms in 2019, treating the coup as a Gülen operation; he denied it. The state religious directorate, the Diyanet, had its imams in 38 countries report on Gülen followers, and Interpol refused 773 Turkish arrest requests as political. Before that, prosecutors many now link to the movement had jailed hundreds in the 'Sledgehammer' and 'Ergenekon' coup-plot trials, including a former army chief and three opposition MPs. Those cases collapsed: Sledgehammer evidence was found forged, and in 2016 the appeals court found no evidence Ergenekon existed. The older roots lie with nationalist networks. Alparslan Turkes, whose party's youth wing is the Grey Wolves, an ultranationalist movement, was deputy prime minister in the 1970s, when NATO's secret 'stay-behind' unit, the Counter-Guerrilla, sat inside the army. In 1996 a car crash at Susurluk killed a police chief and a Grey Wolves fugitive in the same car as an MP; a parliamentary inquiry found state bodies had used the Grey Wolves. The conditions score is 7.52 out of 10. Turkey is the sponsoring state in 'Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement' and 'Governments that export religion', and belongs to 'The anticommunist web, 1945–1990', 'Governments and industries inside international bodies', 'Churches and movements placing members in the state' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Turkiye.imp: For people in Turkey, these cases show each network that gained a foothold in the courts or police being used against rivals, then purged, with ordinary officials losing their jobs on the strength of alleged links. Some convictions were later found to rest on forged evidence. Watch how 'membership' is proven in court and how many dismissed officials win their cases.

Turkmenistan.d: Turkmenistan's documented case is about schools closed and men jailed after closed trials. The Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network known for its schools abroad, opened schools in Turkmenistan in the 1990s. In 2011 the government closed or nationalised most of them. In late 2016 more than 100 people, most with some link to the movement, were detained. According to a joint statement by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and the Norwegian Helsinki Committee, 18 men were then convicted in closed trials and given 12 to 25 years for inciting hatred and involvement in a criminal organisation. Because the trials were closed, the evidence against them has not been made public. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, also has a recorded presence. The conditions score is 8.41 out of 10, among the highest: power is held tightly within the state (9.0) and there is almost nothing to check it (2.2). Turkmenistan belongs to 'Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement', as a country that closed schools, and to 'Churches and movements placing members in the state'.
Turkmenistan.imp: For people in Turkmenistan, the case shows people jailed for long terms after trials no one outside could watch, for links to a school network. With no free press or independent courts, citizens cannot test the charges. Watch for further arrests of people linked to foreign schools or religious groups.

United Arab Emirates.d: The United Arab Emirates has used its money and police to gain a place at the top of Interpol, the international police body whose 'Red Notices' ask police worldwide to arrest someone. Through a foundation set up in 2013, the UAE gave Interpol about $54 million, reported to equal the regular contributions of the other 194 member countries combined. Critics, including a report by former UK chief prosecutor David Calvert-Smith, said the money helped it host the 2018 General Assembly and win the 2021 presidency; Interpol rejected that. On 25 November 2021 Major General Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi, inspector general of the UAE Interior Ministry, was elected Interpol president, serving until November 2025. Two Britons, Matthew Hedges and Ali Issa Ahmad, say he was responsible for their torture in UAE custody, and complaints also cite the activist Ahmed Mansoor. In March 2022 French anti-terrorism prosecutors opened a preliminary inquiry; the UAE denies the accusations. At home, the government treats the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement, as a threat. In July 2013 the Federal Supreme Court jailed 56 Emiratis, many from the Islah group, for plotting to take power by infiltrating schools, universities and ministries, and acquitted 26; Islah denies ties to the Brotherhood. In November 2014 the cabinet listed both as terrorist. The oldest case: by July 1991 Abu Dhabi's government and ruling family owned 77% of BCCI, a bank closed that year for fraud, and a US Senate inquiry found Abu Dhabi had hidden what it knew from auditors. The UAE is also home to Privinvest, a shipbuilding group. The conditions score is 5.69 out of 10. It belongs to 'Governments and industries inside international bodies', 'Banks that carried the hidden money', 'Global firms buying governments', 'Movements that sought the state itself' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
United Arab Emirates.imp: For people in the UAE, and for those who have been held there, the case shows an official accused of overseeing torture leading the world's police network after large donations from his government. At home, people tied to a banned movement were jailed for seeking influence in schools and ministries. Watch the French inquiry and how Interpol handles Emirati requests.

Uzbekistan.d: Nothing is documented for Uzbekistan on this map yet, so this is an estimate. One organisation has a recorded presence: Chinese police 'overseas service stations', offices linked to Chinese police that are said to monitor Chinese citizens abroad. Three are likely present but undocumented: the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network known for schools; Hizb ut-Tahrir, a party seeking a caliphate; and the Grey Wolves, a Turkish ultranationalist movement. The conditions score is 6.58 out of 10, fairly high: unelected actors are well embedded (7.0) and checks are weak (3.8). As a best guess, the most likely routes in are Turkish networks through schools and religious groups, and Chinese security networks through business and diaspora ties.
Uzbekistan.imp: People in Uzbekistan have no documented case on this map. Neighbouring countries have closed Gülen schools and jailed people for movement links, and Uzbekistan's government has long cracked down on religious groups. Watch for foreign police activity and how membership in banned groups is defined and prosecuted. Ordinary believers and students are the ones most exposed when such definitions are loose.

Vietnam.d: Vietnam's one documented case is the government labelling an exile political party as terrorist. Viet Tan, the Vietnam Reform Party, is a pro-democracy party founded by Vietnamese exiles in 1982 and based in the United States. On 4 October 2016 Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security, the police and security ministry, designated it a terrorist organisation, saying it trained people to enter Vietnam and plotted sabotage. Human rights groups and foreign governments dispute this, and the US government has said there is no evidence that Viet Tan is a terrorist group. Vietnamese courts have jailed people accused of being members. This is the Vietnamese government's designation, not the finding of an independent forum. Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life, also has a recorded presence. The conditions score is 6.11 out of 10: the ruling party is well embedded in every part of the state (7.0) and institutions are of middling strength (4.8). Vietnam belongs to 'Exposure, purge and reversal', as a government that banned an organisation.
Vietnam.imp: For people in Vietnam, the case shows that a terrorism label can be used against a political party that operates abroad, and that people at home can be jailed for being accused of membership. There is no independent court to test the label. Watch who is prosecuted under it and on what evidence.

Yemen.d: Yemen's documented case shows a foreign government placing an ally at the top of the state, and losing it. The Southern Transitional Council (STC) was formed in May 2017 with help from the United Arab Emirates to seek a separate state in Yemen's south. In April 2022 it joined the eight-member Presidential Leadership Council that leads Yemen's internationally recognised government, and its leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, became a vice-president. After an STC offensive in December 2025 and a Saudi-backed counter-offensive, al-Zubaidi fled to the UAE in January 2026 and was removed from the council. A delegation in Riyadh, the Saudi capital, announced the STC's dissolution; its UAE-based spokesman rejected that. The Muslim Brotherhood, Hezbollah, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force with its allied militias also have a recorded presence. The conditions score is 8.04 out of 10: armed and unelected actors are deeply embedded (8.0) and there is almost nothing to check them (1.9). Yemen is a target country in 'Governments buying officials in other countries'.
Yemen.imp: For people in Yemen, the case shows rival foreign governments, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, deciding through their allies who sits in the country's leadership. Iran backs other armed groups. Ordinary Yemenis have no vote in any of it. Watch who replaces al-Zubaidi on the council and whether the STC's dissolution holds.

Australia.d: Australia now has laws against foreign interference, and in December 2023 a jury returned the first conviction under them. Di Sanh Duong, a Melbourne community leader, was found guilty of preparing a foreign interference offence. Prosecutors said he used his roles in Chinese community groups to get close to Alan Tudge, then acting immigration minister, while hiding links to the Chinese Communist Party's United Front Work Department, which works to win over people outside the party, and to China's Ministry of State Security. He was sentenced to 2 years 9 months. Earlier cases centre on one donor, Huang Xiangmo, a property developer who chaired a council for 'peaceful reunification' of China described as a peak body for United Front-linked groups. With associates he gave about AU$2 million to Labor and over AU$1 million to the Liberal Party. Labor senator Sam Dastyari let a Huang-linked company pay his legal bills, backed China's position on its borders against party policy, and reportedly warned Huang his phone was probably tapped; he resigned in early 2018. In February 2019 the government cancelled Huang's residency on advice from ASIO, the domestic intelligence agency. In 2022 the New South Wales anti-corruption commission found that $100,000 in cash delivered to NSW Labor in 2015 came from Huang, disguised as donations from restaurant staff. A separate case shows private consultants inside government. In 2013 the Treasury hired a partner at PwC, one of the 'Big Four' accounting firms, to advise on laws against multinational tax avoidance; he shared confidential plans with at least 53 PwC partners. A Senate committee found PwC covered it up; its chief executive left and its government arm was sold for $1. Police raided PwC in 2024; no charges have been reported. The Sydney-based Nugan Hand Bank, which collapsed in 1980, and the Round Table, a British imperial network, are background. The conditions score is low at 2.23 out of 10. Australia belongs to 'China's long arm abroad', 'Consultants and lobbyists inside the ministries', 'Private forums where officials meet money', 'Rhodes, Milner and the Round Table network', 'Banks that carried the hidden money' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Australia.imp: For people in Australia, these cases show foreign influence working through political donations, community groups and access to ministers, and a private firm using inside knowledge of tax law to help its clients. Courts, ASIO and anti-corruption bodies brought these out. Watch whether the PwC police inquiry leads to charges and how donations from people with foreign-government ties are policed.

Fiji.d: Fiji has asked China to withdraw police officers who worked inside its national force, but it is keeping the agreement that put them there. In 2011, during military rule, Fiji signed a police cooperation agreement with China. From 2013 China's Ministry of Public Security attached two officers at a time to the Fiji Police Force, and in 2021 it posted a police liaison officer to its embassy. In 2017 Chinese police, working with local officials, arrested 77 Chinese nationals in Fiji and flew them to China. In March 2024 Home Affairs Minister Pio Tikoduadua said Fiji had asked China to withdraw its embedded officers but would keep the agreement, reviewing it every six months. Fijian officers continue to train in China. The Shincheonji Church of Jesus, a Korean sect, also has a recorded presence; India's RSS, a Hindu nationalist organisation, is likely present but not documented. The conditions score is 4.31 out of 10, middling. Fiji is a target country in the pattern 'China's long arm abroad'.
Fiji.imp: For people in Fiji, the case shows a foreign police force working from inside their own, and carrying out mass arrests and removals on Fijian soil. The officers are gone but the agreement stays. Watch what the six-monthly reviews decide and what Fijian officers bring back from training in China.

Kiribati.d: In Kiribati, uniformed Chinese police officers work alongside the local police today. Kiribati switched its diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 2019 and asked China for help with policing in 2022. In 2024 the acting police commissioner, Eeri Aritiera, confirmed to Reuters that up to a dozen uniformed Chinese police officers work with local police on six-month rotations. They do community policing, give martial-arts training and provide IT support for a crime database. The arrangement was made openly between the two governments and is acknowledged by Kiribati's police. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, also has a recorded presence. The conditions score is 3.52 out of 10, on the lower side: few hidden actors in the state (1.5) and middling institutions (4.5). Kiribati is a target country in the pattern 'China's long arm abroad', alongside Fiji, the Solomon Islands and Vanuatu.
Kiribati.imp: For people in Kiribati, foreign police are now part of everyday policing, including the database that records crimes. The arrangement is public, but how information is shared, and with whom, is not. Watch what happens to that crime data and whether the rotations become permanent. Kiribati's own police have confirmed the arrangement, so it can be asked about in public.

Marshall Islands.d: Nothing is documented for the Marshall Islands on this map yet, so this is an estimate. Marshall Islands.imp: People in the Marshall Islands have no documented case on this map. In a small country, a few people's decisions can change national policy.

Watch for policing or security deals and for funds given directly to members of Congress. Watch who funds government programmes and any shift in diplomatic ties. Because so few people hold office, ordinary residents can more easily ask their MP directly about such offers.

New Zealand.d: New Zealand's cases are mostly about private networks whose members have reached high office, and two MPs who left parliament over China concerns. David Seymour, Deputy Prime Minister since 2025 and Minister for Regulation since 2023, worked in the 2000s for Canadian think tanks including the Frontier Centre for Public Policy, a partner of the Atlas Network, a US-based group linking free-market think tanks worldwide. Atlas's chair, Debbi Gibbs, is the daughter of a co-founder of his ACT party. Ruth Richardson, finance minister from 1990 to 1993, is listed as a member of the Mont Pelerin Society, a private forum of free-market economists, and sat on its board in 2018–20. Jacinda Ardern, prime minister from 2017 to 2023, is listed by the German Bundestag's research service as a participant in the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme. In each case, membership is documented but no forum has found that the network directed government decisions. The China case: Jian Yang, a National Party MP from 2011 to 2020, had been a Communist Party member and taught at Chinese military institutions that trained intelligence linguists. Media reported in 2021 that he retired after intelligence agencies raised concerns, and that Ardern and opposition leader Todd Muller agreed Labour MP Raymond Huo would leave for the same reason. At a livestreamed budget hearing in August 2022, the prime minister's secretary said China had provided SBD20.9 million (about US$2.49 million) spent in 2021, and that 39 of the 50 MPs were paid in two tranches, on 22 November and 13 December. Sogavare survived a no-confidence vote that December. Wale accused him of using the money to stay in power; his office denied it. China sent its first police advisers in February 2022 and signed a security agreement letting Honiara ask for Chinese police and military personnel. In 2025 Chinese police began a local trial of the 'Fengqiao' model of community surveillance policing, suspended after local objections. The conditions score is 6.39 out of 10: hidden actors are well embedded (7.5) and checks are weak (4.7). The Solomon Islands is a target country in 'China's long arm abroad'.

Austria.d:
Austria's most recent cases run through Moscow. On 19 December 2016 the leaders of the Freedom Party (FPÖ) signed a cooperation pact with United Russia, Vladimir Putin's ruling party. FPÖ ministers then sat in government from 2017 to 2019. The pact lapsed at the end of 2021 when party leader Herbert Kickl chose not to renew it. Karin Kneissl, foreign minister from 2017 to 2019 on the FPÖ's nomination, had Putin at her wedding in 2018. In 2021 the Russian government put her on the board of Rosneft, Russia's state oil company; she resigned in 2022 and now lives in Russia, working at St Petersburg State University.

The roots go back to the early Cold War. In 1951 trade unionist Franz Olah set up a secret anti-communist force disguised as a hiking and social club, the OeWSGV, funded through front companies. It ran until 1964. Olah became Interior Minister, the minister in charge of the police, in 1963 and resigned in 1964 over misuse of union funds. In 1996 Austrians learned the US had hidden more than 80 weapons caches on their soil without telling the government.

Turkey's reach is the third thread. Austria's 2015 Islam law bans foreign funding of religious bodies. In 2018 the government moved to close one Turkish mosque, dissolve a body running six others, and review the permits of about 40 imams employed by ATIB, the Austrian branch of Turkey's state religious authority, the Diyanet. Since 2019 the salute of the Grey Wolves, a Turkish nationalist youth movement, is banned. A 2020 police operation against suspected Muslim Brotherhood networks, Operation Luxor, searched about 60 addresses; a court ruled the searches unlawful in 2021. Former chancellor Sebastian Kurz is listed as a WEF Young Global Leaders alumnus, a selection rather than a finding of influence. Austria appears mostly as a target country, in seven patterns including Russia's networks, Turkey's long arm and the anticommunist web.
Austria.imp: For people in Austria, the clearest lesson is that a governing party can sign an agreement with a foreign ruling party, and a former foreign minister can join a foreign state company's board, all openly and within the law. Voters see these ties only when parties disclose them. Watch who takes jobs with foreign state companies after leaving office, how the ban on foreign funding of religious bodies is enforced, and whether courts keep checking police raids, as they did with Operation Luxor.

Belgium.d:
Brussels is home to the European Union's institutions, so much of what happens in Belgium touches all of Europe. Two bribery cases inside the European Parliament are open now. The first, called Qatargate, began on 9 December 2022, when Belgian police seized about €1.5 million in cash and arrested Greek MEP Eva Kaili, one of Parliament's 14 vice-presidents. Prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid to influence Parliament, with money passing through Fight Impunity, a Brussels human-rights NGO run by former Italian MEP Pier Antonio Panzeri. Panzeri took a plea deal in 2023; Kaili and the others deny the charges, and in February 2026 the Brussels Court of Appeal ruled the case can go ahead. The second involves Huawei, the Chinese telecoms firm. Prosecutors allege MEPs were paid to sign a 2021 letter against limits on foreign 5G equipment. Eight people have been charged, and in June 2026 Parliament lifted the immunity of Italian MEP Fulvio Martusciello, who denies wrongdoing.

Foreign states also reach in through religion. Saudi Arabia ran the Great Mosque of Brussels under a rent-free lease from 1967 until the government ended it in 2018. In 2020 the Justice Minister refused the new management state recognition after State Security found members tied to Moroccan intelligence and one employed by Turkey's Diyanet. In 2023 newspapers reported that former Flemish senator Frank Creyelman took money from a Chinese intelligence officer; a gap in Belgian law prevented prosecution.

At the top of the EU, Health Commissioner John Dalli was made to leave in 2012 after an associate asked snus maker Swedish Match for €60 million. Former Commission president José Manuel Barroso became Goldman Sachs International's chairman in 2016, which an ethics committee cleared. In 2025 the EU court annulled the Commission's refusal to release Ursula von der Leyen's texts with Pfizer's CEO. Five commissioners and NATO chief Mark Rutte are on the 2025 list for Bilderberg, a private conference with no public record.

The Cold War roots came out in a 1991 Senate inquiry into Belgium's secret stay-behind network, funded through secret NATO payments. Belgium sits in the patterns on foreign money in Europe's parliaments, China's and Turkey's reach, lobbyists in ministries, private forums, the anticommunist web, and exposure and reversal.
Belgium.imp: For people in Belgium, and everyone the EU governs, the lesson is that money from foreign governments and companies can reach lawmakers through charities, gifts and travel, and is usually found only when police search offices. Belgian law has gaps: a former senator reported to have been paid by Chinese intelligence could not be charged. Czech Republic.d:

Estonia.d:
Estonia is cutting the Moscow ties of its Orthodox church. The Estonian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate has about 150,000 faithful. In January 2024 the state refused to renew the residence permit of its head, Metropolitan Eugene, calling his support for Russia's war a security risk; he left on 6 February 2024. In May 2024 the parliament, the Riigikogu, declared the Moscow Patriarchate an institution that supports Russian military aggression, and in 2025 it tightened the churches law to cut foreign control.

Money is the second story. In September 2017 the OCCRP reporting network and partner newspapers published 16,000 leaked transactions showing about $2.9 billion moved in 2012–2014 through four UK shell companies with accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch. Almost half came from an Aliyev-linked account at the International Bank of Azerbaijan. Recipients included Bundestag member Karin Strenz and Slovenian MP Zmago Jelinčič, and payments reached people who defended Azerbaijan in PACE, the Council of Europe's assembly of MPs.

Top office-holders also sit in private forums. Kaja Kallas was on the official 2024 list for Bilderberg, a private yearly conference with no public record, while prime minister; weeks later EU leaders nominated her as the EU's foreign policy chief, a post she has held since December 2024. Economy minister Erkki Keldo is in the WEF's Young Global Leaders class of 2025. Estonia appears in the patterns on Russia's networks, foreign money in Europe's parliaments, exported religion, private forums, and governments purging networks. Its conditions scores are strong: embedded actors 2.0 out of 10, resilience 8.0.
Estonia.imp: For Estonians, the main pressure comes from Moscow through a church with about 150,000 faithful whose head the state has now expelled. Finland.d:
Finland's present-day entries are about private forums. President Alexander Stubb, in office since 1 March 2024, lists membership of the WEF's Young Global Leader Network (2009) on his official CV. The larger case is older. After the Moscow Armistice of 19 September 1944, Colonel Valo Nihtilä and Lieutenant Colonel Usko Haahti of the operational department of Finnish Military Headquarters began hiding weapons across the country, planned for 8,000 men but estimated to equip about 35,000. Between 5,000 and 10,000 people took part. The scheme was exposed in spring 1945 to the Allied Control Commission. The security police questioned more than 5,000 people, and under a retroactive law of January 1947, 1,488 were convicted, most receiving one to four months in prison.

Finland appears in the patterns on private forums and the anticommunist web. Its conditions scores are among the strongest on the map: embedded actors 1.5 out of 10, resilience 8.4.

France.d:
Several French cases are still running. Since 2022 the National Financial Prosecutor has investigated McKinsey, the US consulting firm, after a Senate inquiry found the state's use of consultants since 2017 'sprawling and opaque'; on 4 September 2026 French and Belgian prosecutors announced a €65 million seizure. The Grey Wolves, youth movement of a nationalist party in Turkey's governing alliance, have been banned in France since November 2020. A May 2025 government report called the Muslim Brotherhood a threat to national cohesion working at municipal level, while finding no sign that Muslims in France want an Islamic state; the federation it named rejects the findings. In 2014 Marine Le Pen confirmed her party took a €9 million loan from a Moscow bank; she says it was private money. The Uber Files, leaked in 2022, suggest that Emmanuel Macron as economy minister helped Uber against cabinet opponents; he said he was proud to support the company.

Freemasonry runs through French government. From 1901 to 1904 the War Minister used reports from Grand Orient de France lodges, 18,818 files out of about 27,000 officers, to block Catholic officers from promotion; the exposure brought down the government in 1905. Manuel Valls, later prime minister, was a Grand Orient member from 1989 to 2005, according to L'Express. In May 2025 Macron made the first presidential visit to the Grande Loge de France; he is not documented as a member.

The Cold War left more. Le Cercle, a private network, was founded here in 1952–53 by former prime minister Antoine Pinay with Konrad Adenauer and Franz Josef Strauss. The CIA funded the Paris-run Congress for Cultural Freedom, with offices in 35 countries, for more than ten years. Generals formed the OAS, a secret army, after a failed 1961 putsch. The Gaullist SAC militia, founded by de Gaulle's Africa adviser Jacques Foccart, was dissolved in 1982 after its members murdered a police inspector and his family.

Courts upheld Scientology's fraud conviction in 2012, and a 2018 inquiry found members of the Council of Europe's assembly working for Azerbaijan. France hosts Interpol and is the lodge side of the pattern on French lodges and African presidencies.
France.imp: For people in France, the cases show three routes into the state: consultants shaping policy inside ministries, foreign money reaching parties through loans and lobbying, and private networks of lodges, forums and militias linking people in office. Most came to light through Senate inquiries, leaks and trials rather than routine disclosure. Watch the McKinsey investigation, who lends money to parties, and how the government uses its power to dissolve groups, applied to the SAC in 1982 and the Grey Wolves in 2020.

Germany.d:
Several German cases are before the courts now. Since 2024, 26 people around Heinrich XIII Prinz Reuss, a 'Reichsbürger' group that denies the legitimacy of the Federal Republic, have been on trial over a plan to storm the Reichstag. Among them is Birgit Malsack-Winkemann, a Berlin judge and former AfD Bundestag member whom prosecutors say was to be justice minister; no verdict had been reported as of April 2026. Munich prosecutors are investigating AfD politician Petr Bystroň over suspected cash from Voice of Europe, a Russian-funded network; he denies it and has not been charged. In September 2025 Jian Guo, an aide to AfD MEP Maximilian Krah, was jailed for 4 years 9 months for spying for China's Ministry of State Security. In 2021 the Bundestag lifted the immunity of two CDU MPs, Karin Strenz and Axel Fischer, over money from Azerbaijan. Former chancellor Gerhard Schröder chaired the board of Rosneft, Russia's state oil company, until 2022; that year the Bundestag closed his ex-chancellor's office.

Foreign states' religious bodies are another thread. DITIB runs about 900 mosques with imams paid as Turkish civil servants; a 2017 inquiry into imams spying on Gülen supporters was dropped for lack of evidence. In 2024 Germany banned the Islamic Centre Hamburg, seen as aligned with Iran's government. Domestic intelligence has watched Scientology since 1997, and in 2020 put Uniter, a network founded by a former special-forces soldier, under surveillance.

Private forums reach the top. Ludwig Erhard joined the free-market Mont Pelerin Society in 1950 as economics minister. Angela Merkel and Annalena Baerbock are listed in WEF leadership programmes. The 2025 Bilderberg list names economy minister Katherina Reiche and Bundestag President Julia Klöckner; the 2024 list named Friedrich Merz.

The roots run deep. Historian Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke states that Rudolf Hess and Hans Frank belonged to the Thule Society, a Munich group formed in 1918, before rising in the Nazi Party, and calls lists including Hitler spurious. Radio Free Europe broadcast from Munich on CIA money until 1971–72. In 1991 the government confirmed it had ordered the BND's stay-behind network dissolved. Germany appears in patterns on China's and Russia's reach, foreign money in parliaments, Turkey's long arm, private forums and the anticommunist web.
Germany.imp: For people in Germany, the cases show foreign states reaching into parliament through cash, aides and party ties, and conspiratorial networks forming among soldiers, police and even a judge. Most were found by prosecutors and intelligence services and are still before the courts, so guilt is settled in only some. Watch the Reuss trials, the Bystroň inquiry, which former leaders take foreign state jobs, and which ministers sit in private forums.

Greece.d:
Greece's present-day entry is a single meeting: Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, in office since 2019, is on the official list for the June 2025 Bilderberg meeting in Stockholm, a private conference with no public record. The deeper story is how a secret society of army officers took the state. IDEA, the Holy Bond of Greek Officers, was formed in 1945 by officers who had served in the collaborationist Security Battalions; its 1952 manifesto called dictatorship the only solution for Greece. Several leaders of the 21 April 1967 coup, including Georgios Papadopoulos, were members, and IDEA members took key posts. During the coup the LOK special forces, part of NATO's stay-behind network after 1952, took over the Defence Ministry. The colonels ruled until 1974. In 1975 Papadopoulos, Stylianos Pattakos and Nikolaos Makarezos were sentenced to death for high treason, commuted to life. In 1990 the defence minister confirmed that a stay-behind branch, Operation Sheepskin, had operated until 1988.

A later story concerns the police. After the May 2012 election, polling stations used by Attica police officers showed just over 20% for the far-right Golden Dawn, against about 6% at civilian stations nearby, and in 2013 a Council of Europe commissioner said he had strong evidence of ties between police and the party. In 2020 an Athens court found its leaders guilty of running a criminal organisation 'dressed in the mantle of a political party', in a trial that included the 2013 murder of rapper Pavlos Fyssas; in March 2026 an appeal court upheld 42 convictions. Greece appears in the patterns on sworn brotherhoods, the anticommunist web and private forums. Its conditions scores are weak: embedded actors 7.5 out of 10, resilience 5.1.
Greece.imp: For Greeks, the record shows how far this can go: a sworn society of officers prepared a coup and ran the country for seven years, and decades later a party convicted as a criminal organisation drew strong support inside the police. Both ended through the courts. Loyalty networks inside the army and police are what ordinary people cannot easily see. Watch police links to extremist groups and which leaders attend private forums.

Hungary.d:
Hungary lets Chinese police officers patrol alongside its own. In mid-February 2024 Interior Minister Sándor Pintér and China's Minister of Public Security reached an agreement that lets Chinese officers join Hungarian police in tourist areas and at large events. The ministry denies that Chinese 'police stations' exist in Hungary, though the human-rights group Safeguard Defenders listed two in Budapest, in the Józsefváros and Kőbánya districts. Safeguard Defenders describes such stations as being used to pressure people wanted by China to return.

The second case involves Russia. Béla Kovács sat in the European Parliament for Jobbik, a Hungarian nationalist party. Prosecutors accused him of spying on EU institutions for Russia, and Parliament lifted his immunity on 14 October 2015. In September 2022 Hungary's top court, the Curia, sentenced him in absentia to five years in prison for espionage; he lives in Russia.

Other bodies with a recorded presence include Opus Dei, the Order of Malta, the Legion of Christ, the Trilateral Commission and the Mont Pelerin Society; Scientology, Ordo Iuris and the Medvedchuk network are likely present. Hungary appears as a target country in the patterns on China's long arm, Russia's networks, governments buying officials abroad and foreign money in Europe's parliaments. Its conditions scores are weak: embedded actors 7.5 out of 10, resilience 4.8.
Hungary.imp: For Hungarians, the patrol agreement puts foreign police on Hungarian streets under a deal between two governments, and the public cannot see what those officers do or whom they speak to. The Kovács case shows a sitting MEP could be accused of spying for a foreign state and leave for that state before a court ruled. Watch the terms of police deals with foreign states and who oversees them.

Iceland.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Iceland yet, so this is an estimate. The Mont Pelerin Society, an international society of free-market economists, has a recorded presence. NATO's Cold War stay-behind network, the secret structure built across member states to resist an occupation, is marked as likely but undocumented. Iceland's conditions scores are among the strongest on the map: embedded actors 1.0 out of 10, resilience 8.2. The best guess is that any past route in ran through the stay-behind network, and that the risk today is low.
Iceland.imp: For Icelanders, the map shows no documented case and strong defences. The open question is historical: whether a stay-behind network existed here and who was in it. Watch for any release of Cold War defence or NATO records, which is how such networks came to light in several other European countries.

Ireland.d:
Ireland's present-day links are to the World Economic Forum. Simon Harris, a former Taoiseach (prime minister), was in the WEF's Young Global Leaders class of 2025 while Tánaiste (deputy prime minister), foreign minister and defence minister. Leo Varadkar was named to the 2018 class while Taoiseach, and was on the official Bilderberg list in 2024, weeks after stepping down. In October 2022 the foreign ministry ordered a Chinese 'overseas service station' on Capel Street, Dublin, run for the Fuzhou city police, to close; the group Safeguard Defenders reported that such stations are used to pressure people wanted by China to return.

The older story is a Catholic brotherhood. The Knights of Saint Columbanus, an Irish Catholic order of laymen, had members at the top of government. In 1948 Taoiseach John A. Costello was a member, and with other cabinet members who were Knights his government gave Maynooth seminary a special annual grant. Labour TD William Davin, also a Knight, is reported to have countered support in government for the Mother and Child health scheme, which Archbishop John Charles McQuaid opposed. Justice Minister Seán MacEoin reportedly assured the Order's Supreme Council that efforts would be made to prevent conflict between Church and State. Members also sat in the civil service, including Dublin's chief planner and the Taxing Master of the Courts. These accounts rest chiefly on biographies by John Cooney (1999) and Anthony Jordan (2007).

Ireland appears in the patterns on sworn brotherhoods, private forums, China's long arm, and governments shutting such operations. Its conditions scores are moderate: embedded actors 4.0 out of 10, resilience 7.4.
Ireland.imp: For people in Ireland, the Knights case shows how a members-only religious brotherhood could count a Taoiseach, ministers and senior civil servants among its members, with the public learning of it decades later through biographies. Today's links are more open: WEF selections are announced, and the Dublin station was closed once it was reported. Watch which office-holders join private networks, and whether foreign police operate here without permission.

Italy.d:
Italy has the longest record on this map, 51 cases, and parts of it are still in the courts. In 2025 Italy's top court made final a life sentence for Paolo Bellini over the 2 August 1980 Bologna station bombing, which killed 85 people; the appeal judges called Licio Gelli, head of the P2 lodge, 'the knowing financier of the massacre'. Gelli died in 2015, never tried for it. The Lega's 2017 cooperation pact with Putin's United Russia was, Il Foglio reported, tacitly renewed to 2027; its leader Matteo Salvini is deputy prime minister. Qu Dongyu, a former Chinese vice-minister, heads the Rome-based UN food agency, the FAO.

P2 (Propaganda Due) is the centre of the story. On 17 March 1981 finance police searching Gelli's factory found a list of 962 names: 44 members of parliament, ministers, 195 military officers and the heads of all three intelligence services. Prime Minister Arnaldo Forlani's government fell that May. A parliamentary commission led by Tina Anselmi called P2 criminal and subversive, and a 1982 law dissolved it and banned secret associations that seek to interfere with public bodies. Banco Ambrosiano, chaired by P2 member Roberto Calvi, collapsed in 1982 with a $1.3 billion hole tied to the Vatican Bank; Calvi was found hanged under a London bridge. Silvio Berlusconi, later prime minister three times, was on the list; a court found in 1990 that he had testified falsely about it, but an amnesty had extinguished the offence. Courts acquitted Gelli and others of conspiracy against the state.

Gladio, NATO's secret stay-behind network, overlapped with this. Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti disclosed it in 1990, and military intelligence put its membership at 622.

Lodges still come up. In 2017 the Anti-Mafia Commission found 193 lodge members in organised-crime proceedings; the European Court of Human Rights later ruled its seizure of lodge lists a privacy breach. The P3 case brought convictions in 2018 under the 1982 law. Roberto Formigoni, political voice of the Catholic movement Communion and Liberation, governed Lombardy from 1995 to 2013 and was convicted of corruption in 2019, a ruling about bribes, not the movement. Italy is the centre of the patterns on lodges in police and courts, the anticommunist web and banks that carried hidden money.
Italy.imp: For Italians, the record shows a secret lodge that counted ministers, generals and every intelligence chief as members, and courts that took more than four decades to reach findings on the Bologna bombing. A law now bans secret associations that try to influence public bodies, and prosecutors still use it. Who belongs to which lodge stays hidden; even a parliamentary seizure of lists was ruled a privacy breach. Watch party pacts with foreign ruling parties and lodge links in mafia cases.

Latvia.d: Latvia's Orthodox Church is now, by law, independent of Moscow, and the state must be told whenever it appoints a bishop. That is a recent change. Until 2022 the Latvian Orthodox Church was a self-governing part of the Russian Orthodox Church, the church led by the Patriarch in Moscow. On 9 September 2022, on a bill tabled by President Egils Levits, the Saeima, Latvia's parliament, amended the law so that the church answers to no church authority outside Latvia, and required that the President's chancery be told of its bishops' appointments. As of mid-2026 no Orthodox church anywhere had recognised the new status. The second case concerns a seat in the European Parliament, where laws for the whole EU are voted. Tatjana Ždanoka, co-chair of the Latvian Russian Union, sat there from 2004 to 2024. In January 2024 leaked emails published by The Insider and partner outlets showed her reporting to officers of the FSB, Russia's main security service, from at least 2004. Latvia's State Security Service opened a criminal case on 22 February 2024 for possible cooperation with Russian intelligence and searched her property in July 2024. In April 2024 the European Parliament penalised her for breaking its code of conduct. This is an investigation, not a conviction. On the map Latvia appears as a target country in the patterns on Russia's networks in Europe, governments buying officials abroad, and foreign money inside Europe's parliaments; as a place where a foreign state's church operated, in "Governments that export religion"; and as a state that pushed back, in "Exposure, purge and reversal".
Latvia.imp: For people in Latvia, both cases show the state acting against Moscow's reach: one through a change in the law, the other through a criminal investigation. What ordinary voters could not see was the contact itself; the leaked emails cover about twenty years in which Ždanoka held a seat in Brussels and Strasbourg. Things to watch: where the State Security Service case ends up, and whether any other Orthodox church comes to recognise the Latvian church's new status.

Liechtenstein.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Liechtenstein yet, so this entry is an estimate. The only organisation with a recorded presence is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic religious order that is also recognised as a sovereign body in international law and keeps its own diplomats. The conditions scores are among the lowest in Europe: few powerful actors embedded in the state (1.0 out of 10) and strong resilience (8.4), meaning institutions well placed to resist capture. Our best guess is that any influence here would come quietly, through diplomatic and social ties such as the Order's, rather than through members placed in office. That is a guess, not a finding.
Liechtenstein.imp: No case of a secret society or foreign network working inside Liechtenstein's government appears in the sources this map uses. The scores describe a state that would be hard to capture. That is not proof nothing happens; it means nothing has come to light so far. If something did surface, the place to look would be the people around foreign diplomatic missions and the firms that register in the country.

Lithuania.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Lithuania yet, so this entry is an estimate. Several organisations have a recorded presence: Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life; the Sovereign Military Order of Malta; Tradition, Family, Property (TFP) and its successors; and the Atlas Network of think tanks. Poland's Ordo Iuris legal institute and Russia's Russkiy Mir Foundation are likely present but unrecorded. The conditions scores read as fairly healthy: actors embedded in the state 4.0 out of 10, resilience 7.4. As a best guess, the likeliest route in is through legal networks like the one Ordo Iuris built in Poland, or Russian cultural funding.
Lithuania.imp: For people in Lithuania there is no documented case on this map of these groups reaching into government. The neighbours show what to look out for: in Poland, a founder of Ordo Iuris became deputy foreign minister and later acting head of the Supreme Court; in Latvia, an MEP was investigated as a Russian intelligence contact. Those are the kinds of paths worth watching here.

Luxembourg.d: Luxembourg still has no verdict on who set off a wave of bombs in the 1980s. Between May 1984 and April 1986, 18 bombs went off around the country, hitting sites such as the power company Cegedel's pylons. In 2013 two former members of the Gendarmerie's mobile brigade (BMG), an armed police unit, Jos Wilmes and Marc Scheer, went on trial for them. Their defence argued the attacks were the work of NATO's "Stay Behind" network, the secret Cold War units set up across Western Europe to resist a Soviet invasion, often called Gladio. In court, a 2006 recording was played of Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, Justice Minister Luc Frieden and intelligence (SREL) chief Marco Mille speculating about Stay Behind involvement. Prosecutor Robert Biever said 88 of 125 pieces of evidence had disappeared. The trial was suspended in 2014. Later, eight former gendarmerie and public-force officers were sent to trial for giving false testimony, not for the bombings. The country also appears in the banking story. BCCI, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, was registered in Luxembourg, with its operating centre in London, until regulators in several countries closed it on 5 July 1991. Le Cercle, a private foreign-policy club, and the Trilateral Commission also have a recorded presence. Luxembourg sits in two patterns: "The anticommunist web, 1945–1990", as a documented case, and "Banks that carried the hidden money", as a bank's headquarters.
Luxembourg.imp: For people in Luxembourg, the Bommeleeër case shows how hard it is to hold a state's own security services to account: the accused were police officers, much of the evidence went missing, and the only charges that followed were for false testimony. The bank case shows how a small financial centre can serve as the legal home of a bank run from somewhere else. Watch for any further court steps on the bombings, and for how the country registers foreign-run financial firms.

Malta.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Malta yet, so this entry is an estimate. Organisations with a recorded presence are the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order that keeps its own diplomatic service; Huawei, the Chinese telecoms company; and the Swedish company Swedish Match. The United Grand Lodge of England, the governing body of English Freemasonry, is likely present but unrecorded. Malta's conditions scores are the weakest among the small states in this group: a high level of powerful actors embedded in the state (7.5 out of 10) and only middling resilience (5.1). As a best guess, the likeliest route in is through business: firms and investors winning access to ministers, rather than secret societies placing members.
Malta.imp: For people in Malta, no case is recorded here, but the scores suggest the state is more open to capture than its neighbours of similar size. The thing to watch is who meets ministers and on what terms, especially where foreign companies are involved. A missing case on this map means nothing has been documented from our sources, not that nothing is happening.

Moldova.d: In August 2025 a Moldovan court sentenced Evghenia Guțul, the elected governor of Gagauzia, an autonomous region in the country's south, to seven years in prison for using undeclared Russian money to finance her party. That party was the Șor Party, led by businessman Ilan Shor, whose network is headquartered in Moldova. On 19 June 2023 Moldova's Constitutional Court declared the party unconstitutional for serving a foreign state's interests. Guțul had won the governorship as its candidate in 2023 and met Vladimir Putin in March 2024. At the same hearing the party's former secretary was sentenced for handing out 9.8 million lei to pay protesters. An earlier case ran the other way, with Moldova's own security service acting for a foreign government. Turkey's government calls the movement of preacher Fethullah Gülen a terrorist group. On 6 September 2018 Moldova's Security and Intelligence Service (SIS) detained seven Turkish teachers and managers of the Gülen-linked "Orizont" school network and sent them to Turkey, saying they were suspected of ties to an Islamist group. In June 2019 the European Court of Human Rights ruled in Ozdil and Others v. Moldova that the arrests were neither lawful nor necessary and amounted to an illegal transfer, and ordered Moldova to pay €25,000 to each applicant. Moldova appears as a target country in "Russia's networks in Europe and Africa", as a country that handed people over in "Turkey's long arm", and in "Exposure, purge and reversal". Russia's Russkiy Mir Foundation is likely present but unrecorded.
Moldova.imp: For people in Moldova, these cases show two foreign governments reaching into the state by different routes: Russian money behind a party that won a regional government, and Turkish pressure that led the country's intelligence service to hand teachers over without lawful grounds. Courts caught both, but only after the fact. Watch how parties are funded, who pays for protests, and whether security services act on foreign requests outside the law.

Monaco.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Monaco yet, so this entry is an estimate. The only organisation with a recorded presence is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic religious order that is recognised as a sovereign body in international law and keeps its own diplomats. The conditions scores are mixed: a modest level of powerful actors embedded in the state (3.5 out of 10) and middling resilience (5.8). As a best guess, any influence here would run through wealth and private social circles in a small state where business and government sit close together, rather than through organisations placing members in office.

If something were happening, it would most likely be visible in who gets close to the palace and the government, and on what terms.
