Montenegro.d: Montenegro's prime minister, Milojko Spajić, is a member of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders class of 2025. The World Economic Forum, the organisation behind the yearly Davos meeting of business and political leaders, picks people under about 40 each year for this programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Spajić was named while serving as head of government. That is the only case on the map for Montenegro, and it is a membership, not a finding of wrongdoing or of influence over decisions. Other organisations with a recorded presence are the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with its own diplomatic service, and Aum Shinrikyo, the Japanese religious group now known as Aleph and Hikari no Wa. The conditions scores are on the weak side: a high level of powerful actors embedded in the state (7.0 out of 10) and middling resilience (4.8). Montenegro belongs to the pattern "Private forums where officials meet money", where it counts as a country with a member placed in office.
Montenegro.imp: For people in Montenegro, the case means the head of government takes part in a private leadership network run with the Davos forum while in office. That is legal and public, but what is said in such programmes is not reported to voters. With the weak conditions scores, the thing to watch is whether contacts made in private networks show up later in contracts, appointments or policy.

Netherlands.d: The Netherlands is where the Bilderberg Meeting began, and its royal family still appears on the list. Bilderberg is a private yearly conference of about 130 European and North American politicians, executives and academics, held under the Chatham House rule, so nothing said there is published. It was founded in 1954 by Prince Bernhard, grandfather of King Willem-Alexander, and the King is on the official lists for 2024 and 2025; minister David van Weel was also on the 2025 list. The King is also listed among alumni of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network for people under about 40, and Ruben Brekelmans, then defence minister, was named to its class of 2025. Two cases involve foreign governments. A parliamentary inquiry chaired by CDA MP Michel Rog reported on 25 June 2020 that donors from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar funded Dutch mosques to spread a hardline Salafi Islam it called anti-democratic, including €2.5 million to The Hague's As-Sunnah mosque (2010–17), and that Turkey's Diyanet, whose preachers are Turkish civil servants, has strong political influence over Turkish-Dutch mosques. In November 2022 foreign minister Wopke Hoekstra ordered two Chinese "overseas service stations" closed because China had never notified the Dutch government of them. The leaked Uber Files show former EU commissioner Neelie Kroes helping Uber lobby Dutch politicians, including Prime Minister Mark Rutte, during her cooling-off period after leaving office. She denies wrongdoing. The roots go back to the Cold War. From 1945 to 1992 a secret stay-behind network, the I&O units, recruited several hundred citizens and kept dozens of weapons caches. Prime Minister Ruud Lubbers told parliament about it in November 1990, and in February 2021 Rutte and defence minister Ank Bijleveld acknowledged it in a letter to relatives. According to de Volkskrant, the government covered up the theft of some of its guns, later used by members of Willem Holleeder's gang. The Netherlands appears in six patterns, among them "Private forums where officials meet money" and "China's long arm abroad".
Netherlands.imp: For Dutch residents, the cases show several kinds of outside reach: foreign governments funding religious life and running unofficial offices, a former commissioner lobbying for a company, and heads of state and ministers attending private forums whose talks are not recorded. Parliament and ministers acted on some of this, through an inquiry and closure orders. Watch who funds mosques and community bodies, who lobbies ministers after leaving office, and who sits on the Bilderberg and Davos lists each year.

Norway.d: Norway's case on this map is from the Cold War. In 1978 police found an arms cache and radio equipment at a mountain cabin and arrested businessman Hans Otto Meyer, who said Norwegian intelligence had supplied the weapons. The find exposed part of Norway's stay-behind network, known as ROC: one of the secret units NATO countries set up after the war to resist a Soviet occupation. Defence Minister Rolf Hansen then said the network "was not in any way answerable to NATO and had no CIA connection". Twenty years earlier, in 1957, intelligence chief Vilhelm Evang had protested to NATO about stay-behind activity by officers at the alliance's Kolsås headquarters; that dispute was settled in 1958 with assurances on how the networks would be run. Other organisations with a recorded presence are Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life, the Trilateral Commission and the Mont Pelerin Society, a society of free-market economists and thinkers. Bilderberg and the World Economic Forum are likely present but unrecorded. The conditions scores are strong: few actors embedded in the state (1.5 out of 10) and high resilience (7.9). Norway belongs to the pattern "The anticommunist web, 1945–1990" as a documented case.
Norway.imp: For people in Norway, the case shows that a secret armed network existed inside the state, outside public knowledge, until a police search turned it up. The government's answer was to deny foreign control rather than to open the files. The country's strong scores mean present-day capture is unlikely, but the lesson is that security services can run hidden structures for decades.

Poland.d: Poland's foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, in office since December 2023, is on the official guest lists of the Bilderberg Meeting for both 2024 and 2025. Bilderberg is a private yearly conference of about 130 European and North American politicians, executives and academics, where nothing said is published. Finance minister Andrzej Domański was on the 2024 list. The longer story concerns Ordo Iuris, a Catholic legal institute headquartered in Warsaw that writes draft laws and legal arguments. Aleksander Stępkowski co-founded it in 2013 and chaired its board. In November 2015 the new Law and Justice government made him deputy foreign minister for legal and treaty affairs; he left the Ordo Iuris chair a month later and was recalled in August 2016. That year Ordo Iuris drafted a near-total abortion ban, which the Sejm, Poland's parliament, rejected on 6 October 2016 after nationwide protests. Stępkowski was appointed to the Supreme Court in February 2019 with no prior judicial experience, and on 15 May 2020 President Andrzej Duda made him acting First President of the court, its head. Gazeta Wyborcza reported in 2023 that Przemysław Wipler, elected to the Sejm for the Confederation party that October, is a supernumerary of Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life. In 2024 he became vice-chair of the inquiry into the previous government's use of Pegasus spyware. One case is criminal. In January 2019 Polish authorities arrested Wang Weijing, a senior Huawei employee, and Piotr Durbajło, a cybersecurity expert who had worked for the Internal Security Agency, and charged both with working for Chinese intelligence. Both pleaded not guilty; their trial opened in Warsaw in June 2021, closed to the public. Poland appears in "Churches and movements placing members in the state", "China's long arm abroad" and "Private forums where officials meet money".
Poland.imp: For people in Poland, the clearest case is a single person moving from a legal campaign group into the foreign ministry and then to the head of the Supreme Court, the court that settles the country's highest legal disputes. Membership of Ordo Iuris or Opus Dei is lawful. What voters cannot easily see is how drafting work done outside government carries into it. Watch who writes draft laws, who is appointed to the courts, and the outcome of the Huawei trial.

Portugal.d: Portugal's place on this map comes mostly from the dictatorship years. In September 1966, under António Salazar's Estado Novo regime, Aginter Press was set up in Lisbon. It presented itself as a news agency but trained members in bombing and sabotage. It was run by Yves Guérin-Sérac, a former French officer and member of the OAS, the French underground army that fought Algerian independence. Its documents were found at the end of 1974, after the Carnation Revolution that ended the dictatorship, when Guérin-Sérac and his associates left the country. The trail later led to Italy. Magistrate Guido Salvini, investigating the 1969 Piazza Fontana bombing in Milan, told the Italian parliament's commission on terrorism in 1997 that his inquiries confirmed links between Aginter Press and the neo-fascist groups Ordine Nuovo and Avanguardia Nazionale, and that Aginter instructors taught Avanguardia Nazionale members to use explosives in Rome in 1967–68. A newer case concerns the World Economic Forum, the organisation behind the Davos meetings. It lists José Manuel Durão Barroso, then foreign minister, among its 1993 "Global Leaders for Tomorrow", the forerunner of its Young Global Leaders programme. He became Prime Minister in 2002 and president of the European Commission from 2004 to 2014. Membership is a WEF selection; no forum has found the network directed his decisions. Portugal belongs to "The anticommunist web, 1945–1990", where Aginter Press is headquartered, to "Exposure, purge and reversal", and to "Private forums where officials meet money".
Portugal.imp: For people in Portugal, the Aginter case shows how a dictatorship's security apparatus could host a bombing school dressed up as a press agency, and how its work only came out when the regime fell and its papers were found. The Barroso case is of a different kind: a public listing in a private leadership network. Watch for which Portuguese officials join such networks while in office.

Romania.d: Romania's one case rests on a single news report. In September 2019 Newsweek România, citing anonymous Masonic sources, reported that Mihai Fifor, then interim interior minister and deputy prime minister, joined Freemasonry in 2008 through Loja Armonia and later Loja Basarab, and that General Constantin Florea, head of the Gendarmerie, the armed police force, belonged to Loja Basarab. The interior ministry runs the police; the Gendarmerie handles public order and protests. Neither man had declared membership in his interest declaration, which the magazine said the law required. Fifor neither confirmed nor denied it. Costin Mihalache, head of the Government Chancellery and a former foreign-intelligence (SIE) officer, said he had been a Mason but no longer was. Freemasonry is a lawful fraternal organisation; the question raised was disclosure, not membership itself. Other organisations with a recorded presence include Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life, the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, the US-funded broadcaster Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, and Azerbaijan's so-called "caviar diplomacy" network for courting European politicians. The Gülen movement and The Fellowship, a US Christian prayer network, are likely present but unrecorded. The conditions scores are middling: actors embedded in the state 4.5 out of 10, resilience 5.9. Romania appears in the pattern "Lodges inside police forces and courts" as a documented case.
Romania.imp: For people in Romania, the case raises a simple question: whether the officials in charge of the police and the Gendarmerie belonged to lodges they had not declared. The report rests on one outlet and unnamed sources, so it is not proven. Watch whether interest declarations list such memberships, and whether any official body checks them.

Russia.d: Russia appears on this map mainly as a sponsoring state, the home of networks that reach into other countries. Headquartered here are the Russkiy Mir Foundation, set up in 2007; the Wagner Group and the defence ministry's Africa Corps; the Prigozhin disinformation network; the state energy companies Rosneft and Gazprom; the Viktor Medvedchuk influence network; and the Russian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate. The Voice of Europe network, sanctioned by the Czech government in March 2024, paid European politicians. Russia's use of Interpol, the body through which police forces share wanted-person alerts, is under watch now. Interpol refused Russia's requests for a Red Notice against financier Bill Browder as "predominantly political". In 2018 US senators said Interpol vice-president Alexander Prokopchuk, a Russian Interior Ministry general, had abused Red Notices; he lost the presidency vote. On 10 March 2022, after the invasion of Ukraine, Interpol stopped Russia's bureau sending alerts directly to other countries and put it under enhanced supervision. In January 2026 the BBC reported leaked files showing Interpol received more complaints about Russia than any other country, and that some extra checks were dropped in 2025. At home, the state bans foreign groups. In July 2015 it declared the US National Endowment for Democracy "undesirable", the first group banned under that law; no court or independent body has found NED worked inside Russian institutions. In November 2015 a Moscow court banned the Church of Scientology of Moscow, upheld by the Supreme Court in June 2016. The roots go back to 1917. Alexander Kerensky was Secretary General of the Grand Orient of Russia's Peoples, a Masonic body, until mid-1917, and served that year as justice minister, war minister and then Prime Minister of the Provisional Government. Historians describe most of the lodge's members as associated with that government. Russia appears in nine patterns, mostly as sponsor or headquarters.
Russia.imp: For people in Russia, the map shows a state that uses its own institutions, including police channels and courts, against groups and critics, while funding networks abroad. Bans on foreign organisations are the government's own assertions. Watch how Interpol handles Russian requests now that some checks have been dropped, and which foreign groups are next named "undesirable".

San Marino.d: Nothing is documented on this map for San Marino yet, so this entry is an estimate. The only organisation with a recorded presence is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic religious order that is recognised as a sovereign body in international law and keeps its own diplomats. The conditions scores are middling: powerful actors embedded in the state score 5.0 out of 10 and resilience 5.3. As a best guess, the likeliest route in for outside influence would be through banking and business ties with neighbouring Italy, rather than through secret societies placing members in office.
San Marino.imp: For residents of San Marino, no case is recorded on this map. The middling scores suggest a state with some exposure. In a very small country, watch who holds several roles at once, in business and government, and where its banks' money comes from. A missing case here means nothing has been documented from the sources this map uses, not that nothing is going on.

Serbia.d: Serbia's place on this map rests on events more than a century old, from a time when sworn societies of army officers decided who ruled the country. On 11 June 1903, Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as "Apis", and junior officers stormed the royal palace in Belgrade and killed King Alexander Obrenović, Queen Draga and others, bringing the Karađorđević dynasty to the throne. In 1911 Dimitrijević and fellow officers founded the secret society Unification or Death, the Black Hand, which Britannica describes as dominating the army and pressuring the government through intimidation. In 1913 Apis became chief of intelligence of the Serbian General Staff. Many scholars hold that he sanctioned the 1914 Sarajevo assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the killing that set off the First World War, with the Black Hand supplying weapons and training. In 1917 Prince Regent Alexander had him court-martialled at Salonika for treason; he and two others were shot on 26 June 1917 and more than 200 members were jailed. In 1953 Serbia's Supreme Court retried the case and acquitted them for lack of proof of the alleged plot. A rival society, the White Hand, was founded in 1912 by officers led by Petar Živković; Crown Prince Alexander later joined. After the Black Hand was broken, it gained influence over him. When King Alexander I suspended the constitution on 6 January 1929 with White Hand support, Živković became Prime Minister, serving until 1932. Serbia belongs to "Sworn brotherhoods that chose who governed" and "Exposure, purge and reversal". The conditions scores today are weak: actors embedded in the state 8.0 out of 10, resilience 4.9.
Serbia.imp: For people in Serbia, this is the background rather than the present: no current case is recorded. It shows how officers' secret societies once decided who ruled, by murder and by backing a royal dictatorship. The weak conditions scores today mean powerful actors sit close to the state. Spain.d: Spain hosted the Bilderberg Meeting in Madrid in 2024, a private yearly conference of about 130 European and North American politicians, executives and academics where nothing said is published. The official list named foreign minister José Manuel Albares and economy minister Carlos Cuerpo; King Felipe VI was reported to have attended although he was not on the list. The deeper story is about Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life, and Franco's dictatorship. In February 1957 Franco made two Opus Dei members ministers: Mariano Navarro Rubio at finance, which decides how the state spends its money, and Alberto Ullastres at trade. Both served until 1965 and drove the Stabilisation Plan that opened Spain's closed economy. Navarro Rubio then became governor of the Bank of Spain; Ullastres headed Spain's mission to the European Communities until 1976. Laureano López Rodó ran the development plans and was briefly foreign minister; Gregorio López-Bravo was industry and then foreign minister. Historians count 8 Opus Dei members among Franco's 116 ministers, none before 1957. In July 1969 the MATESA scandal broke: a textile-machinery firm owed about 10 billion pesetas in export credits from a state bank. Former ministers Navarro Rubio, Juan José Espinosa San Martín and Faustino García-Moncó were charged, and Franco pardoned them before any verdict. The October 1969 cabinet that followed had eleven members with ties to Opus Dei. After democracy returned, Jorge Fernández Díaz, reported to be an Opus Dei supernumerary, ran the interior ministry, in charge of the police and Guardia Civil, from 2011 to 2016. José María Aznar, Prime Minister from 1996 to 2004, is listed among the World Economic Forum's 1993 "Global Leaders for Tomorrow". In 1990 defence minister Narcís Serra opened an inquiry into whether Spain had a secret NATO stay-behind network; former prime minister Leopoldo Calvo Sotelo said the Franco regime "itself was Gladio". Spain appears in four patterns, most heavily in "Churches and movements placing members in the state".
Spain.imp: For people in Spain, the record shows a religious organisation's members running the economy under a dictatorship, and a corruption case closed by pardon before any verdict. Switzerland.d: Switzerland is home to many of the bodies this map follows: the World Economic Forum, the World Health Organization, FIFA, the International Olympic Committee, the Club of Rome, the Mont Pelerin Society, and commodity traders Glencore, Gunvor and Trafigura. A committee chaired by Swiss health official Thomas Zeltner reported in July 2000 that tobacco companies had run an "elaborate, well financed, sophisticated and usually invisible" effort to undermine WHO tobacco control; its work led into the 2003 tobacco treaty. In June 2010 the Council of Europe's assembly voted 60-1 that the H1N1 flu response wasted public money, finding "grave shortcomings" in transparency that raised concerns about drug-industry influence, though it found no proven control. In 2020 the Gates Foundation, a private US charity, was the WHO's second-largest contributor, mostly earmarked for its chosen programmes. FIFA, world football's governing body, is based in Zurich. Attorney General Michael Lauber, whose office was investigating FIFA corruption, met FIFA president Gianni Infantino in 2016 and 2017 without keeping records. He was found to have misled his oversight body and left office in 2020. A criminal case against Infantino was closed without charges in October 2023. The roots are in the Cold War. In November 1990 a parliamentary inquiry found a secret organisation, P-26, outside parliamentary and government control, with up to about 1,000 members and about 54.3 million francs of federal money spent from 1979. It was dissolved that month. Judge Pierre Cornu's report found it lacked legal legitimacy and cooperated extensively with British intelligence; only a summary was published, and the full report stays sealed until 2041. Switzerland appears in "Governments and industries inside international bodies", "The anticommunist web" and "Exposure, purge and reversal".
Switzerland.imp: For people in Switzerland, the cases show that the global bodies hosted in the country are themselves targets of industry and private money, and that the federal prosecutor's closeness to one of them cost him his job. United Kingdom.d: In February 2026 the High Court upheld the Metropolitan Police's new rule that its officers and staff must declare Freemasonry. By then 397 had declared membership, most of them Freemasons. Freemasonry is a lawful fraternal society; the long argument has been about whether police and judges should say if they belong. The trail runs back through Operation Countryman's inquiry into London detectives (1978–82), journalist Stephen Knight's The Brotherhood (1984), a Commons committee in 1997 that called for registration, a declaration rule for new judges and police from 1998, and its end for judges in 2009 after 205 masons were counted among 3,808 judges. The 2021 Daniel Morgan Panel found no corrupt masonic channels in that murder case but urged confidential disclosure. Current cases involve foreign states. Private forums run through the record: Le Cercle chaired by MPs on the Foreign Affairs Committee, Health Secretary Wes Streeting at Bilderberg 2025, and Blair, Brown and Cameron in WEF leadership programmes. United Kingdom.imp: For people in the UK, the record shows influence arriving through several doors: secret or private memberships among police and judges, foreign governments paying or courting politicians, and firms placing staff or former leaders close to ministers. Watch the Met's declaration rule, the lobbying rules for former ministers, and who attends private forums while in office.

With a small cabinet, aid and diplomatic ties are where an outside group would find the easiest access, so those are worth following.

Suriname.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Suriname yet, but its conditions scores are worrying. On a scale of 0 to 10 it scores 8.5 for how far unelected or outside actors are already built into the state, and only 3.2 for resilience, meaning courts, press and parliament are weak checks. Two organisations are recorded as present: the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order of knights, and the National Endowment for Democracy, a grant-maker funded by the US Congress. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist movement from India, is likely present but undocumented. As a best guess, the likeliest route in is through groups already close to the state, where weak oversight hides a great deal.
Suriname.imp: For people in Suriname, the blank record should not be read as an all-clear. The scores say outside and unelected actors already have a strong place in the state and that the institutions meant to expose them are weak, so a case could exist without anyone having documented it. Watch which foreign-funded groups, religious movements and diaspora organisations gain regular access to ministers, and whether anyone, from parliament or the press, is able to ask about it.

Argentina.d: Argentina today is led by Javier Milei, who took office as president in December 2023. Before entering politics he won the 2018 Liberty Prize of Fundación Atlas and spoke at events of partners of the Atlas Network, a US-based network that funds and trains free-market think tanks around the world. In August 2025 the network credited its Argentine partners with helping push his deregulation, tax and labour reforms; that is the network's own claim. An earlier link ran through Mauricio Macri's party, PRO, which absorbed the Atlas think tank Fundación Pensar in 2015, the year Macri won the presidency. On the other side of politics, former president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner must stand trial for aggravated cover-up. In 1994 the AMIA Jewish centre in Buenos Aires was bombed, killing 85 people, and Argentine courts charged Iranian officials. In 2013 her government signed a pact with Iran on questioning the suspects, and in December 2024 the Supreme Court upheld the order to try her over it. The deepest roots go back to the 1970s and Propaganda Due, or P2, a secret Italian Masonic lodge run by Licio Gelli. When Italian police seized Gelli's membership lists in 1981, Argentine names were on them: interim president Raúl Lastiri; social welfare minister José López Rega, whose ministry funded the Triple A death squad blamed for about 1,500 deaths; foreign minister Alberto Vignes; economy minister Celestino Rodrigo; navy chief Admiral Emilio Massera; and General Guillermo Suárez Mason, who commanded the army corps around Buenos Aires and later ran the state oil company YPF. In 1974 a decree drafted by Perón and Vignes gave Gelli a top state honour and a post at the embassy in Italy, with diplomatic passports. Massera and Suárez Mason were convicted of dictatorship crimes and pardoned in 1990. In 2016 an Argentine court convicted 15 officers, including ex-dictator Reynaldo Bignone, in the first trial centred on Operation Condor, the dictatorships' cross-border repression network. A 1992 US indictment of the bank BCCI cited a $500,000 'political' payment to central bank officials. Argentina belongs mainly to the patterns on the anticommunist web, lodges inside the security forces, and exposure and reversal, with newer entries under private forums and foreign governments.
Argentina.imp: Argentines have seen hidden networks close to power more than once. In the 1970s a secret foreign lodge counted a president, ministers and military chiefs as members, and the public learned of it only when the lists were seized in Italy. Today's links are open but hard to measure: foreign-funded think tanks say they help shape a sitting government's reforms, which is lawful. What to watch is who drafts laws and decrees, who funds the groups behind them, and whether cases such as the AMIA cover-up trial reach a verdict.

Bahamas.d: The one entry for the Bahamas is a finished story from the early 1980s, and it shows the islands' role as a place where foreign banks booked money. Banco Ambrosiano Overseas in Nassau was a subsidiary of Roberto Calvi's Banco Ambrosiano, an Italian bank. Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, president of the Vatican Bank (the IOR, which manages money for the Holy See), had been one of its directors. When Ambrosiano collapsed in 1982, Bahamian banking authorities suspended the Nassau bank's operations. The Nassau and Luxembourg units owed about half of the $1.2 to 1.4 billion that had been lent to shell companies in Panama. Nothing on the map shows a Bahamian official taking part. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, is also present. The country sits in the pattern of banks that carried hidden money, as a booking centre, and under exposure and reversal, because its regulator shut the unit down.
Bahamas.imp: For Bahamians, the risk shown here is not officials joining a secret group but outsiders using the banking system to move money out of sight. In 1982 the regulator acted once the parent bank had failed. What to watch now is how well the regulator knows who really owns and runs the banks and companies registered in Nassau, and whether it acts before a collapse rather than after one.

Bolivia.d: Bolivia's two documented cases both go back to the coup of 17 July 1980, when General Luis García Meza seized power with the backing of Argentina's junta, in what became known as the 'cocaine coup'. Neither case concerns the present government; they are the background to how the country remembers that period. The first is the case of Luis Arce Gómez, García Meza's interior minister and chief of repression. In July 2019 a Rome appeals court gave him a life sentence in the Operation Condor case, the trial over the South American dictatorships' joint campaign against opponents across borders. The verdict is still subject to Italy's top court. The second rests on a single journalist. Robert Parry wrote that the Unification Church, the movement founded by Korean preacher Sun Myung Moon, published a photo of Moon's aide Bo Hi Pak meeting García Meza after the coup, and quoted Pak: 'I have erected a throne for Father Moon in the world's highest city.' Parry also wrote, without naming a source, that the church's political arm CAUSA ran joint operations with the junta, and that later Bolivian investigations found Moon's group had invested about US$4 million in the coup. He cited another author for García Meza's attendance at a congress of the regional branch of the World Anti-Communist League. Bolivia sits in the anticommunist web pattern and the pattern of churches and movements placing members in the state. Opus Dei, the Order of Malta and Tradition, Family, Property are also present.
Bolivia.imp: For Bolivians, the record here is about a dictatorship that ended long ago, yet one of its ministers was sentenced only in 2019, and abroad. The claim that a foreign church helped pay for the coup rests on one writer and has not been tested in court. For today, it shows that foreign groups can back a seizure of power and that justice may come late and from outside. Watch who funds the armed forces, the police and political movements, especially from abroad.

Brazil.d: Brazil's Congress today has an organised religious bloc. The Evangelical Parliamentary Front, a registered cross-party caucus of mostly Pentecostal members, lists 213 of 513 deputies and 26 of 81 senators; most vote with the conservative side and a few sit on the left. One party, Republicanos, was founded in 2005 by pastors of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, a Pentecostal church started by Bishop Edir Macedo in 1977. Its president, Bishop Marcos Pereira, is a vice-president of the Chamber. Macedo's nephew Marcelo Crivella, also a bishop, was a minister and mayor of Rio, was arrested in a kickback inquiry days before his term ended in 2020, and has sat as a federal deputy since 2023. André Mendonça, a Presbyterian pastor, sits on the Supreme Federal Court, and pastor Damares Alves sits in the Senate. Belonging to a church is not wrongdoing; the map records where members hold office. Other networks reach office too: Kim Kataguiri, whose protest movement worked with a partner of the Atlas Network (a US network of free-market think tanks), is a federal deputy, and Racial Equality Minister Anielle Franco was chosen in 2024 as a Young Global Leader of the World Economic Forum. The roots run back to the 1960s. A CIA-linked institute, IBAD, paid for opposition campaigns in the 1962 election, which a congressional inquiry investigated. Historians describe the Catholic group Tradition, Family, Property as helping set the stage for the 1964 coup, and the director of a US-funded labour institute later claimed its trainees were 'intimately involved', a claim historians doubt. In 2014 federal prosecutors released army files they called the strongest proof of Brazil's role in Operation Condor; the armed forces deny it. Later cases show money crossing borders: the US Senate found that the bank BCCI secretly owned a Brazilian bank through nominees, some close to President Sarney; ex-governor José Maria Marin was convicted in the FIFA bribery case; Rio governor Sérgio Cabral testified he paid $2 million for Olympic votes and Olympic chief Carlos Nuzman was sentenced in 2021; and in 2024 the trader Trafigura pleaded guilty to bribing Petrobras officials. Former president Lula's Car Wash convictions were annulled in 2021 because the trial court lacked jurisdiction. Brazil is home to several groups on the map and belongs above all to the churches-in-the-state pattern.
Brazil.imp: For Brazilians, the clearest present-day fact is that a large, organised church bloc sits in Congress, and pastors and bishops have held seats in the cabinet and on the top court. That is lawful and public, but it means church priorities can shape laws on schools, families and rights. Past cases show foreign money and companies reaching elections, the state oil company and sports bodies. Watch how the evangelical front votes as a bloc, who funds campaigns, and whether corruption cases survive appeal.

Canada.d: Canada's current story is about foreign governments working through people inside the country. In January 2025 a public inquiry led by Justice Marie-Josée Hogue found that China is the 'most active' state interfering in Canada, using diplomats, proxies and the United Front Work Department, the Communist Party body that builds influence over overseas Chinese communities. It named India second and cited intelligence that Indian proxies may have given, and may still give, illicit money to Canadian politicians. It found no 'traitors' in Parliament, though a committee of parliamentarians had reported in 2024 that some unnamed members were 'semi-witting or witting' participants. China and India reject the findings. After Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar was shot dead in Surrey in 2023, Canada expelled six Indian diplomats in 2024, saying Indian agents used the Lawrence Bishnoi gang against Sikhs in Canada, and in 2025 it listed the gang as a terrorist entity. Several specific cases have thinned out: the police probe of alleged Chinese 'police stations' closed without charges, the elections commissioner found no breach of election law in MP Han Dong's 2019 nomination, and in May 2026 a judge acquitted ex-RCMP officer William Majcher of helping China, a verdict prosecutors are appealing. Older networks were homegrown. Four prime ministers belonged to the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity, and every Toronto mayor in the first half of the 20th century was an Orangeman. A secret francophone order, 'La Patente', placed members in federal posts until an insider exposed it in 1964. In Saskatchewan a Klan claiming 40,000 members stirred the issues that helped unseat the Liberals in 1929, though no alliance was proven. Two Governors General, Earl Grey and John Buchan, came from Cecil Rhodes's and Lord Milner's imperial circles. In 1992 the Church of Scientology of Toronto was convicted of planting members in the provincial police and Attorney General's offices, and in 2019 the ethics commissioner found Prime Minister Trudeau broke conflict law by pressing his Attorney General over SNC-Lavalin's bribery prosecution. Canada is mainly a target country in the patterns on China and on governments buying officials abroad, and a long-running case of sworn brotherhoods.
Canada.imp: For Canadians the main concern now is foreign states reaching into elections and diaspora communities: pressure on relatives abroad, money routed to candidates, and violence against activists. Public inquiries have confirmed the pattern but named few people, and several cases ended without charges, so voters cannot see which nominations or donations were touched. Watch party nomination contests, donations, and whether the Hogue inquiry's 51 recommendations are carried out.

Chile.d: Chile's president since 11 March 2026, José Antonio Kast, belongs to the Schoenstatt Movement, a Catholic lay movement founded in Germany in 1914 that has many shrines in Chile; BBC Mundo reported that he and his siblings were raised under its guidelines. His under-secretary of justice, law professor Luis Silva, is a numerary of Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life. Both memberships are lawful. Under President Piñera, Opus Dei member Joaquín Lavín ran education, and Cristián Larroulet moved from Libertad y Desarrollo, a think tank in the Atlas Network of free-market groups, to a top cabinet post. The background is the dictatorship of Augusto Pinochet. From the mid-1950s a US aid scheme, later funded by the Ford Foundation, trained 126 Chilean economists through the University of Chicago and Santiago's Catholic University. Their plan, 'El ladrillo', became the junta's economic programme in 1975, and graduates ran the economy, finance and planning ministries and the Central Bank: Sergio de Castro, Pablo Baraona, Miguel Kast (the president's brother), Sergio de la Cuadra and Rolf Lüders. Chile's intelligence service DINA, under Manuel Contreras, called the founding meeting of Operation Condor in Santiago in November 1975. A truth commission found in 1991 that DINA held prisoners at Colonia Dignidad, a German sect compound where some residents helped torture them. Contreras's conviction for the 1976 car-bomb killing of Orlando Letelier in Washington was upheld in 1995, and Pinochet was indicted for Condor crimes in 2004 but died in 2006 without being convicted. In the late 1960s, President Frei's government banned the Catholic group Tradition, Family, Property. Salvador Allende was a Freemason; no lodge direction of his government is documented. Chile is the coordinating centre of the anticommunist web, the clearest case of trained technocrats running an economy, and a current case of churches and movements placing members in the state.
Chile.imp: For Chileans, two things stand out. Under the dictatorship, a small group of economists trained through a foreign programme was placed in charge of the economy, without any public vote on their plan. Today members of Catholic movements hold the presidency and the second post in the justice ministry, which is lawful but worth following for its effect on laws on families, schools and rights. Watch who is appointed to economic and justice posts, and which networks they come from.

Guatemala.d: Guatemala's recent history is the story of an international anti-corruption commission that worked and was then shut down. CICIG, the International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala, was set up by a 2006 agreement with the UN to help local prosecutors take apart criminal networks inside the state. In 2015 it and the Public Ministry exposed 'La Línea', a customs-bribery ring reaching Vice-President Roxana Baldetti and President Otto Pérez Molina. Congress lifted his immunity 132 to 0, he resigned on 2 September 2015, and in December 2022 both were sentenced to 16 years; he was released on bond in January 2024. When CICIG began investigating the financing of President Jimmy Morales's campaign, Morales refused to renew its mandate, deployed armed forces near its offices and in January 2019 ended the agreement. The Constitutional Court ruled against him, but the commission's mandate ended in September 2019. A second case comes from football. Héctor Trujillo, a judge and general secretary of Guatemala's football federation, was arrested in Florida in 2015 and pleaded guilty in the US FIFA bribery case. The roots lie in the Cold War. Mario Sandoval Alarcón, a leader of the World Anti-Communist League, was vice-president from 1974 to 1978; historians link his party, the MLN, to killings by the Mano Blanca death squad. Guatemala belongs to the patterns of international bodies, the anticommunist web, and exposure and reversal.
Guatemala.imp: For Guatemalans, the record shows both sides: an outside body helped prosecutors reach a sitting president, and a later president removed that body while it was investigating him. Without it, prosecuting powerful officials depends on local institutions that score 4.0 out of 10 for resilience. Watch who controls the Public Ministry and the courts, and whether corruption cases opened under CICIG reach final verdicts.

Honduras.d: Honduras has two documented cases, and both are finished. The first is from the early 1980s, when General Gustavo Álvarez Martínez commanded the armed forces. He headed the Association for the Progress of Honduras (APROH), which brought business leaders and officers together. According to the Library of Congress country study, APROH received a US$50,000 contribution from a front group for the Unification Church, the movement founded by Korean preacher Sun Myung Moon. The Christian Science Monitor reported in March 1984 that APROH and its allies had taken control of university, professional, teacher, labour and peasant bodies. Fellow officers ousted Álvarez on 31 March 1984, and APROH declined. The second case involves a former head of state. Rafael Callejas, president from 1990 to 1994, later ran the Honduran football federation. Indicted in the US FIFA case in 2015, he pleaded guilty in 2016 to taking $500,000 in bribes for media and marketing rights; FIFA banned him for life, and he died in 2020. Honduras belongs to the patterns of churches and movements placing members in the state, and of governments and industries inside international bodies. Its conditions scores are high: 8.5 out of 10 for embedded actors and 3.9 for checks.
Honduras.imp: For Hondurans, these cases show two routes: a military chief using a civic association, partly funded from abroad, to take over unions and professional bodies, and a former president selling access inside an international sports body. Both came to light through outsiders, a US study and US prosecutors. With weak checks at home, watch who controls unions, universities and professional associations, and whether local courts act on foreign findings.

Jamaica.d: Jamaica's one documented case shows how far a foreign bank reached into a government's finances. Under Prime Minister Edward Seaga, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), an international bank later indicted in the United States, handled Jamaica's US commodity financing and most of the government's foreign-currency accounts. A BCCI officer told the US Senate: 'we handled every penny that came into or out of Jamaica in terms of foreign currency.' The Senate's 1992 report lists loans of $33.9 million to the Bank of Jamaica, the central bank, and $45.4 million to the state oil firm Petrojam. No Jamaican official is recorded on the map as charged. The United Grand Lodge of England and the Rhodes Trust, which funds Rhodes Scholarships, are probably present. Jamaica belongs to the patterns of banks that carried hidden money and of exposure by a parliament or commission, here a foreign one.
Jamaica.imp: For Jamaicans, the case shows that a single foreign bank once held most of the state's foreign-currency money and lent heavily to the central bank and the state oil company, and that the public learned the details from a US Senate report. Watch where government reserves and state-company accounts are held, who chooses the banks, and whether those choices are published.

Mexico.d: Mexico's open case today is that of Emilio Lozoya, who ran Pemex, the state oil company, from 2012 to 2016. He is accused of taking about $10 million in bribes from Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group. Arrested in Spain and extradited in July 2020, he denies the charges and was moved from prison to house arrest in February 2024; no verdict has been reported. The other cases concern religious groups close to power. El Yunque is a secret Catholic organisation founded in Puebla in 1953. In 2003 journalist Álvaro Delgado wrote that it had members among leaders of the PAN party and in President Vicente Fox's cabinet; PAN officials called this 'pure fiction'. Guanajuato governor Juan Manuel Oliva and his chief of staff were named as members and denied it, and in 2007 a former mayor of Puebla named PAN leader Manuel Espino and claimed the group controlled four state governments, which the party denied. None of these claims has been tested in court. From another part of the political map, in 2019 a senator from a party allied with Morena asked for the Palacio de Bellas Artes, and it hosted a homage for the 50th birthday of Naasón Joaquín García, leader of the Guadalajara church La Luz del Mundo. The arts institute said it had been told it was an opera gala. García was arrested in Los Angeles weeks later and in 2022 pleaded guilty to child sexual abuse. Mexico is home to El Yunque, La Luz del Mundo and the Legion of Christ, and belongs to the patterns of churches and movements placing members in the state and of global firms buying governments.
Mexico.imp: For Mexicans, the record shows two routes: company money reaching the people who ran the state oil company, and religious groups with access to parties and public venues. Claims about El Yunque have circulated for two decades with no proof either way, which shows how hard such networks are to see. Watch the Lozoya case for a verdict, how Pemex contracts are awarded, and how parties of every side treat powerful church leaders.

Nicaragua.d: In Nicaragua today, a Russian ministry runs a police training centre. Russia's Interior Ministry opened it in Managua in October 2017, with Russia's ambassador and the president's son Laureano Ortega Murillo at the opening. It gives courses to Nicaraguan police and later to officers from Central America and the Caribbean. On 15 May 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned it, saying it trains officials of the Ortega-Murillo government in the Russian government's 'playbook of oppression' and is a key actor in repressing civil society. Earlier cases show outside money arriving from other directions. In 1984 to 1988 the National Endowment for Democracy, a US foundation funded by Congress, put about $2 million into Nicaragua's civic opposition, about half of it to the newspaper La Prensa, run by Violeta Chamorro. In October 1989 the US House approved $9 million more before the February 1990 election, which Chamorro's coalition won. NED says its grants are public and nonpartisan. In 1985 Daniel Ortega's government cancelled the licence of a local unit of Roberto Calvi's Banco Ambrosiano, which had provided funds to both the Somoza government and the Sandinista opposition. Nicaragua belongs to the patterns of Russia's networks, governments buying officials abroad, intelligence money behind NGOs, and banks that carried hidden money. Its conditions scores are severe: 9.0 out of 10 for embedded actors and 2.0 for checks.
Nicaragua.imp: For Nicaraguans, the main present concern is that a foreign government helps train police who, according to the US Treasury, are used against civil society. With checks this weak, there is little local way to see what is taught or to whom. Past cases show money from the United States and from foreign banks funding sides in Nicaraguan politics. Watch who trains the police and soldiers, and who funds parties and the press.

Panama.d: Panama's documented cases date from the 1980s, when General Manuel Noriega commanded the Panamanian Defense Forces. In early 1982 he opened an account at the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), an international bank later indicted in the United States, in the name of the Defense Forces. The US Senate's 1992 report found he held about $25 million in it at its peak, mostly in cash deposits, including one deposit of about $4 million. BCCI also lent to his associates and absorbed about $10 million in losses. The same report found that Noriega had BCCI pay off the mortgage of Nicolás Ardito Barletta, his chosen presidential candidate, who became president in 1984. Panama's banks also appear in other countries' stories on this map: Banco Ambrosiano's Latin American units lent to Panamanian shell companies, and Peru's central bank kept reserves at BCCI-Panama. Opus Dei, the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, the National Endowment for Democracy and Odebrecht are also present. Panama belongs to the patterns of banks that carried hidden money and of exposure by a parliament or commission, here a foreign one.
Panama.imp: For Panamanians, the record shows a military commander using a foreign bank to hold millions in an account in the army's name and to pay a presidential candidate's mortgage, with the details coming out only through a US Senate inquiry. Panama's use by outsiders as a place to register companies and hold accounts, seen in other countries' cases here, is the point to watch: who really owns companies registered there, and how banks report large cash deposits.

Paraguay.d: Paraguay's most recent case involves a former president. On 26 January 2023 the US Treasury sanctioned Horacio Cartes and the sitting vice-president, Hugo Velázquez, for corruption, saying both 'have ties to members of Hizballah', the Lebanese armed movement and party that the US designates as a terrorist organisation, and that their representatives collected bribes at Hizballah's private events in Paraguay. The US lifted the sanctions on Cartes and several of his companies in 2025. The roots lie in the dictatorship of Alfredo Stroessner. On 22 December 1992 lawyer Martín Almada and judge José Agustín Fernández found the records of Stroessner's secret police in a police station outside Asunción. These 'Archives of Terror' proved that Operation Condor existed; they include a letter from Chile's intelligence chief inviting Paraguayan officials to a secret meeting in Santiago in November 1975. Paraguay's Truth and Justice Commission used them to document 9,923 people who suffered 14,338 violations. The US Senate's BCCI report says the bank's Paraguay ties grew from Saudi businessman Ghaith Pharaon's friendship with Stroessner, and lists a $5 million central bank deposit in 1989. In 2000 representatives of Sun Myung Moon's Unification Church bought about 600,000 hectares in the north, including the town of Puerto Casado; in 2005 the Senate voted 24 to 14 to expropriate 52,000 hectares for the town's roughly 6,000 residents. Paraguay belongs to the patterns of the anticommunist web, banks that carried hidden money, and Iran's armed allies.
Paraguay.imp: For Paraguayans, the cases show outside actors reaching the top of the state by different routes: a foreign bank through a dictator's friendship, a foreign church through land purchases large enough to include a whole town, and, according to the US, an armed foreign movement through bribes at private events. The US later lifted its sanctions on Cartes. Watch land sales to foreign buyers, money flows in the Tri-Border Area, and whether Paraguayan courts examine the US findings.

Peru.d: Peru's recent presidents have been tried one after another over money from Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group that in 2016 admitted paying $788 million in bribes in a dozen countries. In October 2024 Alejandro Toledo, president from 2001 to 2006, was sentenced to 20 years for taking about $35 million for the Interoceanic Highway contract. In April 2025 Ollanta Humala, president from 2011 to 2016, and his wife Nadine Heredia were each sentenced to 15 years for money laundering linked to Odebrecht; both deny it, and Heredia left for Brazil under diplomatic asylum. Religious and fraternal networks also sit close to power. Rafael López Aliaga, who describes himself as a celibate member of Opus Dei, was mayor of Lima until 2025 and took a Senate seat in July 2026. In July 2025 a TV programme reported that Eduardo Arana, then prime minister, holds the 33rd degree of Scottish Rite Freemasonry and that a lodge member was hired as a consultant while Arana was justice minister; Arana said membership is no grounds to assume favours. Earlier, Opus Dei numerary Rafael Rey served as production and defence minister, and Opus Dei bishop Juan Luis Cipriani was named a state mediator in the 1996 to 1997 hostage crisis; the Truth and Reconciliation Commission later said he never questioned abuses by state forces, which he rejected. The older roots are financial and military. Peru's central bank placed up to $270 million of reserves at BCCI-Panama by 1987, and a 1991 US indictment alleged $3 million in bribes for the deposits, which the named officials denied. A Lima unit of Banco Ambrosiano guaranteed Peru's 1982 Exocet missile purchase. A Rome court gave former military ruler Francisco Morales Bermúdez a life sentence in absentia in 2019 in the Operation Condor case. Peru belongs to the patterns of global firms buying governments, churches and movements in the state, and banks that carried hidden money.
Peru.imp: For Peruvians, the cases show that one foreign company paid its way to successive presidents, and that it took foreign confessions and years of trials to bring this out. Membership of Opus Dei or a lodge is lawful, but when officials hire fellow members or favour their groups, the public rarely finds out. Watch who wins large public works contracts, whom officials appoint as advisers, and whether the convictions hold on appeal.

Trinidad and Tobago.d: Jack Warner, once one of the most powerful men in world football and a former Trinidad cabinet minister, is wanted in the United States on fraud charges, and Trinidad's High Court blocked his extradition on 23 September 2025. To see why his case is on this map, start with FIFA, the body that runs world football and decides who hosts the World Cup, and CONCACAF, the confederation that runs the game in North and Central America and the Caribbean. Warner was a FIFA vice-president and CONCACAF president until 2011. From 2010 he also sat in Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar's cabinet, first as Minister of Works and Transport, which handles roads and public building, and then as Minister of National Security, in charge of police and defence. He resigned from the cabinet on 21 April 2013. Three days earlier, a CONCACAF Integrity Committee report had concluded that he committed fraud against CONCACAF and FIFA. In May 2015 US prosecutors indicted him for wire fraud, racketeering and money laundering, including a $10 million payment tied to South Africa's bid for the 2010 World Cup, and FIFA banned him for life. He has not been tried. Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life, is also recorded as present, and the United Grand Lodge of England and the RSS, a Hindu nationalist movement from India, are likely present but undocumented. Trinidad belongs to the pattern of governments and industries inside international bodies, as the home of an official who held a top international post and national office at the same time.
Trinidad and Tobago.imp: For people in Trinidad and Tobago, the Warner case shows how one person can hold power in an international body and in the national cabinet at once, with the money of the first sitting beside the public contracts and police powers of the second. The charges against him have never been tested in a court, and Trinidad's own High Court has kept him from being sent abroad for trial. The question to keep asking is whether ministers hold outside posts, and who checks the money that flows through them.

United States.d: Right now, several private bodies sit unusually close to power in Washington. The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, organised Project 2025, a plan for running the government; Russ Vought, who wrote its chapter on the president's own offices, runs the budget office, and a CNN review found six cabinet secretaries wrote for it or contributed. On 29 May 2025 President Trump wrote that he had used the Federalist Society, a network of about 70,000 conservative lawyers, as his 'recommending source' on judges; 43 of his first 51 appeals-court nominees were members. Under the previous president, nearly 70 staff of the Center for American Progress, a Democratic think tank, left for administration posts, including chief of staff Ron Klain. ALEC, which brings state lawmakers and corporations together to write 'model bills', handed out 32 new ones in December 2024. Bob Menendez, once chair of the Senate committee that shapes arms sales and aid, is in prison after a jury found him guilty in 2024 of acting as an agent of Egypt. The roots are old. In 1826 a Masonic sheriff helped abduct William Morgan, who planned to expose Masonic rituals; the sheriff was convicted. In 1854 the Know Nothings, a secret anti-Catholic order, took the governorship and all 40 state Senate seats in Massachusetts. In the 1920s the Ku Klux Klan helped elect governors in Indiana, Colorado and Oregon, and Klansman Hugo Black went on to the Supreme Court. Through the twentieth century, members of Skull and Bones, a Yale secret society, held the presidency, the CIA and the Treasury, and a 1977 study counted more than half of 502 senior foreign-policy officials as members of the Council on Foreign Relations, a private New York forum. During the Cold War the CIA paid for students, unions and foundations; the Senate's Church Committee found its money in at least 108 of 700 large foundation grants in 1963-66, and after 1983 the National Endowment for Democracy took over part of that work openly. Foreign governments work the other way: South Korea's intelligence agency paid members of Congress in the 1970s, and Chinese state proxies placed an agent in New York's governor's office, according to charges against Linda Sun, whose trial ended in a mistrial in December 2025. The United States is the headquarters for many of these bodies, a target country, and the coordinating and funding centre of the Cold War networks.
United States.imp: For people in the United States, much of this is legal and public: think tanks writing plans, legal networks proposing judges, corporations sitting with state lawmakers to draft bills. What voters rarely see is who wrote a bill or chose a nominee before it reached them. Both major parties draw staff from such bodies. Foreign governments also work through former officials, donors and local politicians, and several of those cases ended in pardons, dismissals or mistrials. Watch who drafts the laws your legislators file and who recommends the people appointed to judge them.

Uruguay.d: The documented cases for Uruguay all lead back to its years of military rule, and the most recent ones are court verdicts against the men who ran that state. In July 2019 a Rome appeals court gave life sentences to 24 people in the Operation Condor case, among them Juan Carlos Blanco, Uruguay's former foreign minister, the official who speaks for the country abroad; the verdict was subject to review by Italy's highest court. Operation Condor was the plan under which South American military governments of the 1970s hunted opponents across each other's borders, and the Rome case covered the disappearance of 43 people, 23 of them Italian citizens. At home, Gregorio Álvarez, former army commander and Uruguay's last de facto president, was sentenced in October 2009 to 25 years for 37 homicides, including disappearances; several victims had been moved to Argentina in 1978 under Condor, and the Supreme Court upheld the sentence in 2011. Two other cases show outside networks finding a footing during the dictatorship. In 1981 the movement of Sun Myung Moon, a Korean church leader, bought 49% of Banco de Crédito, one of the oldest banks, and founded a daily paper that declared itself 'fully identified' with the military government. The bank closed in 2002, and a parliamentary commission found it had lent about US$100 million of its US$600 million in loans to Moon-linked companies. The same year, Licio Gelli, head of Propaganda Due (P2), a secret Italian Masonic lodge, hid in Montevideo; police seized his files, reportedly on a CIA tip. Uruguay sits in the anticommunist web, in churches placing members in the state, and among countries where parliament exposed a case.
Uruguay.imp: For people in Uruguay, these cases are mostly history, and the country now scores well on resilience, at 7.5 out of 10. The record shows what happened when the military held power and nobody could question it: a foreign church could buy into a major bank, and a fugitive lodge leader could keep his files in Montevideo. The bank's losses came to light only after it failed. The courts are still the place where that period is answered for.

Venezuela.d: Venezuela today has the conditions that let hidden networks work unchecked. On a scale of 0 to 10 it scores 9.0 for how far unelected or outside actors are built into the state, and only 1.9 for resilience, the strength of the courts, press and parliament that would catch them. Only two cases are documented, from opposite sides. The first goes back to 1984. Tradition, Family, Property (TFP) is a Catholic movement, founded in Brazil, that campaigns against left-wing politics. After parents complained that it cut teenagers off from their families, a three-month investigation under President Jaime Lusinchi found Venezuela's TFP was operating outside the constitution, and the government was reported to plan a ban. Whether a ban took effect is not confirmed. The second is from the 2002 coup against Hugo Chávez. Cedice Libertad, the Caracas think tank tied to the Atlas Network, a US-based network of free-market think tanks, had received regular grants since 1998 from a core institute of the National Endowment for Democracy, a US body funded by Congress; one grant letter lists money for Cedice to advocate 'a change in government'. Cedice's director signed the decree of Pedro Carmona's short-lived coup government, which dissolved the National Assembly and the Supreme Court. Influence also runs the other way: a US jury convicted former congressman David Rivera in May 2026 for secretly lobbying to ease sanctions on the Maduro government under a $50 million contract with the US arm of Venezuela's state oil company. Opus Dei, the Order of Malta and Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction firm, are recorded as present. Venezuela belongs to the patterns of private forums meeting officials and of churches placing members in the state.
Venezuela.imp: For people in Venezuela, the scores mean that if outside or unelected groups are shaping decisions, very little stands in the way and little is likely to be exposed. The record shows foreign money backing one side of the country's politics and the state oil company paying for lobbying abroad on the other. Neither came to light through Venezuelan institutions. Watch where foreign grants go, and how state companies spend money outside the country.

Kosovo.d: Kosovo's former intelligence chief, Driton Gashi, was sentenced in 2023 by the Basic Court in Pristina to four years and eight months for abuse of office. The case goes back to 29 March 2018. Turkey's government calls the movement of preacher Fethullah Gülen a terrorist group and has pursued its members abroad since a 2016 coup attempt. That day Kosovo police and intelligence officers seized five teachers and a doctor whom Ankara accused of Gülen links and flew them to Turkey on a private plane. Prime Minister Ramush Haradinaj said he had not been told, and sacked the interior minister and the intelligence chief. The case shows a foreign government getting a country's own security service to act for it, with the head of government left out. It belongs to the pattern "Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement", where Kosovo counts as a country that handed people over, and to "Churches and movements placing members in the state". The conditions scores are borrowed from North Macedonia, because Kosovo is not scored by the source index; they read as middling-to-weak, with actors embedded in the state at 6.5 out of 10.
Kosovo.imp: For people in Kosovo, the case shows that the intelligence service could hand residents to a foreign state without the prime minister knowing. A court later punished its chief, which is the accountability that did happen. Watch how security services answer to elected government and whether foreign requests to remove people go through courts.
